After that they are sorted, because they often belong to several farmers. The animals then spend the winter in the **barn** or on lower pastures.

begriffe.erklaerung: The French word for the Alpabzug in French-speaking Switzerland.
A large, forged cowbell with a deep sound.
Traditional festive clothing of a region.
The handing out of the sheep to their owners after the alpine summer.

gewusst: A large Treichel can weigh several kilograms.
The families often tie the cows’ headdresses from hundreds of flowers days before the festival.
Some Alpabzüge are broadcast live on television.

teile.einleitung: The American mink is a small marten-like animal that lives by the water. Originally it comes from North America. It was brought to Europe for fur farming, escaped from farms in some places and today lives wild in many areas.
wichtigste: The American mink is a small member of the weasel family from North America.
It is also called the mink.
It swims and dives very well and lives on rivers, lakes and coasts.
It was brought to Europe for fur farming.
Escaped animals have gone wild in many countries of Europe.
In Europe it threatens native animals such as the European mink.
It is regarded in Europe as an invasive species.

abschnitte.text: The **American mink** belongs to the weasel family, like the polecat, stoat and otter. Including the tail it is about 50 to 70 centimetres long and usually weighs less than one and a half kilograms. Its dense fur is dark brown to almost black and shiny. On the chin it usually has a small white patch. Between the toes it has small **webs**.

Originally the mink lives in almost the whole of **North America**, from Alaska to Florida. It lives by streams, rivers, lakes, marshes and sea coasts. It swims and dives superbly and hunts in the water and on land. It eats fish, crayfish, frogs, mice, water voles and birds together with their eggs. Mostly it is out at dusk and at night and lives as a loner.

Because of its soft, valuable **fur**, the mink has been bred on farms since the late 19th century. From about the 1920s, minks also came to Europe to fur farms. Through breeding, there are today many fur colours, from white through silver grey to black. Mink fur coats were long regarded as a sign of wealth. Because of animal welfare, keeping animals for fur is today banned or strongly restricted in many countries of Europe.

Minks have escaped again and again from fur farms, and sometimes they were also released on purpose. In this way wild populations arose in many countries of Europe, for example in Scandinavia, Great Britain, Spain and Germany. Because it does not originally live here, it is regarded as an **invasive species**. On islands and by lakes it eats many waterbirds, eggs and water voles. Especially affected is the much rarer **European mink**, which is being displaced by the American mink.

In Switzerland there are no large wild populations of the American mink, and it is only rarely observed. There are practically no fur farms here because of strict animal welfare rules. Furs sold in Switzerland must be **declared** according to their origin and the way the animals were kept. Wildlife experts nevertheless watch whether minks from neighbouring countries are spreading.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of slender predators such as polecat, badger, otter and mink.
An animal or plant that was brought by humans into a foreign area and harms native species there.
Keeping animals on farms in order to sell their fur.
Another name for the American mink.

gewusst: The American mink is larger and stronger than its European relative and therefore displaces it.
In 2020, millions of farmed minks were killed in Denmark because the coronavirus had spread among them.

teile.einleitung: Brachiation is a special kind of movement in which an animal swings from branch to branch with its arms. The masters at it are the gibbons in the rainforests of Asia. Children on the playground copy it too on the monkey bars.
wichtigste: Brachiation means swinging from branch to branch with the arms.
The word comes from the Latin brachium, the arm.
Gibbons are the best swingers in the animal kingdom.
For it you need long arms, hook-shaped hands and very mobile shoulders.
Orangutans and spider monkeys also swing, but more slowly.
Humans too can swing hand over hand thanks to their mobile shoulders.

abschnitte.text: In **brachiation** the animal hangs under a branch and swings onwards with its arms. It reaches alternately with the left and the right hand for the next branch. The legs are hardly used. The name comes from the Latin word **brachium**, which means arm. In German this movement is also called Schwinghangeln.

When swinging, the body swings back and forth like a **pendulum**. The momentum carries the animal to the next grip, so little strength is used. Very fast swingers even let go completely in between and fly a stretch through the air. For this to work you need long arms, strong shoulders and a **shoulder joint** that can turn in every direction.

The **gibbons** of South-East Asia are the world champions of brachiation. Their arms are much longer than their legs, and their hands work like hooks. They swing at lightning speed through the treetops and manage leaps of several metres. Orangutans also swing, but move more slowly and carefully. In South America spider monkeys swing and use their prehensile tail as a fifth hand to help.

On the playground, on the **monkey bars**, you do exactly what gibbons do. Gymnasts on the high bar or climbers on an overhang use similar movements. In sports such as ninja courses, too, swinging is an important exercise. In doing so you quickly notice how much strength there is in your hands and shoulders.

Researchers are interested in brachiation because it reveals a lot about our body. Humans too have a very mobile shoulder joint and can raise their arms above their head. We inherited that from **ancestors** who climbed in trees. So the swinging of the apes also explains why we can throw a ball or hang from a bar.

begriffe.erklaerung: Movement by swinging with the arms from branch to branch.
A small ape from Asia with very long arms.
The joint that connects the arm to the body.
A tail with which an animal can hold on as with a hand.

gewusst: Gibbons can swing through the trees at over 50 kilometres per hour.
In gibbons the arms are so long that they almost touch the ground when walking upright.
The ladder for swinging on the playground is called monkey bars in English.

teile.einleitung: The Białowieża National Park lies in the east of Poland on the border with Belarus. It protects one of the last large primeval forests in the lowlands of Europe. It is famous above all for the European bison, the largest land animals in Europe.
wichtigste: The Białowieża National Park lies in Poland, right on the border with Belarus.
It is part of the Białowieża Forest, one of the last lowland primeval forests in Europe.
Free-living European bison live in the forest, the European relatives of the American bison.
The national park was founded in 1932 and is one of the oldest national parks in Europe.
Since 1979 the area has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The forest continues on the Belarusian side, where it is called Belovezhskaya Pushcha.
Many trees are allowed to grow old, fall over and rot here without people interfering.

abschnitte.text: The national park lies in the north-east of Poland in the Podlaskie Voivodeship. It is only a part of the much larger **Białowieża Forest**, which extends across the border into Belarus. The whole forest is larger than the canton of Zug and much flatter than Swiss forests. The village of Białowieża is the starting point for visitors.

In a **primeval forest** the forest has grown for thousands of years almost without interference by people. Here stand huge oaks, limes, spruces and hornbeams, some of which are several hundred years old. Fallen trunks stay where they lie and become a habitat for fungi, beetles and mosses. This **deadwood** is important for countless species. In the most strictly protected area you may only travel with a guided tour.

abschnitte.titel: The rescue of the European bison
abschnitte.text: The **European bison** used to be numerous in the Białowieża Forest. During the First World War and afterwards the last free-living animals were poached, and by about 1921 the bison was wiped out here. The species was bred up again with animals from zoos. From 1952 bison were released into the forest again. Today several hundred animals live here again, and Białowieża is the most important area for the European bison in the world.

Besides the bison, wolves, lynxes, elks, red deer, wild boar and beavers live in the forest. There are also many rare bird species, for example nine different species of woodpecker. The world of insects, fungi and lichens is especially rich. Many of these species need old trees and deadwood, which are hardly found in ordinary managed forests.

Hundreds of years ago the forest was already a hunting ground of the Polish kings and later of the Russian tsars. That is why it was never completely cleared. In 1932 the Polish national park was created, and in 1979 it was added to the **UNESCO World Heritage** list. Later the World Heritage Site was extended to the Belarusian part. There has been repeated dispute over the felling of trees in the rest of the forest between nature conservation and forestry.

In Białowieża visitors can go to a museum and hike on nature trails. In a show enclosure you can watch bison safely. The strictly protected part of the primeval forest may only be entered with an official guide. This prevents too many people from disturbing the delicate nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: A forest that has developed almost without interference by people.
The European wild ox, a close relative of the American bison.
Dead trees and branches that stay where they lie and offer food and homes to many living things.
A list of especially valuable natural and cultural sites of the world that are to be protected.

gewusst: All of today's European bison descend from only twelve animals that had survived in zoos.
The Białowieża Forest lies in two countries, so the national border runs right through the primeval forest.
Some oaks in the forest are over 400 years old.

teile.einleitung: Buffalo are large, strong wild oxen that live in Africa and Asia. They include the African buffalo and the water buffalo. The American bison are often called buffalo, but they are a different group of animals.
wichtigste: True buffalo live in Africa and Asia.
Bison in North America and Europe are not true buffalo.
The African buffalo is among the most dangerous animals in Africa.
The water buffalo became a domestic animal in Asia thousands of years ago.
Buffalo are plant eaters and usually live in herds.
Real mozzarella is made from buffalo milk.

abschnitte.text: Buffalo are **wild oxen** with massive bodies and large, curved horns. The group includes the African buffalo, the Asian water buffalo and smaller species such as the anoas of Indonesia. They are related to our domestic cattle, but belong to genera of their own. Bison, by contrast, have a hump and a mane and live in North America and Europe.

The **Cape buffalo** or African buffalo lives in savannas and forests of Africa south of the Sahara. A bull can grow about 1.7 metres high and weigh over 800 kilograms. Its horns grow together on the forehead into a thick shield. It is one of the “Big Five”, the five animals that were regarded as especially dangerous in big-game hunting in the past.

The **water buffalo** comes from South and South-East Asia and loves marshes, rivers and mud holes. In Asia it was tamed several thousand years ago and still helps today with ploughing the rice fields. It supplies milk, meat and leather. Wild water buffalo, which are called arni, have become very rare today.

African buffalo often live in large **herds** with hundreds of animals. If an animal is attacked by lions, other buffalo come to its help and attack the big cats. Buffalo eat grass and have to drink regularly, so they stay near water. Oxpeckers, small birds, often sit on their backs and pick ticks out of the fur.

In Switzerland too there are water buffalo today on some farms. Their fat-rich milk is made mainly into **mozzarella**, as is the tradition in southern Italy. Water buffalo are robust and also cope well with damp pastures. In nature reserves they are sometimes used to keep wet meadows open.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wild-living animal from the cattle family, for example a buffalo or a bison.
Five large animals of Africa: lion, leopard, elephant, rhinoceros and buffalo.
A large group of animals of the same species that lives and travels together.
A small African bird that picks ticks and insects from the fur of large animals.

gewusst: The African buffalo can remember hunters and sometimes attack them from ambush.
The real Mozzarella di Bufala from Italy is made from water buffalo milk.
Water buffalo can sink almost completely into the water until only the nose and eyes show.

teile.einleitung: Basilisks are lizards from Central and South America that can do something unbelievable: they run across water. That is why they are also called Jesus Christ lizards. Their name comes from a mythical creature in old legends.
wichtigste: Basilisks are iguana-like lizards from the rainforests of Central and South America.
They can run across the surface of water on two legs.
They slap their feet on the water so fast that pockets of air form.
Water striders, by contrast, are held up by surface tension.
Males often carry striking crests on the head, back and tail.
Basilisks eat insects, small animals and fruit.

abschnitte.text: Basilisks are slim lizards with very long hind legs and a long tail. Including the tail, large animals grow to about 80 centimetres long, with the tail making up most of that. The males have **skin crests** on the head, back and tail. The **plumed basilisk** is bright green, while the brown basilisk is more brown with pale stripes. Four species belong to the genus.

When a basilisk has to flee, it rears up and runs across the water on its hind legs. On its toes it has **fringes of skin** that enlarge the surface of the foot. It slaps its feet powerfully downwards, which creates a pocket of air under the foot. Before this collapses, it has already pulled the foot out again. A water strider, on the other hand, is so light that the **surface tension** of the water holds it up.

Basilisks live in the tropical forests from Mexico to Ecuador and Colombia. They like to stay on branches and stones on the banks of rivers and streams. When in danger they jump into the water and run away or dive. They are also good **swimmers** and can stay underwater for a while. Young, light animals manage longer distances when running on water than heavy adults.

Basilisks eat mainly insects, spiders and worms. Larger animals also hunt small frogs, lizards or fish and eat fruit and flowers. The females lay their eggs in a pit in the damp ground. The young hatch after a few months and are independent straight away. They can run on water just after **hatching**.

The basilisk was originally a **mythical creature** from legends, a kind of king of snakes with a deadly gaze. The lizard got this name because of the crest on its head, which is reminiscent of a crown. The name Jesus Christ lizard has a background too: the Bible tells that Jesus walked on water. Basilisks are also popular in zoos and terrariums.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of lizards that also includes iguanas and chameleons.
A force that makes the top layer of water act like a thin skin.
A glass container in which reptiles or amphibians are kept.

gewusst: A young basilisk can run several metres across water without sinking.
On land, basilisks run faster on two legs than on four.
If a human wanted to run on water like this, they would have to run at over 100 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: Omnivores are animals that eat both plants and animals. They are not fussy and can adapt well to different habitats. We humans are omnivores too.
wichtigste: Omnivores eat plant and animal food.
The technical word for omnivores is omnivorans.
Baboons, wild boar, brown bears and foxes are omnivores.
Humans, too, are omnivores by nature.
Omnivores have teeth that can cut and grind.
Because they eat many things, they find food almost everywhere.
Besides omnivores there are plant eaters and meat eaters.

abschnitte.text: An omnivore feeds on plants and on animals. Experts say **omnivore**, which comes from Latin and means roughly devouring everything. By contrast, **herbivores** such as cows eat only plants, and **carnivores** such as cats eat almost only meat. Omnivores therefore stand somewhere in between.

abschnitte.titel: Examples from all over the world
abschnitte.text: Baboons are omnivores: they eat grasses, fruit and roots, but also insects and sometimes small mammals. Chimpanzees, raccoons and rats also eat almost everything. Many birds such as crows and gulls take grains, worms and even waste. In Switzerland, the **wild boar**, red fox, badger and brown bear are typical omnivores.

Omnivores mostly have **mixed teeth**. At the front sit incisors for biting off and canines for holding. At the back, broad molars grind up the plant food. In humans you can feel these different tooth shapes well in your own mouth.

Omnivores can adapt well to new places. If there are no berries in winter, they simply eat insect larvae or carrion. That is why foxes and crows today even live in the middle of cities such as Zurich or Bern. This **adaptability** helps them to get through difficult times too.

For hundreds of thousands of years, humans have fed on fruit, seeds, roots and meat. That is why our body can digest very different food. Today many people decide for themselves whether they eat meat or eat a **vegetarian** or vegan diet. For a healthy diet, variety is above all important.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for an animal that eats everything.
An animal that eats only plants, for example a roe deer.
An animal that mainly eats other animals, for example a lynx.
All the teeth of an animal or human together.

gewusst: Despite its size, the brown bear often eats more plants than meat.
Wild boar dig up the ground with their snouts to find roots, worms and mice.
Even some fish, such as the carp, are omnivores.

teile.einleitung: A bee colony is a large community of honey bees that lives together in a hive. Every bee has its task, and only together can the colony survive. That is why people often compare the bee colony with a single large living creature.
wichtigste: A bee colony consists of a queen, many workers and in summer also drones.
In summer several tens of thousands of bees live in a colony.
The workers take on different tasks depending on their age.
Bees from the same hive share a common hive scent.
Sick or too old bees are carried out of the hive by others.
In winter the colony survives as a dense cluster that keeps itself warm.
If the colony gets too big, it divides by swarming.

abschnitte.text: In the **bee colony** there are three different kinds of bee. The **queen** lays all the eggs. The workers are females that do not lay eggs and do all the other jobs. The **drones** are the males, they have no sting and do not collect food. Their only task is mating with a young queen.

In summer several tens of thousands of bees live in a bee colony, often 30,000 to 50,000. Among them are one queen and a few hundred to a few thousand drones. In winter the colony shrinks to about 5,000 to 15,000 bees. Summer bees live only about six weeks, because they wear themselves out with work. Winter bees, by contrast, live for several months.

A young worker begins as a **cleaner bee** and cleans the comb cells. After that she feeds the larvae as a nurse bee. Later she builds combs, processes nectar into honey or guards the entrance as a guard bee. Only in the last weeks of her life does she fly out as a **forager bee** and fetch nectar, pollen and water. This order can change when the colony urgently needs certain helpers.

All the bees of a hive carry a shared **hive scent**. By it the guards at the entrance recognise strange bees and fend them off. Dead, sick or very old bees are carried out of the hive by the others. This protects the colony from disease. In the brood nest the bees keep the temperature quite precisely at about 35 degrees by fanning with their wings or shivering with their muscles.

abschnitte.titel: The year in the bee colony
abschnitte.text: In spring the colony grows quickly. If it gets too big, it raises new queens, and the old queen leaves with some of the bees as a swarm. In late summer the drones are no longer fed and are driven out of the hive, which is called the **drone cull**. In winter the bees sit close together as a winter cluster and live off the honey. In spring the cycle begins again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female bee that does not lay eggs and does all the jobs in the colony.
A shared smell by which bees recognise their hive mates.
A group of living things that work together so closely that they function like a single creature.
In late summer the male bees are driven out of the hive.

gewusst: A bee colony can collect far more than 100 kg of nectar in a year.
Beekeepers often call the whole colony simply “der Bien”.

teile.einleitung: Bastet was a goddess in ancient Egypt who was shown as a cat or as a woman with a cat's head. She was seen as the protector of the home, the family and mothers. Because of her, cats were revered in Egypt and treated especially well.
wichtigste: Bastet was a goddess in ancient Egypt.
She was usually shown as a cat or as a woman with a cat's head.
Earlier she was also depicted with a lion's head.
Her most important place of worship was the city of Bubastis in the Nile Delta.
Cats were linked with Bastet and revered.
Many cats were mummified after their death.

abschnitte.text: Bastet was one of the most popular **goddesses** of ancient Egypt. She was seen as the protector of the home, of women, of children and of fertility. In pictures she often holds a **sistrum** in her hand, a rattle instrument for music and dance. Sometimes kittens lie at her feet. She was seen as a daughter of the sun god Ra.

In the early times of Egypt, Bastet was shown with a **lion's head**, like the fierce goddess Sekhmet. Over the centuries she became more and more the gentle house cat. From around the first millennium BC she was known above all as the cat goddess. In this way she stood for the peaceful, protective side. Sekhmet, by contrast, remained the dangerous lioness.

The centre of worship was the city of **Bubastis** in the eastern Nile Delta. There stood a large temple to the goddess. The Greek historian Herodotus reported on a huge festival to which thousands of people travelled by boat every year. Near Bubastis large **cat cemeteries** were also found. Today the ruins lie near the city of Zagazig in Egypt.

Cats were very useful in Egypt because they kept mice, rats and snakes away from granaries and houses. Because they were linked with Bastet, they were under special protection. According to reports from antiquity, anyone who killed a cat was severely punished. When a house cat died, the family mourned it. Many cats were embalmed as **mummies** and dedicated to the goddess as an offering.

Egypt is one of the areas in which the house cat developed from the wild **African wildcat**. Bastet is today one of the best-known figures of Egyptian mythology. Small bronze figures of Bastet can be seen in many museums around the world. She also often appears in books, films and games. The Egyptian religion with its many gods is no longer practised today, but it is an important part of history.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female being who is worshipped in a religion.
A body preserved by embalming.
An ancient Egyptian rattle instrument with small metal plates.
The wild cat of Africa from which our house cat descends.

gewusst: Archaeologists found hundreds of thousands of cat mummies in Egypt.
In the 19th century many tonnes of cat mummies were shipped to England and used there as fertiliser.
The name Bastet probably has to do with a word for an ointment jar.

teile.einleitung: The beehive is the home of a colony of honey bees. Here the bees build their combs, raise the next generation and store their honey. Today most honey bees live in wooden boxes that beekeepers provide for them.
wichtigste: The home of many honey bees is called a beehive.
In the beehive the bees build combs out of wax and make honey.
Wild honey bees live in tree holes.
Beekeepers today usually keep bees in wooden boxes, called Beuten.
In the past woven straw baskets, known as skeps, were widespread.
In Switzerland there are many bee houses in which several colonies live side by side.
The bees fly in and out through the entrance hole.

abschnitte.text: A **beehive** is the dwelling of a colony of honey bees together with its combs. The German word Bienenstock comes from “Stock”, that is a hollow tree trunk in which bees used to live. In technical language the box that the beekeeper provides is called a **Beute**. In everyday speech, though, people usually simply say beehive or bee box.

In nature honey bees look for a sheltered hollow space, usually a hole in an old tree. There they hang their combs from top to bottom. They seal cracks with **propolis**, a sticky resin that they collect from buds. In Europe today there are only a few wild colonies of honey bees left. Many other species of bee, the wild bees, live by contrast alone in holes in the ground, plant stems or deadwood.

In the past bees were kept in hollow tree trunks or in woven straw baskets, the **skeps**. To harvest the honey, the combs often had to be destroyed. In the 19th century boxes with movable wooden frames were invented. Now the beekeeper could take out single combs, inspect them and harvest the honey without harming the colony.

In Switzerland the **Swiss box** was long widespread, which is opened from the back like a cupboard. It usually stands in a bee house in which many colonies live side by side. Today many beekeepers use **stackable hives**, in which boxes are stacked on top of each other. On top, the honey chamber is added in summer, and below lies the brood nest with the queen.

Inside it is dark and warm, in the brood nest about 35 degrees. The bees arrange their stores skilfully: in the middle lies the brood, around it pollen and further out and above the honey. At the **entrance hole** guards keep watch. In winter the bees huddle together as a cluster and stay in the hive until it is warm enough outside again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for the box or container in which a bee colony lives.
A sticky resin with which bees seal cracks in the hive.
The entrance through which the bees fly into and out of the hive.
A small house in which several bee boxes stand side by side.

gewusst: A beehive is called a Beute in the technical language of beekeeping, although no prey (which is what Beute also means in German) is hidden inside it.
Propolis works against bacteria and fungi and so protects the whole hive.

teile.einleitung: In biological pest control, natural enemies are used against pests instead of spraying poison. Ladybirds, for example, eat aphids, and tiny parasitic wasps lay their eggs in the eggs of harmful insects. In this way nature helps itself.
wichtigste: Biological pest control uses the natural opponents of pests.
To reduce aphids naturally, beneficial animals such as ladybirds and birds are encouraged.
Lacewing larvae and hoverfly larvae also eat many aphids.
In Switzerland parasitic wasps are used against the European corn borer.
In greenhouses predatory mites help against spider mites.
The method spares other animals, the water and the soil.
Introduced foreign beneficial animals can, however, become a problem themselves.

abschnitte.text: A **pest** is a living thing that damages crops, stores or trees. In **biological pest control** it is fought with its natural enemies, the **beneficial animals**. These include predatory insects, spiders, birds, hedgehogs, but also fungi and bacteria. The aim is not to wipe out the pest completely, but to make it so rare that it hardly does any damage.

There are many natural enemies of aphids. A **ladybird** eats dozens of aphids a day, and its larvae even more. The larvae of the lacewing, called aphid lions, and the larvae of hoverflies are also big aphid eaters. Tits feed their young with many caterpillars and insects. Anyone who has hedges, wild flowers and nest boxes in the garden attracts such helpers.

On many Swiss maize fields tiny **parasitic wasps** of the genus Trichogramma are released. They lay their eggs in the eggs of the European corn borer, a moth whose caterpillars damage the maize. In greenhouses vegetable growers use **predatory mites** against spider mites and thrips. In vineyards scent substances are released that confuse male grape moths so that they cannot find females.

Biological methods spare bees, birds, waters and the soil. The pests also do not become resistant, as is often the case with poisons. However, beneficial animals work more slowly and need knowledge and good timing. It becomes dangerous when foreign species are introduced: the **harlequin ladybird** was brought to Europe as a beneficial animal and today pushes out native ladybirds. In Australia the cane toad was introduced against beetles and has become a plague there.

Instead of spraying at once, it is worth waiting a few days, because beneficial animals often come by themselves. Light infestation can be rinsed off with a jet of water. Wild corners, deadwood and insect hotels offer beneficial animals shelter. An **earwig pot** with wood wool, hung upside down in a fruit tree, attracts earwigs, which eat aphids at night.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal or living thing that eats or fights pests.
A living thing that damages the plants, stores or animals of people.
A small wasp that lays its eggs in other insects or their eggs.
An introduced species that spreads strongly and pushes out native species.

gewusst: Some parasitic wasps are smaller than half a millimetre.
In its life a ladybird can eat several thousand aphids.

teile.einleitung: Beauveria brongniartii is a fungus that attacks and kills insects. Farmers in Switzerland use it deliberately against the grubs of the cockchafer, which damage meadows and pastures. This is a form of biological pest control without chemical poison.
wichtigste: Beauveria brongniartii is a fungus that makes insects ill.
It is used for the biological control of grubs.
Grubs are the larvae of the cockchafer and eat plant roots.
The fungal spores are brought into the soil on barley grains.
The fungus attacks almost only cockchafers and is harmless to people and pets.
In Switzerland the method was developed in part by the research station Agroscope.

abschnitte.text: Beauveria brongniartii is a **mould fungus** that occurs naturally in the soil. It belongs to the **insect-pathogenic** fungi, that is fungi that make insects ill. It is specialised above all in cockchafers and their larvae. It is named after the French naturalist Brongniart. A close relative is Beauveria bassiana, which attacks many different insects.

The tiny **spores** of the fungus stick to the skin of a grub. They germinate and grow through the hard body covering into the inside. There the fungus spreads until the larva dies after a few weeks. After that it grows out of the dead animal as a white fluff. That is why people speak of the **white muscardine**: the dead larvae look as if covered in cotton wool.

The cockchafer lives as a **grub** in the soil for three to four years. There it eats the roots of grasses, vegetables and fruit trees. In bad years whole meadows turn brown and can be lifted off like a carpet. Pastures and meadows in mountain regions are especially affected, for example in Uri, the Grisons or Thurgau. For the farmers this means less fodder for their animals.

The fungus is multiplied in the laboratory on barley grains. This so-called **fungal barley** is brought a few centimetres deep into the soil with a seed drill. There the fungus keeps growing and attacks the grubs. It often stays active in the soil for many years. In this way a single treatment protects a meadow for a long time.

Biological pest control manages without chemical **insecticides**. Other animals such as earthworms, bees or birds are not harmed. The fungus is also harmless to people and pets. The method is therefore also allowed in organic farming. It shows how damage to plants can be reduced with the help of nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thick, curved, white larva of the cockchafer that lives in the soil.
Fighting pests with natural opponents such as fungi or beneficial insects.
A tiny seed-like cell from which a new fungus grows.
A chemical agent that kills insects.

gewusst: As early as the 19th century the Italian Agostino Bassi discovered that a Beauveria fungus causes a disease in silkworms.
A grub covered with the fungus looks as if it had been rolled in sugar.
Because the fungus survives in the soil, it can also attack the grubs of the next generation of cockchafers.

teile.einleitung: The beaver is the largest rodent in Europe and a real master builder of nature. With its sharp teeth it fells trees and builds dams and lodges. In Switzerland it once died out, but today it lives again on many rivers and lakes.
wichtigste: The European beaver is the largest rodent in Europe and weighs about 20 to 30 kg.
It lives on streams, rivers and lakes and is usually active at dusk and at night.
Beavers eat only plants, for example bark, twigs, herbs and water plants.
Beavers usually live monogamously in fixed pairs with their young.
In the 19th century the beaver was wiped out in Switzerland because of its fur and castoreum.
From 1956 beavers from abroad, for example from France and Scandinavia, were resettled in Switzerland.
When a beaver meets a person, it usually flees quickly into the water.
With lodges and dams it changes the landscape greatly and creates habitat for many other animals.

abschnitte.text: A fully grown beaver is about one metre long with its body, and in addition comes the flat, scaly tail, the **paddle**. It weighs about 20 to 30 kg. Its gnawing teeth are orange at the front because they contain iron and are therefore especially hard. They keep growing all its life. The beaver oils its dense fur with a secretion from a gland so that it stays waterproof. On the hind feet it has webbing.

Beavers need calm waters with banks on which willows, poplars and other broadleaved trees grow. They build a **beaver lodge** out of branches and mud or dig a den into the bank. The entrance is always under water so that enemies cannot get in. If the water is too shallow, the beaver dams it up with a **beaver dam**. A beaver territory can extend over one to several kilometres of bank.

The beaver is a pure plant eater. In summer it eats mainly herbs, grasses and water plants. In winter it gnaws the bark off branches and trees. To reach the twigs in the treetop, it fells whole trees. Before winter it stores a supply of branches under water, the so-called food raft.

A beaver pair usually stays together for life. In early summer about two to four young are born, called **beaver kits** or young beavers. They can swim after only a few days. The young stay with the family for about two years and help with building. After that they look for a territory of their own, often many kilometres away.

In the past beavers lived on almost all Swiss waters. Because of hunting for fur, meat and the scent secretion **castoreum**, the beaver had died out by the beginning of the 19th century. Between 1956 and 1977 beavers from France and Norway were released in various places. Since 1962 the beaver has been protected in Switzerland. In a count in 2022 about 4,900 beavers lived in Switzerland again, above all on the Central Plateau.

Beavers bring many advantages: their ponds hold back water and offer frogs, dragonflies and fish a habitat. Sometimes, however, they undermine riverside paths, flood fields or fell fruit trees. The authorities then try to find a balance with fences, wire mesh round trees or pipes through dams. In cases of great damage farmers partly receive compensation.

begriffe.erklaerung: The flat tail of the beaver, covered with scales, which serves as a rudder when swimming.
A strong-smelling secretion with which beavers mark their territory.
Mammals with continually growing gnawing teeth, for example mice, squirrels and beavers.
The area that a beaver family lives in and defends against strange beavers.

gewusst: A beaver can stay under water for up to 20 minutes.
A beaver can fell a tree 50 cm in diameter in one night.
When danger threatens, the beaver slaps its paddle loudly on the water to warn its family.

teile.einleitung: The Bengal tiger, also called the royal Bengal tiger, is the form of tiger that occurs especially often in India. It is a mighty hunter with orange fur and black stripes. Today most of the wild tigers in the world live in India.
wichtigste: The Bengal tiger lives mainly in India, but also in Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.
It is also called the royal Bengal tiger.
Males can weigh over 200 kilograms.
Every tiger has its own unique stripe pattern.
In India in 2022 an estimated 3,700 wild tigers lived.
The tiger is the national animal of India and Bangladesh.
White tigers are Bengal tigers with a special inherited trait.

abschnitte.text: The Bengal tiger is one of the largest big cats in the world. Males grow to about three metres long including the tail and usually weigh between 180 and 260 kilograms, while females are clearly lighter. Its fur is orange with black **stripes**, and the belly and the insides of the legs are white. The stripe pattern is different in every animal, similar to a fingerprint. Rarely **white tigers** occur, which are pale because of a special inherited trait.

Bengal tigers live in India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan. They are found in dry and damp forests, in tall grassland and in mangrove swamps. The **Sundarbans** on the border of India and Bangladesh are the largest mangrove area in the world. There tigers even swim back and forth between the islands. India is today home to about three quarters of all wild tigers worldwide.

The tiger is an **ambush hunter**: it sneaks up on its prey and pounces on it from a short distance. It hunts mainly deer such as sambar and chital, but also wild boar and young buffalo. It usually hunts at dusk or at night. A tiger can eat a great deal of meat at one meal and then fast for several days. It lives as a **loner** in a large territory.

After a gestation of about three and a half months, the tigress usually gives birth to two to four young. The young are blind at first and weigh only about one kilogram. The mother raises them alone and teaches them to hunt. At about two years old the young tigers leave their mother. Then they look for their own **territory**.

About a hundred years ago there were still tens of thousands of tigers in India, but through hunting and the destruction of their habitat there were fewer and fewer. In 1973 India started the protection programme **Project Tiger** and set up many tiger reserves. Since then the populations have recovered. Even so, the tiger is still highly endangered, above all through poaching and conflicts with people. Well-known protected areas are, for example, the national parks of Ranthambore and Bandhavgarh.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large cat such as a tiger, lion or leopard.
An animal that sneaks up and surprises its prey.
Trees that grow in salty water on tropical coasts.
The illegal hunting of protected animals.

gewusst: Tigers are very good swimmers and like to go into the water, unlike most cats.
The skin under a tiger's fur is striped too.
The roar of a tiger can be heard for kilometres.

teile.einleitung: The beaver lodge is the home of a beaver family. From the outside it looks like a big heap of branches and mud on the bank. Inside is hidden a dry living chamber that can only be reached from under water.
wichtigste: A beaver lodge is a structure made of branches, twigs, mud and stones.
From the outside you often see a big heap of branches and mud on the bank.
The entrance is under water so that enemies such as foxes cannot get in.
Inside there is a dry living chamber above the water level.
In the lodge the beavers sleep during the day and raise their young.
Fresh air gets into the living chamber through the loose roof.
Where the bank is high, beavers often dig only a den instead of building a lodge.

abschnitte.text: The **beaver lodge** is the beaver's dwelling. It is made of many branches and twigs that the beaver seals with mud, earth and plant remains. From the outside it looks like an untidy heap of wood. A large lodge can be several metres wide and over a metre high. A beaver family often uses it for many years.

Inside there is a **living chamber** that stays dry above the water level. The floor is padded with wood shavings and grass. From the water one or more tunnels lead up into the chamber. The entrances lie **under water** and are therefore hardly reachable for foxes, dogs or wolves. At the top the roof is built a little more loosely so that fresh air gets in.

Not every beaver builds a free-standing lodge. If the bank is high and firm, it digs a **bank den**, that is a den with a tunnel into the bank. If the roof collapses, it patches it with branches, and what is called a mixed den arises. Free-standing lodges are seen mainly on flat banks and in beaver ponds. In Switzerland many beavers live in bank dens on river banks.

Beavers are usually out and about at dusk and at night. During the day they sleep in the lodge. In early summer the young are born here and grow up protected. In winter it stays much warmer in the lodge than outside, even when the lake is frozen over. Under the ice the beavers then swim to their store of branches.

In Switzerland the beaver is protected, and its structures must not simply be destroyed either. Anyone who discovers a beaver lodge should keep their distance and not disturb the animals. Dogs should stay on the lead nearby. If a lodge causes problems, experts from the cantons decide what to do.

begriffe.erklaerung: The dry room in the beaver lodge in which the family sleeps.
A den that the beaver digs into a high bank.
The height to which the water reaches in a lake or river.

gewusst: In winter you can sometimes see steam rising above an occupied beaver lodge.
Beavers repair their lodge constantly and in this way build it ever bigger over the years.

teile.einleitung: The harlequin ladybird, also called the Asian ladybird, is a beetle from East Asia that is now also widespread in Switzerland. It was brought to Europe to fight aphids and then spread by itself in the wild. There it can push out native species of ladybird.
wichtigste: The harlequin ladybird comes from East Asia.
It has moved into Switzerland and can push out native species.
It is also called the Asian ladybird.
It was used to fight aphids.
Its colours and the number of spots vary a great deal.
In autumn it often seeks shelter in houses in large groups.
It also eats the larvae of other ladybirds.

abschnitte.text: The harlequin ladybird is about 5 to 8 millimetres long, and so a little bigger than many native species. Its colour varies a lot: yellow, orange, red or black with red spots. It can have no spots at all or up to about 20. Often there is a typical pale marking behind the head that looks like an **M** or a **W**. Because of this colourful variety it is also called the **harlequin ladybird**.

Its home is **East Asia**, for example China, Japan and Korea. Because it eats very many aphids, it was used in North America and Europe as a beneficial insect in greenhouses. From there it got out into the open and spread strongly. In Switzerland it was first recorded in the wild in 2004, and today it occurs almost everywhere on the Central Plateau.

The harlequin ladybird is a great **aphid eater**, and one larva eats hundreds of aphids. If it and its larvae find too few aphids, they also eat the eggs and larvae of other ladybirds. In this way it competes with native species such as the **seven-spot ladybird**. In autumn it also likes to eat ripe, sweet fruit such as grapes.

In autumn the beetles often gather in their hundreds on bright house walls. They creep through cracks in window frames and spend the winter in houses and attics. They are harmless to people, but can sometimes give a slight nip. When in danger they release a yellow, bad-smelling liquid that can leave stains.

Because the harlequin ladybird multiplies so strongly, it counts as an **invasive species**. It also brings a fungal parasite that is harmless to itself but can harm native species. In vineyards, beetles that are pressed with the grapes can give the wine an unpleasant taste. Today it is no longer released as a beneficial insect in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: An introduced living thing that spreads strongly and pushes out native species.
An animal that eats pests and so helps people.
A tiny insect that sucks plant sap.
A colourful jester figure from the theatre, after which the beetle is named.

gewusst: For defence, ladybirds release bitter drops from the joints of their legs, which is called reflex bleeding.
A single harlequin ladybird can eat thousands of aphids in its lifetime.
Because it can reproduce several times a year, the harlequin ladybird quickly becomes common.

teile.einleitung: An aquarium is a glass container of water in which you keep fish, plants and other water animals and can watch them. To keep the animals well, an aquarium needs plants, a filter and regular care. Large public aquariums even show sharks, rays and whole underwater worlds.
wichtigste: An aquarium is a small, artificial habitat under water.
There are freshwater aquariums and marine aquariums.
Plants produce oxygen and give the fish shelter.
A pump or a filter with aeration provides enough oxygen.
Fish need plants or other hiding places where they can retreat.
The water should be partly changed regularly, for example every week.
Goldfish need a large tank and company of their own kind.

abschnitte.text: The word **aquarium** comes from the Latin “aqua” for water. It means a container, usually made of glass, in which water creatures are kept. In a **freshwater aquarium** live fish from rivers and lakes, such as goldfish, guppies or neon tetras. In a **marine aquarium** swim animals from the sea, for example clownfish among corals.

A **filter** sucks in water, cleans it of dirt and returns it. A pump or a filter with aeration makes sure that enough oxygen gets into the water. Tropical fish also need a heater, while goldfish prefer cool water. A lamp replaces sunlight so that the plants can grow.

Water plants are very important in an aquarium. They produce oxygen and take waste substances out of the water. At the same time, plants, stones and roots give the fish **hiding places** where they can rest and feel safe. Without places to retreat to, many fish become stressed and ill.

Fish release waste into the water, which becomes poisonous over time. Useful **bacteria** in the filter turn these substances into less harmful ones. Even so, you should change part of the water regularly, for example every week. A new aquarium must first run for a few weeks without fish so that these bacteria can settle in.

Goldfish come from **China**, where they have been bred for over a thousand years. They can live for many years and grow to over 20 centimetres long. Small round bowls are therefore completely unsuitable for them. Goldfish are sociable and should never live alone, and in summer they also feel at home in a garden pond.

Public aquariums show animals from rivers, lakes and oceans. In Switzerland **Aquatis** in Lausanne is well known. It opened in 2017 and is one of the largest freshwater aquariums in Europe. Basel Zoo, too, has a large aquarium complex in its Vivarium. Such aquariums help to get people excited about protecting waters.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that cleans and moves the water in the aquarium.
Replacing only part of the water instead of emptying the whole tank.
Water from rivers and lakes that contains hardly any salt.
A gas that fish take from the water with their gills and need to live.

gewusst: With good care, goldfish can live for more than 20 years.
The first public aquariums appeared around 1850 in England.
Fish have no eyelids and therefore sleep with their eyes open.

teile.einleitung: The adaptive immune system is the learning part of the body’s defence. It recognises very specific disease-causing germs and remembers them for later. Only vertebrates have an adaptive immune system with antibodies.
wichtigste: The adaptive immune system is also called the acquired or specific defence.
Only vertebrates have an adaptive immune system with antibodies.
Invertebrates such as insects have only an innate defence.
The most important cells are the B cells and the T cells.
B cells make antibodies, which mark germs in a targeted way.
Memory cells remember germs that the body already knows.
Vaccinations use this memory to protect against diseases.

abschnitte.text: The body has two defence systems. The **innate defence** reacts quickly, but always in the same way to all intruders. The adaptive immune system, by contrast, adjusts to one very particular germ. Adaptive means able to adapt, and that is exactly what makes it so effective.

Every disease-causing germ has typical features on its surface, called **antigens**. White blood cells, the lymphocytes, recognise these features like a key that fits into a lock. The matching cells then multiply greatly. On the first contact this takes a few days, which is why you are ill for a while at first.

**B cells** make antibodies, which are proteins in a Y shape. The antibodies attach to the germs and mark them so that scavenger cells can destroy them. **T cells** help with control or kill infected body cells directly. Both types of cell arise in the bone marrow, and the T cells then mature in the thymus gland.

After an illness, **memory cells** stay behind in the body, often for many years. If the same germ comes again, the body reacts very quickly and strongly. That is why you usually get diseases such as chickenpox only once. In a **vaccination**, the immune system gets to know the germ without you becoming properly ill.

Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals all have an adaptive immune system. Insects, worms, snails and other invertebrates have no antibodies. They rely on an innate defence, which nevertheless works well. The adaptive immune system probably arose over 400 million years ago in early fish.

The English doctor **Edward Jenner** protected a boy in 1796 against the dangerous smallpox with harmless cowpox. That was the beginning of vaccinations. At the end of the 19th century, researchers discovered antibodies in the blood. Today in Switzerland, children are vaccinated, for example, against measles, mumps and rubella.

begriffe.erklaerung: Proteins in a Y shape that recognise and mark disease-causing germs.
A feature on a germ that the immune system recognises.
A group of white blood cells that includes B cells and T cells.
Defence cells that remember a germ.
A training session for the immune system so that it recognises germs faster.

gewusst: The body can make billions of different antibodies.
In the first months of life, a baby receives antibodies from its mother, partly through breast milk.
In allergies, the adaptive immune system reacts to harmless substances such as pollen.

teile.einleitung: “The Town Musicians of Bremen” is a well-known fairy tale by the Brothers Grimm. In it a donkey, a dog, a cat and a rooster join together because their owners no longer want them. Together, with courage and wit, they drive away a gang of robbers.
wichtigste: The fairy tale comes from the collection “Children's and Household Tales” by the Brothers Grimm.
The four animals are a donkey, a dog, a cat and a rooster.
All four are old and are to be given away or killed by their owners.
They want to become musicians in the city of Bremen.
On the way they chase robbers out of a house in the forest.
In the story they never arrive in Bremen.
In Bremen stands a famous bronze figure of the four animals.

abschnitte.text: An old **donkey** can no longer work and flees from his master in order to become a town musician in Bremen. On the way he meets an old dog, a cat and a rooster, who are in a similar situation. In the evening they discover in the forest a robbers' house with a laid table. They climb on top of each other, make a hellish din together and burst through the window, so that the robbers flee in fright.

abschnitte.titel: The end in the robbers' house
abschnitte.text: In the night the robber chief sends a man back to take a look. In the dark the cat scratches him, the dog bites him in the leg, the donkey gives him a kick and the rooster crows loudly. The robber believes he has been attacked by a witch, a man with a knife, a monster and a judge. The robbers never come back, and the four animals stay living in the house.

The brothers **Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm** collected fairy tales from oral tradition in the 19th century and wrote them down. The Town Musicians of Bremen appeared from the second edition of their “Children's and Household Tales” of 1819. Similar stories about animals that drive off robbers existed earlier in various countries. Today the fairy tale is one of the best-known Grimm tales in the world.

abschnitte.titel: The message of the fairy tale
abschnitte.text: The story shows that together you are stronger than alone. Each animal brings its own **ability**: the donkey his strength, the dog his teeth, the cat her claws and the rooster his loud voice. It also tells us that old animals and people are still valuable. The well-known sentence “You can find something better than death anywhere” gives courage to start anew.

In the city of **Bremen** in the north of Germany the four animals are a landmark. Next to the town hall stands, since 1953, a bronze sculpture by the sculptor Gerhard Marcks, in which the animals stand on top of one another. Many visitors touch the front legs of the donkey, because that is supposed to bring luck. That is why these places gleam brightly, while the rest of the figure is dark.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginative story, often with talking animals or magic, that was passed on orally for a long time.
Two German language scholars who collected and wrote down many fairy tales in the 19th century.
A work of art made of stone, metal or wood that you can look at from all sides.
A well-known building or work of art by which you recognise a city at once.

gewusst: In the fairy tale the four animals never reach the city of Bremen at all.
The pyramid of animals made of donkey, dog, cat and rooster is one of the most photographed subjects in Bremen.
In many languages there are picture books, plays and animated films about the Town Musicians of Bremen.

teile.einleitung: The Bernese mountain dog is a large, friendly farm dog with long, three-coloured fur. It originally comes from the canton of Bern, from the area around the Bernese Oberland and the Bernese countryside. Today it is popular all over the world as a family dog.
wichtigste: The Bernese mountain dog is a large Swiss breed of dog.
It has long, three-coloured fur in black, rusty brown and white.
In the past it helped on farms and pulled milk carts to the dairy.
It is one of four Swiss mountain dogs.
It used to be called the Dürrbächler, after the hamlet of Dürrbach near Riggisberg.
It is regarded as good-natured, calm and fond of children.

abschnitte.text: The Bernese mountain dog is a strong, large dog. Males grow to about 64 to 70 centimetres high, females to about 58 to 66 centimetres. Its long, shiny fur is **three-coloured**: deep black with rusty brown markings on the cheeks and legs and white patches on the chest, head and paws. On the forehead it usually has a white blaze. It is the only one of the Swiss mountain dogs with **long fur**.

In the past the Bernese mountain dog lived on farms in the canton of Bern. It guarded the house and yard, drove cows and pulled small carts with milk churns to the **dairy**. Because it is so strong, it was also called a draught dog. To this day you sometimes see Bernese mountain dogs pulling little carts at festivals. The word **Senn** means an alpine herdsman who makes cheese.

At the end of the 19th century there were only a few such farm dogs left. Enthusiasts began to breed them deliberately and at first called them **Dürrbächler**, after the hamlet of Dürrbach near Riggisberg. The geologist Albert Heim campaigned strongly for the Swiss mountain dogs. In 1907 a breeding club was founded in Burgdorf. Later the breed received the name Bernese mountain dog.

Bernese mountain dogs are calm, good-natured and very devoted. They are usually patient with children and are well suited as **family dogs**. They keep a watchful eye but are not aggressive. Because they are large, they need space, exercise and good training from an early age. They do not especially like heat because of their thick fur.

Four breeds belong to the **Swiss mountain dogs**. Besides the Bernese, they are the Greater Swiss mountain dog, the Appenzeller mountain dog and the Entlebuch mountain dog. All four are three-coloured but differ in size and coat. The Bernese mountain dog is today the best known of them. Unfortunately Bernese mountain dogs have on average a rather short **life expectancy** of about seven to ten years.

begriffe.erklaerung: A Swiss breed of dog that in the past worked for farmers and alpine herdsmen.
An alpine herdsman who tends cows on the alp and makes cheese.
A dog that is male.
A white stripe on an animal's forehead.

gewusst: A fully grown Bernese mountain dog can weigh about 40 to 50 kilograms.
Albert Heim, who promoted the mountain dogs, was actually a geologist and studied the Alps.
Bernese mountain dogs shed a great deal of hair, especially when they change their coat in spring and autumn.

teile.einleitung: Altruism means selflessness. In biology it refers to behaviour in which an animal helps another although it harms itself or takes a risk. For a long time this was a great puzzle for researchers, because according to the theory of evolution every animal should look after itself first.
wichtigste: Altruism means that an animal benefits others and accepts disadvantages of its own in doing so.
Biologically this means that it harms its own reproductive success but benefits other individuals.
Meerkat sentries and warning calls are well-known examples.
Worker bees and ants usually have no offspring of their own.
Kin selection explains why animals help relatives in particular.
In reciprocal altruism, individuals help each other in turn.
The word comes from the Latin alter, which means “the other”.

abschnitte.text: The term **altruism** comes from the Latin word alter, “the other”. Its opposite is egoism. In biology, one speaks of altruism when a behaviour harms one’s own **reproductive success** but benefits other animals. Whether the animal feels or thinks anything in doing so plays no role in this definition. It is only a matter of who has more offspring in the end.

In **meerkats**, one animal often stands as a sentry on a mound while the others eat. If it sees a bird of prey, it gives a warning call. Many birds and marmots also warn others with calls and make themselves more conspicuous in doing so. Vampire bats share blood with hungry group members who found nothing in the night. In honeybees, a worker stings to defend the hive and often dies afterwards.

The British biologist William D. Hamilton found an important explanation in 1964, **kin selection**. Related animals carry many of the same genes. If an animal helps its siblings or nieces and nephews, it indirectly passes on its own genes too. That is why animals help relatives especially often. This explains, for example, why workers in ants and bees raise the young of their mother, the queen.

Sometimes animals that are not related also help each other. The biologist Robert Trivers described **reciprocal altruism** in 1971, that is, help on a give-and-take basis. The idea is simple: today I help you, tomorrow you help me. This works mainly in animals that live in groups for a long time and recognise one another. Vampire bats and many monkeys are examples of it.

Humans, too, help others, often even complete strangers, for example when giving blood or in rescue operations. Researchers study how cooperation and willingness to help arose in evolution. Altruism shows that **cooperation** can be just as important in nature as competition. Some apparently selfless behaviours do, however, also bring the animal a hidden advantage of its own.

begriffe.erklaerung: Selfless behaviour that helps others and harms the helper itself.
How many offspring an animal has and raises in its life.
The explanation of why animals help relatives: because these have many of the same genes.
Mutual, that is, help that is returned later.

gewusst: Even Charles Darwin considered the infertile workers of ants and bees a difficult puzzle for his theory.
A vampire bat that finds no blood for three nights can starve, so sharing is vital for it.

teile.einleitung: Brachycephaly means short-headedness. In breeds of dog such as the pug or the French bulldog, the term describes a short, broad skull with a flat nose. What many people find cute often leads in the animals to breathing problems and other suffering.
wichtigste: Brachycephaly describes a short, broad skull.
It is typical of the pug, the French bulldog, the English bulldog and the Pekingese.
Cats such as the Persian cat can also be affected.
Many short-headed dogs have breathing problems because the airways are too narrow.
You often hear this in snoring and wheezing.
Exaggerated short-headedness counts as breeding that causes suffering.
The word comes from Greek and means short head.

abschnitte.text: The technical term **brachycephaly** comes from Greek: brachys means short and kephale means head. What is meant is a skull that is very short in relation to its width. In dogs it is above all the muzzle that is strongly shortened, and the nose sits almost flat in the face. The opposite is a long, narrow head like that of a greyhound. In humans too people speak of brachycephaly, for example when the back of a baby's head is flattened.

Typical short-headed breeds of dog are the **pug**, the French bulldog, the English bulldog, the boxer, the Pekingese and the Shih Tzu. Among cats the Persian and the Exotic Shorthair belong here. These breeds have become very popular in recent years. Many people like the big eyes and the round face, because they are reminiscent of a baby.

Because the skull is short, the nose, throat and palate have too little room. The nostrils are often narrow and the **soft palate** too long. That is why many of these dogs find it hard to get air, snore, wheeze and can hardly cool down in heat. Vets call this **brachycephalic syndrome**. In addition there are often eye problems, skin infections in the folds and difficulties at birth.

abschnitte.titel: Breeding that causes suffering, and animal welfare
abschnitte.text: When animals are bred in such a way that they suffer because of their appearance, this is called **breeding that causes suffering** (Qualzucht). In Switzerland animal welfare law forbids breeding in which the animals have pain or damage because of such features. Vets and animal welfare organisations call for breeds with a longer muzzle again. Some breeders therefore cross in other breeds so that the dogs can breathe better.

Anyone who wants a dog should find out well about the breed beforehand. With short-headed breeds it is worth looking out for a visible **muzzle** and wide nostrils. A healthy dog breathes quietly even when playing and can run well. In heat you should walk short-headed dogs only in the shade and slowly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short-headedness, that is a short, broad skull.
Breeding in which animals suffer because of their appearance.
The soft rear part of the palate in the throat.
A group of animals of one species with similar appearance.

gewusst: The pug used to look clearly different and had a much longer nose than today.
Many short-headed dogs sleep sitting up or with a toy in their mouth so that they can get air better.
Dogs cool down by panting, and with a short nose this works much worse.

teile.einleitung: Anemonefish, also called clownfish, are small, colourful fish from coral reefs. They live among the poisonous tentacles of sea anemones without being hurt. Through the film “Finding Nemo” they have become world famous.
wichtigste: Anemonefish live in warm coral reefs in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
There are about 30 species.
They live in partnership with sea anemones.
A layer of mucus protects them from the anemone's stinging poison.
All anemonefish hatch as males.
The largest fish in a group is the female.
If the female dies, the largest male becomes the female.

abschnitte.text: Anemonefish are usually only 6 to 15 centimetres long. Many are orange, red, yellow or black and have broad **white stripes**. The best known is the false clownfish, which looks like Nemo in the film. In all there are about 30 species. They belong to the damselfish family.

Anemonefish live in warm, shallow **coral reefs** in the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea and the western Pacific. They do not occur in the wild in the Atlantic. Each group lives in its own sea anemone and hardly ever strays far from it. The anemone is their home, hiding place and nursery. They mainly eat plankton, small crustaceans and algae.

Sea anemones have many tentacles with **stinging cells** that paralyse small fish. Anemonefish are protected by a special **layer of mucus** on their skin. Among the tentacles they are safe from predatory fish. In return they defend the anemone against enemies, clean it and supply it with nutrients from their droppings. Such a partnership for mutual benefit is called **symbiosis**.

All anemonefish hatch as males. In one anemone lives a group with a fixed pecking order. The largest fish is the **female**, the second largest is the only male that breeds. If the female dies, the male changes into a female, and a younger male moves up. This change of sex from male to female is called **protandry**.

The female lays hundreds of eggs on a stone right next to the anemone. The male guards the eggs, fans fresh water over them and removes spoiled eggs. After about a week the tiny larvae hatch and drift in the sea. Later the young fish look for an anemone, which they probably find with their sense of smell.

Since the film “Finding Nemo” in 2003, anemonefish have been very popular as **aquarium fish**. Many animals used to be caught in the sea, but today most are bred. Anemonefish are threatened mainly by the warming of the seas and **coral bleaching**, which also weakens anemones. You can watch anemonefish in Swiss zoos and show aquariums.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two different species living together in a way that benefits both.
Tiny poison capsules that jellyfish and anemones use to paralyse their prey.
A change of sex in which an animal is first male and later female.
An underwater ridge made from the limestone skeletons of tiny coral animals.

gewusst: In real life, Nemo's father would himself have become a female after the mother's death.
Anemonefish can make popping and clicking sounds to communicate.

teile.einleitung: The Adélie penguin is a small black and white species of penguin from Antarctica. With its black head and the white ring around its eyes, it looks as if it were wearing a hood. It is one of the penguins that breed furthest south.
wichtigste: The Adélie penguin lives in Antarctica and is very common there.
It has a black head and a striking white eye ring.
It grows to about 70 centimetres.
Its food consists mainly of krill and small fish.
It builds its nest from small stones.
Adélie penguins breed in huge colonies.
The species is named after Adélie Land in Antarctica.

abschnitte.text: The Adélie penguin is about 70 centimetres tall and weighs around 4 to 6 kilograms. Its back and head are black, and its belly is bright white. Typical is the white **eye ring**, which gives it a surprised look. Like all penguins, it cannot fly, and its wings have become strong **flippers**.

Adélie penguins live all around the whole Antarctic continent. In summer they breed on ice-free, rocky coasts. They spend the winter out on the **pack ice**, where they can hunt in the sea. There are several million breeding pairs, which is why the species is among the most common penguins.

The most important part of their food is **krill**, which are small, shrimp-like crustaceans. Besides that they also eat small fish and squid. When diving, they often hunt at a depth of a few dozen metres. Under water they are quick and agile, whereas on land they waddle rather clumsily.

In the Antarctic spring, around October, the Adélie penguins return to their breeding sites. There they build nests from small **pebbles** so that the eggs do not lie in meltwater. Some penguins secretly steal stones from their neighbours. The female usually lays two eggs, and both parents take turns brooding.

The chicks hatch after about five weeks and at first have a grey, fluffy covering of down. The parents fetch food from the sea and bring it up again for the young. Later the chicks gather in groups called **crèches**. Dangerous enemies are skuas on land and leopard seals in the water.

In 1840 the French explorer Jules Dumont d’Urville named a coastal area of Antarctica after his wife Adèle. That is how the name Adélie Land arose, and later the name of the penguin. Overall the species is not considered threatened. **Climate change**, however, is altering the sea ice and with it the food, which is why some colonies are declining.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of animals that breed together.
Small, shrimp-like crustaceans that live in huge swarms in cold seas.
Floating, pushed-together ice floes on the sea.
Soft, fluffy feathers that keep warm.

gewusst: Adélie penguins travel thousands of kilometres every year between their breeding site and their winter quarters.
Some colonies in Antarctica count hundreds of thousands of penguins.
Penguins drink sea water and get rid of the salt again through a special gland.

teile.einleitung: Anubis is a deity of ancient Egypt who is shown with the body of a man and the head of a jackal. He was responsible for mummification and for accompanying the dead. His image links the religion of the Egyptians with a real wild animal of the desert.
wichtigste: Anubis is a god of ancient Egypt with a jackal's head.
He was responsible for mummification and for accompanying the dead.
The model was a dog-like predator that lived on the edge of the desert.
Today this animal is regarded as the African golden wolf and no longer as a true jackal.
Anubis was often painted entirely black, because black stood for fertile earth and new life.
At the judgement of the dead, Anubis weighed the heart of the deceased on a pair of scales.
The olive baboon is also named after Anubis.

abschnitte.titel: A god with an animal's head
abschnitte.text: The ancient Egyptians showed many of their gods with animal heads. Anubis has the slim head of a **jackal** with a long snout and pointed, upright ears. Sometimes he was also shown as a black dog lying on a chest. Such figures often stood at tomb entrances and were meant to guard the dead.

Anubis was regarded as the inventor of **mummification**, that is, the art of preserving the dead. The priests who embalmed the dead sometimes wore a mask with his head. The Egyptians believed that the body had to be preserved so that the soul could go on living in the afterlife. That is why Anubis was especially important to them.

According to Egyptian belief, every dead person had to appear before a court. Anubis placed the heart of the deceased on a pair of scales. On the other side lay a feather of the goddess **Maat**, who stood for truth and order. If the heart was no heavier than the feather, the soul was allowed to go on into the afterlife. This scene is often painted in the Egyptian **Book of the Dead**.

On the edge of the desert, dog-like predators roamed around the cemeteries looking for food. Perhaps that is why the Egyptians came up with the idea of making such an animal the protecting god of the dead. For a long time this animal was called the golden jackal. Genetic studies showed in 2015 that the animals in North Africa are a species of their own, the **African golden wolf**.

Many statues and wall paintings of Anubis have survived and can be seen in museums all over the world. A black, reclining figure of Anubis from the tomb of **Tutankhamun** is famous, and is now displayed in Egypt. Anubis also often appears in books, films and games. In Switzerland you can see Egyptian art, for example, in the Museum of Ancient Art in Basel.

begriffe.erklaerung: A god or goddess, that is, a being worshipped in a religion.
Preserving a dead body with salt, oils and linen bandages.
The world in which, according to the belief of many people, the soul goes on living after death.
A dog-like predator from North Africa that used to be thought of as a jackal.

gewusst: The ancient Greeks called the city where Anubis was especially worshipped “Kynopolis”, which means City of Dogs.
The black colour of Anubis had nothing to do with mourning, but stood for the fertile mud of the Nile.
In Egypt thousands of dogs were mummified and buried as offerings to Anubis.

teile.einleitung: The wood sandpiper, in German called the Bruchwasserläufer, is a slender wader that breeds in the bogs and marshes of northern Europe. In Switzerland it is seen mainly in spring and late summer, when it rests on migration between its breeding area and Africa. On its long legs it stalks through shallow water and pecks for small animals.
wichtigste: The wood sandpiper is a small wader from the family of sandpipers and snipes.
It breeds in northern Europe and Siberia.
It spends the winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
In Switzerland it occurs mainly on passage.
It eats insects, worms and other small water animals.
Its German name comes from the old word “Bruch” for marsh or bog.

abschnitte.text: The wood sandpiper is about 20 centimetres long, so about as big as a blackbird, but much slimmer. Its back is grey-brown with many pale dots, and the belly is white. It has long, yellowish **legs** and a straight, medium-long bill. Above the eye it has a pale stripe called a supercilium.

The wood sandpiper breeds in Scandinavia, in the Baltic states, in Russia and far into Siberia. There it lives in open **bogs**, marshes and light woods with pools. Its nest is usually well hidden on the ground between grass and dwarf shrubs. Sometimes, though, it also uses old thrush nests in trees.

Wood sandpipers are **migratory birds** and fly thousands of kilometres every year to Africa south of the Sahara. On the way they need resting places with mudflats and shallow water. In Switzerland they rest, for example, at the Fanel on Lake Neuchâtel, at the Bolle di Magadino in Ticino or on flooded fields. In April and May and from July to September you can best watch them here.

The wood sandpiper looks for food in shallow water and in mud. It eats mainly **insects** and their larvae, but also small worms, snails and little crustaceans. In doing so it runs quickly back and forth and pecks the prey from the surface. Sometimes it also probes with its bill in the soft ground.

Typical is its bright, many-syllabled call that sounds like “giff giff giff”. In flight you see its white **rump** and the finely barred tail. It can easily be confused with the green sandpiper, which, however, is darker and shows a stronger contrast between back and belly. Birdwatchers therefore pay close attention to the call, the colour of the legs and the underside of the wings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird with long legs that looks for food in shallow water.
The time when migratory birds fly through a country on their journey and rest there.
An old word for a damp marshy area or bog.
The lower back of a bird directly above the tail.

gewusst: Although it is a wader, the wood sandpiper sometimes breeds high up in old thrush nests.
On its migration the wood sandpiper covers a distance of several thousand kilometres twice a year.

teile.einleitung: The Alpine ibex is a wild climbing artist of the Alps with mighty, curved horns. A good hundred years ago it was almost wiped out. Today thousands of ibex live in Switzerland again, and it is the heraldic animal of the canton of Graubünden.
wichtigste: The Alpine ibex lives in steep rocky regions above the tree line.
The males are called bucks and carry horns up to about one metre long.
Its hooves have a hard rim and a soft, grippy sole.
In the 19th century it was almost extinct in the Alps because it was hunted heavily.
All of today’s Alpine ibex descend from a small remnant population in Italy.
A young ibex is called a kid.
In Switzerland it may be hunted today only according to fixed shooting quotas.

abschnitte.text: The **Alpine ibex** (Capra ibex) belongs to the goat family. A fully grown buck can weigh about 100 kilograms, while the females, the **nannies**, are clearly lighter. The horns of the bucks are much larger than those of the nannies and carry thick cross ridges. Its compact, muscular body makes climbing and jumping in steep rock easier. In winter its fur is thick and greyish brown, in summer shorter and paler.

Ibex climb safely over narrow rock ledges and almost vertical walls. Their special **hooves** with a hard rim and a soft, non-slip sole make this possible. The two toes can spread and so hold on to bumps. In Italy, ibex even climb almost vertical dam walls to lick salt from the stones. Even young kids follow their mother over steep rocks a few days after birth.

abschnitte.titel: Habitat and course of the year
abschnitte.text: The ibex likes best to live in steep rocky regions above the **tree line**, often between about 1,600 and 3,200 metres. In summer it eats grasses, herbs and lichens on mountain pastures. When deep snow lies in winter, it moves to lower, sunny slopes with less snow. There, on steep places where the snow slides off, it still finds a little food. Bucks and nannies mostly live in separate groups outside the mating season.

The mating season, the **rut**, takes place in December and January. Then the bucks fight for the females. They rear up on their hind legs and let their horns crash against each other. After about five to six months, usually a single kid is born in June. In the wild, an ibex can live to be about 16 to 20 years old.

In the past, the ibex was hunted heavily for its meat and for supposed healing powers of horns, blood and bones. At the beginning of the 19th century, only a small group survived in the area of today’s **Gran Paradiso** National Park in Italy.
