In 1906, young animals from there were secretly brought to Switzerland and raised in breeding enclosures such as the Peter and Paul wildlife park in St Gallen. In 1911 the first animals were released in the canton of St Gallen. Because almost all of today’s ibex descend from this small remnant population, their genetic diversity is low.

Today around 17,000 ibex live in Switzerland again (as of about 2020). Many animals from Switzerland were later also brought to neighbouring countries to found new colonies there. The ibex is the **heraldic animal** of the canton of Graubünden. Hunting is not banned today but strictly regulated, with fixed shooting quotas. In this way the populations stay healthy and the mountain forests are not browsed too heavily.

begriffe.erklaerung: The mating season in deer, ibex and chamois.
What a young ibex, chamois or roe deer is called.
The height in the mountains above which no trees can grow.
A female ibex.
The exact number of animals that hunters may kill in a year.

gewusst: From the cross ridges of the horns you can roughly read the age of an ibex, similar to annual rings.
The first ibex for the reintroduction were poached in Italy and secretly brought across the border into Switzerland.
Ibex can jump several metres from a standing start.

teile.einleitung: The Bear Pit is a famous bear enclosure in the city of Bern, where living bears have been kept for centuries. It lies at the end of the Old Town by the Nydegg Bridge over the Aare. Today the old pit is part of the larger Bear Park.
wichtigste: The Bear Pit is the well-known bear enclosure in the city of Bern.
Bern has kept living bears since 1513, because the bear is the city's heraldic animal.
Today's Bear Pit at the Nydegg Bridge dates from 1857.
Before that the Bear Pit lay at various places in the city.
Because the round pit was too cramped, it was often criticised.
Since 2009 the old pit has been linked with the new Bear Park by the Aare.
The Bear Pit is one of the best-known sights of Bern.

abschnitte.text: The bear is the **heraldic animal** of the city of Bern, and since the Middle Ages the city has kept living bears. According to tradition, in **1513** soldiers from Bern brought a living bear home as booty after the Battle of Novara. It was kept in the city moat of the time. Since then bears have belonged to Bern like the Zytglogge.

The first Bear Pit lay at the place that is today called **Bärenplatz**. Over the centuries the bears moved several times, because the city grew. In 1857 the pit was opened at its present place by the **Nydegg Bridge** at the eastern end of the Old Town. It was a round, walled pit with a tree for climbing in the middle.

Generations of families, school classes and tourists visited the Bear Pit. In the past visitors were allowed to feed the bears with carrots that could be bought on the spot. For many guests from all over the world, a visit to the pit is part of every trip to Bern. Nearby is also the **Rosengarten** with a lovely view of the Old Town.

Over time the cramped, stone pit was criticised more and more. Animal protectors complained that the bears had too little space and hardly anything to do there. Bears need soil to dig in, water and hiding places in order to behave in a way that is **suited to their species**. The city therefore decided to build a larger enclosure.

In 2009 the **Bear Park** was opened on the slope down to the Aare. The old Bear Pit was kept and is linked with the new park by a tunnel. Today it serves mainly as a place of retreat and an extra part of the enclosure. The pit is a cultural monument under **heritage protection**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal shown on the coat of arms of a city or country.
In the way that matches the natural needs of an animal.
Legal protection for valuable old buildings.
A stone bridge over the Aare at the eastern end of Bern's Old Town.

gewusst: The Bärenplatz in the middle of Bern is named after the earlier Bear Pit that lay there.
Between 1513 and 1857 the Bear Pit was moved several times to a new place.

teile.einleitung: Bioluminescence means that living things produce light themselves. Fireflies glow on summer nights, and in the dark sea jellyfish, fish and crustaceans flash. The light arises through a chemical reaction in the body.
wichtigste: Bioluminescence is the ability of living things to produce light themselves.
The light arises when the substance luciferin reacts with oxygen with the help of the enzyme luciferase.
The light is cold, hardly any heat is produced in the process.
Some jellyfish can glow in the dark sea.
They glow to confuse enemies or attract prey.
There are especially many glowing creatures in the deep sea.
In Switzerland you can watch fireflies in summer.

abschnitte.text: The word **bioluminescence** is made up of “bios” for life and “lumen” for light. What is meant is light that living things make themselves. Bacteria, fungi, algae, jellyfish, worms, insects, squid and fish can glow. Mammals, birds and flowering plants, by contrast, do not glow by themselves. Glowing is most common in the sea.

In the body of the animals there is a light-producing substance, **luciferin**. An enzyme called **luciferase** makes sure that the luciferin reacts with oxygen. In this process energy is given off as light. Almost no energy is lost as heat, which is why people speak of cold light. It usually glows blue or green, because this light travels furthest in water.

In the **deep sea** no sunlight penetrates, yet it flashes there constantly. A large part of the animals that live at middle depths of the sea can glow. Some **jellyfish** light up when they are attacked and so frighten or confuse their enemies. The deep-sea anglerfish carries a glowing lure in front of its mouth with which it attracts prey. In warm seas tiny algae make the water sparkle when there are waves, which is called **sea sparkle**.

On warm June evenings you sometimes see small points of light at the edge of the woods in Switzerland. They are **fireflies**, also called glow-worms or St John's beetles. In the large glow-worm it is mainly the wingless females that glow in the grass to attract males. The males fly around and look for the lights. Artificial light from street lamps disturbs the beetles in their search for a partner.

Living things use their light for very different purposes. They attract partners or prey, warn enemies or confuse attackers. Some squid glow on the underside so that their shadow cannot be seen from below. Researchers use a glowing protein from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria, the **green fluorescent protein**. For research into it, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded in 2008.

begriffe.erklaerung: A light-producing substance in the body of living things that gives off light when it reacts with oxygen.
An enzyme that starts the light reaction.
The dark part of the sea that sunlight no longer penetrates.
A protein that speeds up chemical reactions in the body.

gewusst: Some fungi glow too, and their faint light used to be called foxfire or glowing wood.
The light of a firefly gives off almost no heat, unlike an old light bulb.

teile.einleitung: Pollination is the process in which pollen gets from one flower to another so that seeds and fruit can form. The wind and many animals help with it, above all bees, bumblebees and butterflies. Without pollination there would be no apples, cherries or strawberries.
wichtigste: In pollination, pollen, the flower dust, lands on the stigma of a flower.
After that fertilisation can take place, and seeds and fruit form.
Many plants are pollinated by insects such as bees, bumblebees and butterflies.
Other plants such as grasses and hazel bushes are pollinated by the wind.
Bees and bumblebees collect nectar and in doing so carry pollen from flower to flower.
Pollen sticks especially well to the fur of bumblebees.
In Switzerland over 600 species of wild bee live that help with pollination.

abschnitte.text: Flowers have male and female parts. In the **stamens** the flower dust forms, also called **pollen**. The female part is called the pistil, and its sticky upper end is the **stigma**. When pollen lands on a stigma, this is called pollination. If the pollen comes from another plant of the same species, this is called cross-pollination.

After pollination a fine tube grows from the pollen grain down through the pistil. In this way the male cell reaches the egg cell in the ovary, and this is **fertilisation**. The fertilised egg cell becomes a seed. The ovary grows into the fruit, for example into an apple or a cherry. Without pollination many flowers stay without fruit.

Many flowers attract animals with colours, scent and sweet **nectar**. When a bee or bumblebee looks for nectar, pollen sticks to its body, and it carries it to the next flower. The fur of bumblebees is especially well suited for this. Butterflies, hoverflies and beetles also pollinate flowers. In other countries even hummingbirds and bats help with pollination.

Some plants do not need animals, because the **wind** spreads their pollen. These include grasses, cereals such as wheat and maize and trees such as hazel, birch and pine. Their flowers are usually inconspicuous and have no scent. Instead they produce huge amounts of light pollen. This pollen in the air triggers **hay fever** in many people in spring.

A large part of our food plants depend on pollinators, for example apples, cherries, strawberries, rapeseed and pumpkins. Most wild flowers, too, could not form seeds without pollination. That is why bees, bumblebees and butterflies are so important for plants and people. Unfortunately many insects are declining, because flower meadows and nesting places are missing and pesticides are used. Anyone who plants native flowers in the garden or on the balcony and lets a corner grow wild helps the **pollinators**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fine flower dust that contains the male cells of a plant.
The sticky upper part of the pistil on which the pollen lands.
A sweet juice in flowers with which plants attract insects.
The joining of a male and a female cell, from which a seed forms.

gewusst: Bumblebees can shake flowers by quickly vibrating their flight muscles so that the pollen falls out, which helps with tomatoes, for example.
Bees can see ultraviolet light and recognise patterns on flowers that are invisible to us.
In greenhouses, bred colonies of bumblebees are often used so that tomatoes form fruit.

teile.einleitung: A honeycomb is a structure made of thousands of small, hexagonal cells made of wax. In these cells young bees grow up, and the bees store honey and pollen in them. The hexagonal shape is so ingenious that people still copy it in technology today.
wichtigste: The cells of a honeycomb are hexagonal.
The combs are made of beeswax, which the bees produce themselves.
In the cells bees raise their brood and store honey and pollen.
Full honey cells are closed with a wax cap.
The hexagonal shape saves wax and still makes the comb very stable.
Drones grow up in larger cells than workers.
The honeycomb shape is also copied in aircraft construction and in packaging.

abschnitte.text: A **comb** is a vertical plate that is covered with cells on both sides. Each cell has six walls and an opening that points slightly upwards so that the honey does not run out. The walls are wafer-thin and made of **beeswax**. Between two combs the bees leave just enough space that they can walk past each other.

Hexagons fit together without gaps, without wasting space. At the same time you need less wall for hexagons than for squares or triangles of the same area. So the bees save valuable wax. In addition, the **hexagonal shape** is very stable, because the forces are distributed evenly. The mathematician Thomas Hales proved in 1999 that the hexagon pattern really is the most economical solution.

The cells are nursery and store room at once. In the **brood cell** the queen lays an egg, from which a larva and later a pupa develops. When the cell is filled with ripe honey, the bees close it with a wax cap. Pollen is packed into other cells and serves as protein food. Worker cells are about 5 millimetres wide, drone cells somewhat larger.

Beekeepers often give the bees wooden frames with a thin sheet of wax, the **foundation**. The hexagon pattern is already pressed into it, and the bees build the cells out further. For the honey harvest the wax cap is cut off. Then the combs are spun in a honey extractor so that the honey flies out. The bees can use the empty combs again.

Engineers copy the honeycomb because it is light and yet stable. **Honeycomb cores** made of aluminium, plastic or cardboard are found in aircraft wings, satellites, skis and doors. Many packages and lightweight boards also contain honeycomb patterns. In nature hexagons are also found in snowflakes and basalt columns.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plate of many hexagonal wax cells in the beehive.
A thin sheet of wax with a pressed hexagon pattern that beekeepers give to the bees.
A comb cell in which a young bee grows up from the egg to hatching.

gewusst: A comb made from a few grams of wax can carry many times its own weight in honey.
When building, bees measure the cell size with their antennae and legs.
Wasps also build hexagonal combs, but out of chewed wood.

teile.einleitung: Blue butterflies, in German called Bläulinge, are small butterflies whose wings often shimmer bright blue. In Switzerland you can often see them on flower meadows in summer. Some species have an astonishing friendship with ants.
wichtigste: Blues are small, often blue-shimmering butterflies.
They are common in Switzerland, above all on flower meadows.
Usually only the males are blue, the females often brown.
Their caterpillars often feed on clover and other legumes.
Many caterpillars live closely with ants.
Several species of blue are rare and endangered today.

abschnitte.text: Blues are small day-flying butterflies with a wingspan of usually 2 to 3.5 centimetres. The upper side of the wings is often bright blue in the **males**. The females are often brown with orange spots. The underside of the wings is grey or brownish and has many small dots that look like eyes. The blue colour arises not through pigment, but through tiny **scales** that bend the light.

Blues live on sunny meadows, pastures, woodland edges and banks. Especially many species are found on **nutrient-poor meadows**, which are little fertilised and have many flowers. In Switzerland several dozen species occur, from the valleys to high in the Alps. The **common blue** is one of the most frequent species.

The caterpillars of many blues feed on **legumes** such as clover, bird's-foot trefoil or vetches. The caterpillars look like small, flat woodlice. Many of them have glands from which a sweet juice comes. The butterflies themselves suck nectar from flowers and sometimes drink water with minerals at damp spots.

Ants like the sweet juice of the blue caterpillars and protect them from enemies in return. In the **large blue butterflies** this goes even further. Their caterpillars let ants carry them into the nest, because they smell like ant larvae. There they are fed or even eat the ant brood until they pupate.

Many species of blue have become rare in Switzerland. The reason is above all that flower-rich nutrient-poor meadows are disappearing, because they are fertilised, built over or no longer mown. Large blue butterflies are especially sensitive, because they need the right plant and the right species of ant. Protected areas and late-mown meadows help these butterflies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A butterfly that flies during the day.
A meadow with little fertiliser and many different flowers.
The larva of a butterfly.
When the caterpillar turns into a pupa from which the butterfly hatches.

gewusst: The blue colour of the blues is a trick of light on the scales and not a pigment.
Caterpillars of the large blue butterflies can deceive ants and have themselves fed in the ant nest.
Blues often sleep upside down on blades of grass, sometimes several side by side.

teile.einleitung: Anacondas are giant constrictor snakes from South America that spend a large part of their lives in the water. The green anaconda is regarded as the heaviest snake in the world. It is not venomous, but crushes its prey with its powerful body.
wichtigste: Anacondas belong to the genus Eunectes in the boa family.
Eunectes means “good swimmer” in Ancient Greek.
The green anaconda is the heaviest snake in the world.
Anacondas live in swamps, rivers and floodplains of South America.
They are not venomous and kill their prey by squeezing.
Anacondas give birth to live young.
In 2024 it was proposed to split the green anaconda into a northern and a southern species.

abschnitte.text: Anacondas make up the genus **Eunectes**, which means “good swimmer” in Ancient Greek. They belong to the boa family (Boidae). The best known are the giant or **green anaconda**, the smaller yellow anaconda and a few other, rare species. Carl Linnaeus was the first to describe the giant anaconda scientifically in 1758, then under the name Boa murina. Its species name murinus is usually interpreted today as “hunting mice”.

The green anaconda is olive green with large, dark spots. Its eyes and nostrils sit on top of its head, so it can breathe and look almost completely underwater. Females are much larger than males and can grow to over five metres long and weigh well over 70 kilograms. This makes it the **heaviest snake** in the world. The longest snake, however, is the reticulated python from Asia.

Anacondas live in tropical **South America** east of the Andes. They are found in the Amazon region, in the Orinoco basin, in the Llanos of Venezuela and Colombia, and the yellow anaconda in the Pantanal. They like slow-flowing rivers, swamps and flooded grasslands. In the water they move elegantly, on land they seem rather clumsy. In dry seasons they sometimes bury themselves in the mud.

Anacondas are **constrictors** and are not venomous. They lie in wait in the water, grab their prey with their mouth and coil around it in a flash. Then they squeeze until the animal dies, and swallow it whole. Large anacondas eat fish, birds, capybaras, caimans and even deer. After a large meal they often do not need to eat again for weeks.

At mating time, several males sometimes coil around one female at the same time, which is called a **mating ball**. Anacondas do not lay eggs but give birth to live young. A female usually gives birth to 20 to 40 young snakes, which are already more than half a metre long. The young are independent from the start and have to watch out for caimans and birds of prey.

The word **anaconda** originally referred to snakes in Sri Lanka, formerly Ceylon. According to one theory it comes from a Tamil expression meaning “elephant killer”. A study from 2024 showed that the northern and southern green anacondas differ by about 5.5 per cent in their mitochondrial DNA. Their lines separated about 10 million years ago. For the northern green anaconda the name **Eunectes akayima** was therefore proposed, and akayima means “big snake”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A snake that coils around its prey and crushes it instead of poisoning it.
A group of closely related species, for example all the anacondas.
The young are born fully developed and do not hatch from eggs in a nest.
The blueprint of a living thing, which is found in every cell.

gewusst: After a large meal, a female anaconda can fast for months.
Anacondas can stay underwater for about ten minutes without breathing.
Female anacondas sometimes eat a male after mating, because they need a lot of energy for the long pregnancy.

teile.einleitung: The white rhinoceros, in German called the Breitmaulnashorn or wide-mouthed rhinoceros, is a huge plant eater from Africa and, after the elephant, the largest land animal in the world. It is called “white” although its skin is in reality grey. With its wide mouth it mows the grass like a living lawnmower.
wichtigste: The white rhinoceros lives in Africa, above all in the southern part of the continent.
After the elephant it is the largest land animal in the world.
A large animal can weigh well over 2 tonnes.
Like most African rhinoceroses it has two horns.
It eats mainly short grass, which it plucks with its wide lips.
Its skin is grey, not white.
Because of poaching for its horn it is severely threatened.

abschnitte.text: The white rhinoceros has a massive body, short, strong legs and thick, grey skin. Large bulls grow about 1.8 metres high and can weigh up to about 3.5 tonnes, with the cows somewhat lighter. On the nose sit two **horns**, of which the front one is usually clearly longer. Typical too is a hump in the neck, in which strong muscles for the heavy head are found.

The white rhinoceros is a **grazer**. With its wide, straight lips it can pluck short grass especially well right at the ground. It usually carries its big head low, almost like a vacuum cleaner over the meadow. An adult animal eats many kilograms of grass every day and drinks, if possible, daily at a waterhole.

Most white rhinoceroses live in Africa, above all in **South Africa**, but also in Namibia, Zimbabwe and Kenya. They like open grass savannas with bushes, waterholes and mud holes. They like to wallow in the mud, because the layer of mud protects against the sun and annoying insects. There are two subspecies: the southern and the northern white rhinoceros.

Females often live with their young and other cows in small groups, while adult bulls are rather loners with a fixed **territory**. The bulls mark their territory with piles of dung and urine. The gestation lasts around 16 months, and then a single calf is born. The young usually walks ahead of the mother, while in the black rhinoceros the calf tends to stay behind its mother.

The biggest problem is **poaching**, because the horn is sold at a high price in some countries, although it consists only of keratin, like our fingernails. The southern white rhinoceros was almost wiped out around 1900, and thanks to strict protection there are again a few thousand animals today. Of the northern white rhinoceros only two females are left in Kenya, and the last male, called Sudan, died in 2018. Experts are trying to save the subspecies with the help of stored egg cells and sperm.

begriffe.erklaerung: A horn substance of which hair and fingernails are also made.
The illegal hunting of protected animals.
A group within an animal species that lives in a certain area and differs slightly.
Rolling in mud to protect the skin.

gewusst: The name “white rhinoceros” probably comes from a word for “wide”, which was wrongly translated as “white”.
Despite its weight, a white rhinoceros can briefly run as fast as about 40 kilometres per hour.
The horn of a rhinoceros is not made of bone and keeps growing all its life.

teile.einleitung: The African elephant, also called the bush elephant, is the largest and heaviest land animal in the world. A bull can grow up to 4 metres tall at the shoulder. It lives in savannas and forests south of the Sahara.
wichtigste: The African elephant is the largest land animal on Earth.
A bull grows up to 4 metres tall at the shoulder and weighs several tonnes.
Its ears are much larger than those of the Asian elephant.
The large ears serve mainly for cooling down.
Usually males and females both have tusks.
An adult elephant eats up to 150 kilograms of food a day.
Its sense of smell is very good, even better than that of a dog.
Young bulls leave the herd when they grow up.

abschnitte.text: A bull grows up to 4 metres tall and is often 6 tonnes in weight, while females are clearly smaller. Most striking are the huge ears, which are much larger than in the **Asian elephant**. The ears have the shape of the African continent, people say jokingly. In African elephants, both sexes usually carry **tusks**.

The ears are criss-crossed by many fine blood vessels. When the elephant fans with its ears, the blood in them cools down. In this way it can cool itself in the hot **savanna**. It also sprays itself with water or wallows in mud, which protects at the same time from sun and insects.

An adult elephant eats up to 150 kilograms of grass, leaves, bark, roots and fruit a day. For this it is busy eating for up to 16 hours a day. It often drinks over 100 litres of water a day. Its **molars** are replaced several times by new ones during its life.

A group of elephants is called a **herd**. It consists of related females and their young and is led by the oldest cow, the **matriarch**. Young bulls leave the herd when they grow up and roam alone or in bachelor groups. As a greeting, elephants twine their trunks together.

An elephant cow is pregnant for about 22 months, longer than any other land animal. At birth the calf weighs about 100 kilograms. At first it can hardly control its trunk and has to practise for a long time until it can move it skilfully. The whole herd helps to protect the calf.

Elephants spread seeds and create waterholes that other animals also use. They are therefore very important for their **ecosystem** in Africa. Because of poaching and loss of habitat, the African elephant is endangered. In Switzerland you can watch African elephants, for example, at Basel Zoo.

begriffe.erklaerung: The oldest and most experienced elephant cow, who leads the herd.
A male elephant.
Long incisor teeth made of ivory that stick out of the mouth.
A habitat with all the plants and animals that depend on one another.

gewusst: Through deep sounds that we cannot hear, elephants can talk to others of their kind several kilometres away.
Despite its size, an elephant can walk almost silently, because a soft cushion lies under its feet.
In the wild, elephants are often 60 years old and more.

teile.einleitung: Barry was a famous rescue dog from the hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass in Switzerland. He is said to have saved more than 40 people from snow and cold in his life. Today you can see him stuffed in the Natural History Museum in Bern.
wichtigste: Barry was a dog from the hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass.
He lived from 1800 to 1814.
He is said to have saved the lives of more than 40 people.
Barry is regarded as the ancestor and model of today's St Bernard dogs.
After his death he was preserved and is on display in the Natural History Museum in Bern.
The well-known story that he was killed by someone he had rescued is a legend.
To this day one dog of the St Bernard breeding programme always carries the name Barry.

abschnitte.text: Barry was a large dog who was born around **1800** in the hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass. The monks there kept dogs that helped them to search for travellers who had lost their way. Barry is said to have saved more than **40 people** in his life. He looked a little smaller and lighter than today's St Bernards.

The **Great St Bernard** is an Alpine pass in the canton of Valais on the border with Italy, at a height of about 2,470 metres. A hospice, a shelter for travellers run by monks, has stood there since the 11th century. In winter the pass is dangerous because of the heavy snow, fog and **avalanches**. From the 17th century at the latest, the monks kept large dogs that found their way in the snow and tracked down buried people.

The story is famous that Barry carried a child to safety on his back. Another legend tells that he was killed by a soldier who mistook him for a wolf. This story is not true, however. In reality a monk took the old Barry to **Bern** in 1812, where he died in 1814.

After his death Barry was preserved and put on display in the **Natural History Museum in Bern**. In 1923 the specimen was reworked and adapted to the appearance of St Bernards at that time. Barry is still one of the best-known exhibits of the museum. There is also a monument to him in a dogs' cemetery near Paris.

Barry is regarded as the most famous representative of the dogs from which the **St Bernard** breed arose. The St Bernard is today the national dog of Switzerland. Since 2005 the **Fondation Barry** has looked after the breeding of the St Bernards from the Great St Bernard. In Martigny in the Valais you can visit the dogs at the Barryland museum and learn more about Barry.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shelter on a pass in which travellers find protection and lodging.
A dog that tracks down buried or missing people.
A dead animal is made to last so that it looks lifelike.
A large Swiss breed of dog, named after the hospice on the Great St Bernard.

gewusst: The famous little barrel round the neck of St Bernards is an invention of painters and was never worn by the dogs on the pass.
On the Great St Bernard a dog is christened Barry again and again to recall the famous rescuer.

teile.einleitung: The Alpine salamander is a small, completely black tailed amphibian that lives in the mountains. It is a true specialist for the harsh climate of the Alps. The most astonishing thing about it: it gives birth to fully formed young and needs no water for it.
wichtigste: The Alpine salamander is glossy black and about 10 to 15 centimetres long.
It lives in damp mountain forests and on stony alpine pastures of the Alps and Pre-Alps.
It gives birth to live, fully developed young instead of larvae.
A pregnancy lasts two to three years, in great heights even longer.
Poisonous skin glands protect it from predators.
It eats insects, spiders, worms and small snails.
In Switzerland the Alpine salamander is protected.

abschnitte.text: The Alpine salamander (scientifically **Salamandra atra**) is deep black all over its body and shines when damp. It grows to about 10 to 15 centimetres long. Its short legs serve it for walking and climbing over stones. On the front legs it has four fingers, on the hind legs five toes. Behind the eyes sit two thick swellings, the **parotoid glands**, in which poison is produced.

The Alpine salamander lives in the **Alps** and some mountain ranges in the Balkans. It usually occurs between about 800 and 2,500 metres above sea level. It likes best damp mountain forests, stream banks and stony alpine pastures with many hiding places. Under stones, roots and in holes in the earth it finds shelter from sun and cold. It spends the winter in winter torpor deep in frost-free crevices.

The Alpine salamander needs moisture, because its skin must not dry out. When it gets very dry, it hides. It almost always avoids the hot midday hours. After a summer thunderstorm, by contrast, you often see many Alpine salamanders on hiking paths. That is why it is also called the **rain newt** in everyday speech.

The Alpine salamander eats insects, beetles, spiders, earthworms and small snails. In this way it helps to regulate small insect populations in the mountains. When threatened, it usually does not flee but stands still and calm. Its **skin poison** tastes bitter and irritates the mucous membranes of attackers. That is why most animals leave it in peace.

Unlike the fire salamander, the Alpine salamander does not lay its larvae in a stream. The young develop completely in the mother’s belly, which is called **live-bearing**. The gestation lasts two to three years, in very high places up to four years. At the end, usually only one or two fully formed little salamanders are born. Because it has so few offspring, populations recover only slowly after losses.

The Alpine salamander is **protected** in Switzerland, like all amphibians. You may watch it, but not catch it or take it away. Dangers for it are roads, drought and the destruction of damp hiding places. Anyone who sees it in nature should not touch it, because it then usually tries to escape slowly or stays motionless.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that can live mostly on land and in water, for example frogs, toads and salamanders.
The young grow in the mother’s body and are born fully formed.
Two swellings behind the eyes in which the salamander makes its poison.
A rigid resting state in the cold season in which the animal uses almost no energy.

gewusst: The Alpine salamander has one of the longest gestation periods of all vertebrates, longer than an elephant.
In the mother’s belly, the young feed on unfertilised eggs and a special nutritive layer.
An Alpine salamander can live to over 15 years old in the wild.

teile.einleitung: The Alpaufzug is the day in early summer on which cows, goats and other animals are brought up to the Alp. In many parts of Switzerland it is a ceremonial procession with bells, traditional costumes and flower decorations. For the farmers, the alpine summer begins with it.
wichtigste: When cows are brought up to the Alp in summer, it is called the Alpaufzug.
Bringing up herds of goats is also called the Alpaufzug.
It usually takes place in June, when enough grass is growing on the Alp.
Some cows wear an extra large flower decoration for the festival.
Other names are Alpauffahrt or, in French, Inalpe.
In the Appenzellerland, the Sennen walk along in colourful costume.
In the Valais, Eringer cows fight for the rank of queen.

abschnitte.text: In early summer, the grass in the valley has been eaten, and on the Alp the snow has melted. Then the farmers bring their animals up to the summer pasture. This journey is called the **Alpaufzug**, Alpauffahrt or, in French-speaking Switzerland, **Inalpe**. It usually takes place in June, and in higher places only at the beginning of July.

In the past all the animals walked on foot, often for many hours. Today some farmers take the animals up by lorry, but many still walk the last part in the traditional way. In the Appenzellerland, children often walk ahead with the goats, followed by the Senn and the cows with their **Schellen** (cowbells). At the end comes a wagon with household goods and the cheese cauldron.

For the festival at the Alpaufzug, some cows wear an extra large **flower decoration**. The Sennen put on their festive costume, in the Appenzellerland with yellow trousers and a red waistcoat. The ringing of the large bells can be heard across the whole valley. Often the Älpler sing a **Zäuerli** to go with it, a natural yodel without words.

In the Valais there is a special custom with the strong **Eringer cows**. When different herds come together on the Alp, the cows measure themselves against each other in harmless wrestling matches. They push each other with their heads until one gives way. The strongest becomes the **queen** of the Alp and leads the herd.

With the Alpaufzug, the summer work on the Alp begins. The Älpler milk every day and make **alpine cheese** from the milk. The animals usually stay up there for about 100 days. In autumn they then return to the valley in the Alpabzug.

begriffe.erklaerung: The French word for the Alpaufzug.
A small, strong breed of cattle from the Valais.
A natural yodel from the Appenzellerland.
A bell that cows wear round the neck.

gewusst: For the wrestling matches of the Eringer cows, there are even large competitions in the Valais with thousands of spectators.
Cows are often visibly pleased to go to the Alp and leap about when let out of the barn.
The Alpaufzug in the Appenzellerland is one of the best-known photo subjects in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The African wild ass is the wild ancestor of our domestic donkey. It lives in the hot, dry deserts of the Horn of Africa. Today it is one of the rarest mammals in the world.
wichtigste: Our domestic donkey descends from the African wild ass.
The wild ass lives in deserts and semi-deserts of north-eastern Africa.
Because its ancestors lived in deserts, donkeys are well adapted to dry, hot regions.
The Somali wild ass has striped legs like a zebra.
It belongs to the horses, like the zebra.
The African wild ass is threatened with extinction.
Probably only a few hundred animals are still left in the wild.

abschnitte.text: The African wild ass is about 1.2 metres tall at the shoulder and has grey to sandy fur. Its belly and legs are pale, and a dark **dorsal stripe** runs over its back. In the **Somali wild ass**, the legs are striped black and white like those of a zebra. With its long ears it hears very well and can give off excess heat.

It lives in stony deserts and semi-deserts in Eritrea, Ethiopia and perhaps still in Somalia. There it is very hot by day, and it hardly ever rains. The wild ass eats tough grasses and shrubs that other animals spurn. It can manage for a long time without water and then drinks a great deal at once.

Wild asses often live alone or in small, loose groups. The stallions defend a **territory** around a waterhole. Because the animals live far apart in the desert, they call over great distances with their loud bray. In danger they can run away fast and with stamina.

abschnitte.titel: From wild ass to domestic donkey
abschnitte.text: About 5,000 to 6,000 years ago, people in north-eastern Africa began to tame wild asses. From this arose the **domestic donkey**, which is still used as a pack animal today. Because its ancestors lived in deserts, it is frugal and well adapted to dry, hot regions. A donkey, by contrast, does not particularly like damp pastures and wet weather.

According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the African wild ass is **critically endangered**. It was hunted, and domestic donkeys and grazing livestock take away its water and food. It also interbreeds with feral domestic donkeys. In zoos, including Basel Zoo, Somali wild asses are kept in a **breeding programme** to preserve the species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dark stripe along the back.
The taming and breeding of wild animals into domestic animals.
A very dry area with sparse plants.
Zoos work together so that threatened animals have healthy offspring.

gewusst: The call of a donkey can be heard for kilometres.
Donkeys and horses can have offspring together, the mule, but it usually cannot have young itself.
The stripes on the legs of the Somali wild ass are a little different in every animal.

teile.einleitung: AMICUS is the national database in which all dogs in Switzerland must be registered. It states which dog belongs to whom. In this way a lost dog can quickly find its way back to its family.
wichtigste: AMICUS is the national dog register of Switzerland.
Every dog in Switzerland must be marked with a microchip and registered in AMICUS.
The database has been in operation since 2016.
In AMICUS, more than half a million dogs are registered.
Anyone who buys or takes over a dog or moves house must report it.
With the chip number, the keeper of a found dog is quickly traced.
The name comes from the Latin word amicus, which means “friend”.

abschnitte.text: **AMICUS** is a Switzerland-wide database for dogs. In 2016 it replaced several cantonal dog databases, for example ANIS. The cantons introduced AMICUS together. In the database, more than half a million dogs are recorded (as of about 2024). The name is Latin and means “friend”.

Every dog must be marked with a **microchip**. This is a tiny chip, about the size of a grain of rice, which the vet injects under the skin at the neck. This has to happen while the puppy is young and before it leaves the breeder. A number is stored on the chip, which can be read with a reader. This number is entered in AMICUS together with the details about the dog.

In AMICUS there are details about the dog such as name, breed, sex, date of birth and coat colour. In addition there are the contact details of the **keeper**. Vets and dog breeders are also recorded. Municipalities use the data to collect the **dog tax**. The data are protected and not publicly visible to everyone.

Anyone who takes over a dog must register with the municipality and have the dog registered to them in AMICUS. A move, sale, loss or death of the dog must also be reported, as a rule within ten days. Many details can be changed online by yourself. Anyone who does not fulfil their duties can be fined. For dogs that travel abroad, a **pet passport** is also needed.

If a runaway dog is found, a vet or the police can read the chip. Through AMICUS, the family the dog belongs to is then found at once. In the case of a dog bite, it can be established which dog was involved. In the case of an **animal disease**, the data help the authorities to act quickly. In addition, AMICUS shows which dog breeds are especially popular in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electronic collection of ordered information.
A tiny electronic chip under the skin with a personal number for the animal.
A charge that you pay to the municipality every year for your dog.
The person who is responsible for a dog.

gewusst: Cats can also be registered in a database, but for them this is voluntary in Switzerland.
A microchip has no battery, and it is supplied with energy briefly only by the reader.
The mixed breed is one of the most common registered dogs in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The St Bernard is a huge dog from Switzerland that became famous for rescuing people in the snow. Monks on the Great St Bernard bred it to find travellers in the mountains. Today it is the national dog of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The St Bernard is a Swiss breed of dog.
It was bred in the hospice on the Great St Bernard.
In the past it helped to find and rescue people in the snow and fog.
The most famous St Bernard was called Barry and rescued over 40 people.
St Bernards are among the heaviest breeds of dog in the world.
There is a short-haired and a long-haired variety.
It is regarded as the national dog of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The St Bernard is a very large, massive dog. Males grow to at least about 70 centimetres high and are often 70 to 90 kilograms in weight. Its fur is white with rusty brown patches or rusty brown with white markings. Typical are the large head, the dark **mask** around the eyes and the hanging lips. There are **short-haired** and long-haired St Bernards.

On the **Great St Bernard** in the Valais, at a height of 2,469 metres, a hospice has stood for about a thousand years. It was founded by Saint Bernard of Aosta, after whom the pass and the dog are named. The Augustinian canons took in travellers there who were crossing the dangerous pass between Switzerland and Italy. From the 17th century they kept large dogs. These accompanied the monks and helped to find people who had lost their way.

The most famous St Bernard was called **Barry** and lived in the hospice from 1800 to 1814. He is said to have saved the lives of over 40 people. After his death he was preserved and is now on display in the Natural History Museum in Bern. Barry, however, looked smaller and lighter than today's St Bernards. In his honour, one dog in the hospice was always given the name Barry.

St Bernards have a very good **sense of smell** and can track down people even under snow. In bad weather they went on patrol with the monks and found the way in the fog. The famous little barrel of brandy round the neck is, however, a **legend** that was invented mainly by painters. Today, lighter dogs such as shepherd dogs are mostly used for avalanche rescues. In addition, rescuers today often come by helicopter.

Since 2005 the **Fondation Barry** in Martigny has looked after the breeding of the hospice dogs. In summer some St Bernards live up at the hospice again, where visitors can see them. In Martigny there is also a museum about the dogs. St Bernards are calm, friendly and patient family dogs. Because of their size, however, they need a lot of space and unfortunately usually live to be only eight to ten years old.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shelter on a pass in which travellers find protection.
A large mass of snow that crashes down a mountainside.
The lips of a dog.
A community of priests who live together according to fixed rules.

gewusst: You can still visit Barry today in the Natural History Museum in Bern.
In the past the breed was also called the Barry dog.
The St Bernard is related to the Bernese mountain dog, and both descend from old Swiss farm dogs.

teile.einleitung: An Alp is a large pasture high in the mountains on which cows, sheep and goats spend the summer. There the Sennen or Älpler (herdsmen) look after the animals and often make alpine cheese. Alpine farming has been part of Swiss culture for centuries.
wichtigste: An Alp is a summer pasture in the mountains.
Cows, sheep and goats spend the summer there, usually about 100 days.
Whoever looks after the animals is called a Senn or Älpler.
On the Alp, sheep keep the grass short and look after the landscape.
Some alpine sheep wear a bell so that you can hear where they are.
In winter the animals live in the valley in the barn or on lower pastures.
On many Alps, alpine cheese is made from the fresh milk.

abschnitte.text: An Alp is a pasture high in the mountains, often between about 1,000 and 2,500 metres above sea level. It usually includes an **alpine hut** and a barn. In summer, fresh, strong grass with many herbs grows there. The time in which the animals are up there is called **summering**.

In early summer, cows, young cattle, goats and sheep are brought up in the Alpaufzug (the ascent to the Alp). Sheep are often out in higher and steeper places than the cows. Some wear a bell or **Treichel** (a large cowbell) so that they are easier to find and you can hear where they are. When it gets cold in autumn, all the animals return to the valley in the Alpabzug (the descent from the Alp).

Whoever looks after the cows on the Alp is called a **Senn** or Älpler, and a woman is called a Sennerin. The day begins very early with milking. After that the milk is often made straight into cheese. Many Älplerinnen and Älpler spend the whole summer up there every year, far from roads and shops.

From the milk of the alpine cows comes the tangy **alpine cheese**. It is traditionally made in a large cauldron over the fire. Well-known kinds are, for example, the Bernese alpine cheese or the L’Etivaz from the canton of Vaud. Because the cows eat alpine herbs, every alpine cheese tastes a little different.

The grazing animals keep the grass short and stop the meadows from becoming overgrown. Without them, bushes and forest would slowly take over the alpine pastures. In this way colourful **alpine meadows** with many flowers and insects are preserved. For walkers, too, the well-kept landscape is a reason to go to the mountains.

On many Alps there are old customs. In Catholic areas of central Switzerland, the Senn calls the **Alpsegen** (the alpine blessing) in the evening through a wooden funnel across the pastures. In autumn, at the Chästeilet (the cheese sharing), the cheese is divided among the farmers. The ascent and the descent are celebrated as a festival in many villages.

begriffe.erklaerung: The summer time in which the animals graze on the Alp.
A man who herds animals and makes cheese on the Alp.
A sung evening prayer that is called out across the Alp.
A large, forged bell for cows.

gewusst: The name of the Alps comes from the same word as the Alp.
For a cow, the way up to a steep Alp is real training, and some need several hours for it.
On some Alps, cheese is still made over an open fire today.

teile.einleitung: The red junglefowl is a wild chicken from the forests of South and South-East Asia. All our domestic chickens are descended from it, including the cockerels on Swiss farms. The wild male still looks very much like a colourful farmyard cockerel today.
wichtigste: The red junglefowl is the wild ancestor of our domestic chicken.
Its scientific name is Gallus gallus.
It lives in woods and thickets in South and South-East Asia.
The male is red-gold in colour and has a tail that shimmers black-green.
The hen is an inconspicuous brown and well camouflaged.
People tamed the red junglefowl several thousand years ago.

abschnitte.text: The **junglefowl cock** has splendid plumage with a red-gold neck, a dark belly and long tail feathers that shimmer black-green. On his head he has a red **comb** and under his beak red wattles. The hen is smaller, brown in colour and has only a small comb. Wild junglefowl are lighter and slimmer than most domestic chickens.

The red junglefowl lives in India, southern China and South-East Asia as far as Indonesia. It lives in woods, bamboo thickets and woodland edges. During the day it looks for food on the ground, and at night it sleeps in **trees** for safety. It can fly well, but usually flees by running into the thicket.

Junglefowl scratch the ground with their feet and eat seeds, grains, fruit, insects and worms. They live in small groups made up of one cock and several hens. The cock crows to mark his **territory** and keep other cocks away. The hen lays a few eggs in a hidden nest on the ground and incubates them alone.

abschnitte.titel: From wild fowl to domestic chicken
abschnitte.text: People tamed the red junglefowl several thousand years ago in **South-East Asia**. From there the **domestic chicken** spread across Asia, Africa and Europe. Through breeding, hundreds of breeds arose that lay far more eggs or provide more meat. While a wild hen lays only a few eggs a year, a laying hen today lays around 300 eggs a year.

The red junglefowl is still quite common in the wild. A problem, however, is that wild fowl often mate with free-ranging domestic chickens. As a result there are fewer and fewer **pure-bred** wild junglefowl. Researchers are therefore trying to preserve the true wild form.

begriffe.erklaerung: The wild species from which a domestic animal was bred.
Taming and breeding wild animals into domestic animals.
The red, serrated flap of skin on the head of chickens.
A group of domestic animals with shared, bred characteristics.

gewusst: There are now more chickens than people in the world, far more than 20 billion.
Chickens are close relatives of the dinosaurs, like all birds.
The red junglefowl is also called the red crested fowl.

teile.einleitung: Woodlice are small, grey animals with seven pairs of legs that you find under stones, leaves and wood. Although they live on land, they are not insects but crustaceans. In the garden they do important work as nature's refuse collectors.
wichtigste: Woodlice are crustaceans and form the order Isopoda, the “equal-footed” ones.
A full-grown land woodlouse has seven pairs of legs that look quite alike.
Land woodlice need moisture and are therefore mostly active at night and at dusk.
They break down dead plant parts and so help to form fertile humus.
The female carries her eggs in a brood pouch on her belly.
Woodlice are completely harmless to people, they can neither sting nor bite.

abschnitte.text: Woodlice are related to crabs and lobsters and belong to the **crustaceans**. The order is called **Isopoda**, in German “Gleichfüsser”, because their legs all look quite alike. Worldwide more than 10,000 species are known, most of which live in the sea or in fresh water. Land woodlice are one of the few groups of crustaceans that have conquered the land.

The body of a woodlouse is flat and covered with hard plates that look like armour. A grown-up land woodlouse walks on seven pairs of legs, and at the front it has two pairs of **antennae**, one of which is tiny. Well-known species in Switzerland are the **common rough woodlouse** and the common shiny woodlouse, which usually grow to one to two centimetres long. The pill woodlouse can roll itself up into a ball when in danger. When a woodlouse grows, it moults in two steps, first the rear and then the front half of the body.

Land woodlice breathe with gill-like organs on their rear legs, which have to stay moist. That is why during the day they hide under stones, bark, leaves or in cellars and only come out at night and at dusk. They often gather in **groups**, because it stays damper there and they are better protected. In dry air they would quickly dry out.

Woodlice eat mainly dead leaves, rotting wood and other plant remains. In doing so they break up the material, and their droppings are broken down further by bacteria and fungi. This produces **humus**, that is, fertile soil in which new plants grow well. Anyone who wants to encourage woodlice in the garden makes heaps of leaves and piles of dead wood and stones.

The female carries her eggs in a **brood pouch** on her belly, which is filled with liquid. The young hatch inside it and only leave the pouch as tiny, fully formed woodlice. Young woodlice at first have only six pairs of legs, and the seventh comes after the first moult. Their enemies include spiders, ground beetles, hedgehogs, shrews and birds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals with a hard shell to which crabs, lobsters and also woodlice belong.
The scientific name of woodlice, meaning equal-footed.
Dark, fertile soil that forms from broken-down plant and animal remains.
A pouch on the female's belly in which the eggs and young grow.

gewusst: The largest woodlice in the world live in the deep sea and can grow to about 50 centimetres long.
Woodlice moult in two halves, so you sometimes see animals that are pale at the back and dark at the front.
Woodlice do not only drink with their mouth, but can also take in water through their rear end.

teile.einleitung: Tapeworms are long, flat parasites that live in the intestines of people and animals. They have no mouth and no gut and take in their food through their whole body surface. Some species grow to several metres long.
wichtigste: Tapeworms belong to the animal phylum of flatworms and form the class Cestoda.
The name comes from the Greek word “kestos”, which means belt.
Several thousand species of tapeworm are known.
A tapeworm holds on in the intestine with its head, the scolex.
Its body consists of a chain of segments, the proglottids.
Tapeworms have no gut and take in food through their body surface.
Almost all tapeworms are hermaphrodites.

abschnitte.text: Tapeworms belong to the animal phylum of **flatworms** and form the class **Cestoda**. The name comes from the Greek word kestos, which means belt, because the worms are long and flat like a ribbon. Several thousand species are known. All are **parasites** that as adults mostly live in the intestines of vertebrates.

At the front sits the small head, the **scolex**, with suckers and, in some species, rings of hooks. With these the worm holds on to the intestinal wall. Behind it lies the neck zone, in which new segments are formed all the time. The whole chain of segments is called the **strobila**, and the individual segments are called **proglottids**.

Tapeworms have neither a mouth nor a gut. They take in their food over their whole body surface from the food pulp of their host. Their special, living body covering is called the **neodermis** or tegument. Tiny, bristle-like extensions, the **microtriches**, greatly increase the surface, much like the villi in our intestine.

Almost all tapeworms are **hermaphrodites**, so each segment has both male and female reproductive organs. The rear, ripe segments are full of eggs and break off. They reach the outside with the droppings. Many tapeworms need an **intermediate host**, such as a cow, a pig, a fish or a mouse, in which the larvae grow.

The beef tapeworm and the pork tapeworm can infect people if they eat raw or insufficiently cooked meat. The beef tapeworm can grow to several metres long. In the past the **fish tapeworm** was also widespread in Swiss lakes, which can be picked up through raw fish. Thanks to meat inspections and thorough cooking, an infection is rare today and can be treated well with medicines.

The **fox tapeworm** is only a few millimetres long, but can be dangerous for people. It lives in the intestines of foxes, sometimes also of dogs and cats, and its larvae normally grow up in mice. If a person happens to swallow eggs, the larvae can damage the liver. In Switzerland people are therefore advised to worm dogs regularly and to wash their hands after working in the garden or the woods.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that lives at the expense of another living thing.
The living thing in or on which a parasite lives.
The head of the tapeworm with suckers and hooks for holding on.
The individual segments of a tapeworm that contain eggs.
A living thing with male and female reproductive organs at the same time.

gewusst: A tapeworm can form new segments every day and so keeps growing.
The fish tapeworm is one of the longest parasites of humans and can grow to more than ten metres long.

teile.einleitung: Arthropleura was a giant, millipede-like arthropod that lived about 300 million years ago. It grew to more than two metres long and is regarded as the largest arthropod that ever lived on land. You can imagine it as a millipede as long as a car is wide.
wichtigste: Arthropleura was a prehistoric arthropod.
It grew to more than two metres long.
It lived in the Carboniferous and early Permian, about 345 to 290 million years ago.
It is related to today's millipedes.
Fossils have been found in Europe and North America.
It was the largest known land invertebrate of all time.
It probably fed mainly on plants.

abschnitte.text: Arthropleura was an **arthropod**, that is, an animal with an outer skeleton and jointed legs, like insects, spiders and crustaceans. Its body consisted of about 30 segments with armour plates. It was flat and broad and could grow to over two metres long and about half a metre wide. This makes it the largest known **invertebrate** that ever lived on land.

Arthropleura lived in the **Carboniferous** and the early Permian, about 345 to 290 million years ago. At that time a large part of Europe and North America lay near the equator. There were huge, damp swamp forests with tree-sized club mosses and horsetails. Coal later formed from these forests.

Complete skeletons of Arthropleura are very rare, and usually only parts of the armour are found. More common are fossilised **trackways**, that is, traces of its many legs in the mud. In 2018 an especially large piece of armour was discovered on the coast of northern England, which could have come from an animal about 2.6 metres long. At the end of 2024 researchers described for the first time well-preserved heads from France, which confirmed the relationship with the **millipedes**.

What Arthropleura ate is not entirely certain. Many researchers think it fed mainly on plant remains, spores and seeds. Perhaps it also ate smaller animals or carrion. Such a large animal probably had hardly any big enemies at that time.

In the Carboniferous the air contained more **oxygen** than today, by estimates more than 30 per cent instead of about 21 per cent. This may have made breathing easier for large arthropods. Relatives of dragonflies with wingspans of around 70 centimetres also lived then. In addition, there were not yet any large land vertebrates that competed with them for food or living space.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals with a hard outer shell and jointed legs, for example insects and spiders.
A period in the history of the Earth about 359 to 299 million years ago with large swamp forests.
Turned-to-stone remains or traces of living things from prehistoric times.
Without a backbone, like insects, worms or snails.

gewusst: Arthropleura was longer than a grown-up person is tall.
The name Arthropleura means roughly jointed sides.
Its tracks are sometimes almost half a metre wide.

teile.einleitung: Bruno was a young brown bear from Italy who in 2006 turned up in Germany as the first wild bear in over 170 years. With the scientific code he was called JJ1, and his brothers JJ2 and JJ3 later moved to Switzerland. The story of Bruno and his family shows how difficult coexistence between bear and people in the Alps can be.
wichtigste: Bruno was a brown bear with the code JJ1.
He was born in 2004 in the Adamello Brenta Nature Park in northern Italy.
His parents Jurka and Joze came from Slovenia and were brought to Italy for a reintroduction project.
In 2006 Bruno travelled across Austria to Bavaria.
Because he killed sheep and came close to houses, he was regarded as a “problem bear” and was shot in 2006.
His brothers JJ2 and JJ3 turned up in Switzerland, and JJ3 was shot in 2008 in the Grisons.
Today the preserved Bruno stands in a museum in Munich.

abschnitte.text: Bruno was a male **brown bear** who was born in 2004 in the Trentino region of northern Italy. Researchers gave him the name JJ1, because he was the first young of the she-bear Jurka and the bear Joze. The media in Germany called him Bruno, and under this name he became famous. He was a young bear who, like many young males, travelled far to look for a territory of his own.

In spring 2006 Bruno moved from Italy across Tyrol to **Bavaria**. He was thus the first wild-living bear in Germany since the year 1835. On the way he killed sheep, raided hen houses and beehives and sometimes came very close to villages. Because he showed no fear of people, politicians spoke of a “problem bear”.

At first people tried to catch Bruno alive with specialists and tracker dogs from Finland, but this did not succeed. At the end of June 2006 he was shot by hunters in the Bavarian Alps near Schliersee. Many people in Germany and Italy were sad or angry about it. Today Bruno is on display as a **preserved specimen** in the Museum Mensch und Natur in Munich.

Bruno's brother JJ2 migrated into Switzerland in 2005 and was the first bear in the country for almost a hundred years. Another brother, **JJ3**, stayed in the Grisons in 2007 and 2008 and kept coming into villages and settlements. Because he was classed as dangerous, he was shot in April 2008, which caused great stir in Switzerland. Since then individual young bears have kept coming from Italy into Switzerland.

The story shows that bears are finding room again in the Alps, but need good rules. It is important that bears do not find rubbish or animal feed, so that they do not get used to people. In Switzerland there are therefore bear-proof **rubbish containers** and protective measures for beehives and sheep. Whether a bear may be removed is laid down in a concept of the Confederation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large predator with brown fur that lives in forests of Europe, Asia and North America.
A bear that has lost its fear of people and looks for food in settlements.
A dead animal that has been made to last and is shown in a museum.
When animals are brought to an area where they used to be extinct.

gewusst: Bruno was the first wild bear in Germany since the year 1835.
Bruno's mother Jurka had apparently taught her young to look for food near people, which is why several of her young stood out.
Tracker dogs from Finland were specially brought to Bavaria to catch Bruno alive.

teile.einleitung: Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans, Bsal for short, is a tiny fungus that kills salamanders and newts. Its name means roughly “salamander eater”. Since it appeared in Europe, it has been a serious threat especially to fire salamanders.
wichtigste: Bsal is a chytrid fungus that attacks the skin of tailed amphibians.
It was discovered in 2013 after almost all the fire salamanders in an area of the Netherlands had died.
The fungus probably comes from Asia.
It was probably brought to Europe with newts from the pet trade.
After an infection, fire salamanders often die within a few days or weeks.
Clean shoes and equipment help to slow its spread.

abschnitte.text: Bsal is a microscopically small **fungus** from the group of chytrid fungi. It lives in water and in damp soil and forms moving spores. These penetrate the skin of **tailed amphibians** such as salamanders and newts. A close relative, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis or Bd, attacks mainly frogs and toads. Bd has already wiped out many frog species worldwide.

The fungus eats holes in the skin of the animals, and open wounds form. For amphibians the skin is vital, because they use it to breathe and take in water. Sick animals become weak, stop eating and soon die. In the **fire salamander** an infection almost always ends in death. Some species of newt, on the other hand, can survive the disease and carry the fungus on.

In the Netherlands the population of fire salamanders collapsed almost completely from about 2010. Researchers looked for the cause and in 2013 described the new fungus. Studies showed that it comes from East Asia. There live newts that exist alongside it without becoming ill. It probably reached Europe through the **pet trade** in such newts.

Today Bsal has been found in the Netherlands, in Belgium, in parts of Germany and in Spain. In Germany, for example, the Eifel and the Ruhr area are affected. Switzerland is watching the situation closely, because many fire salamanders live here too. Experts examine dead salamanders in order to spot an **infection** early. The EU and Switzerland have issued rules for the trade in tailed amphibians.

Anyone who is out in the woods by streams and ponds should clean their shoes well afterwards and let them dry. You should not touch salamanders and newts or move them from one place to another. Pets from a terrarium must never be released. If you find dead salamanders, you can report this to an agency for **amphibian protection**. These simple rules help to protect the threatened animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of tiny fungi that live in water and have moving spores.
Amphibians with a tail, that is salamanders and newts.
A tiny seed-like cell from which a new fungus can grow.
Animals such as frogs and salamanders that live on land and in water.

gewusst: In one area of the Netherlands only about one per cent of the fire salamanders survived.
The scientific name salamandrivorans means “devouring salamanders” when translated.
Bsal can survive in water and in damp soil for a long time.

teile.einleitung: The olive baboon is a large species of monkey from Africa that is named after the Egyptian god Anubis. Its long, dog-like snout is reminiscent of the god's jackal head. It lives in large groups and is the most widespread species of baboon.
wichtigste: The olive baboon is also called the Anubis baboon, after the Egyptian god Anubis.
Because of its olive-greenish fur it is also called the green baboon.
It lives in a broad belt across Africa south of the Sahara.
Olive baboons live in groups that often number several dozen animals.
They eat almost anything: grass, fruit, seeds, insects and small animals.
The males are much larger than the females and have a mane.
The species is not considered endangered today.

abschnitte.text: The olive baboon has dense, grey-brown fur with an **olive-green** sheen. Its face is dark and bare, and the snout is long like a dog's. The males have a mane on the head and shoulders and large canine teeth. They can weigh more than 20 kilograms and are almost twice as heavy as the females. The tail looks as if it were bent in the middle.

Olive baboons live in a broad band from Mali in West Africa to Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania. They are found in **savannas**, open woodland, steppes and even in mountains. This gives them the largest range of all baboons. At night they like to sleep on tall trees or rocks, where they are safe from predators.

Baboons are **omnivores** and very adaptable. They eat grasses, roots, fruit, seeds and tubers. In addition they eat insects, eggs and sometimes small mammals such as young antelopes. Because they are so clever, in some areas they also raid fields and rubbish tips.

Olive baboons live in **troops** made up of several males, many females and their young. In a group there is a clear pecking order. Grooming each other, called **picking lice**, strengthens the friendships between the animals. The females usually stay in the group they were born in for their whole lives, while the males leave as young adults.

The name recalls **Anubis**, the jackal-headed god of the dead of the ancient Egyptians. The sacred baboon of the Egyptians, however, was a relative, the hamadryas baboon, which was linked with the god Thoth. In Ethiopia olive baboons and hamadryas baboons meet and sometimes have young together. In all, six species of baboon are distinguished.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large monkey from Africa that lives on the ground and has a long snout.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
A larger group of monkeys that live and travel together.
The order of who is stronger in a group and gets to eat first.

gewusst: A troop of olive baboons can number more than 100 animals.
Baboons communicate with many different sounds, facial expressions and gestures.
When a baboon yawns and shows its canine teeth, it is often a threat.

teile.einleitung: Ants are small insects that live in huge, well-organised colonies. Each animal has its task, and together they build nests, look for food and defend their colony. There are more than ten thousand species of ants, and you find them almost everywhere in the world.
wichtigste: Ants mostly live in large colonies with one or several queens.
The queen lays almost all the eggs, and most animals in the colony are workers.
Worldwide there are over ten thousand species of ants.
An ant can carry many times its own weight.
Ants communicate mainly with scent substances.
A larva hatches from the egg and pupates before a finished ant arises.
Ants have no ears, they sense vibrations.

abschnitte.text: Ants are mostly only a few millimetres in size, but there are tropical species of over three centimetres. Their body consists, as in all **insects**, of head, thorax and abdomen, and they have six legs. Typical is the narrow “waist” between thorax and abdomen. With their bent **antennae** they smell and feel. Ants have no ears, and they sense vibrations with their legs. Ants are related to wasps and bees.

Ants live in **colonies**, also called an ant state or a nation. The queen lays almost all the eggs. Most animals are workers, which are infertile females. The tasks are shared out: some look after the brood, others work on the nest, still others look for food outside or defend the colony. Males exist only at certain times, and they die soon after mating.

Ants go through a **complete metamorphosis**, like butterflies. From the egg hatches first a white, maggot-like larva without legs. The workers feed and clean the larvae. After that the larva becomes a **pupa**, and some species spin a cocoon for this. The well-known “ant eggs”, which ants carry away in danger, are mostly such pupae.

Ants like to eat other small insects, spiders and dead animals. Many species also love sweet things such as nectar and **honeydew**. This is the sweet juice that aphids give off. Ants therefore protect the aphids and “milk” them with their antennae. In South America, leafcutter ants even grow fungi on chewed-up leaves.

An ant can carry many times its own weight, some species more than ten times. When a worker finds food, she lays a trail to the nest with **scent substances**. The others follow this scent trail, and so long ant trails arise. Many species defend themselves with bites, stings or by squirting **formic acid**. Together, ants are so strong that they can overpower much larger prey.

In Switzerland there live well over a hundred species of ants. Their nests can be found in the forest, in meadows, under stones and in the garden. Well known are the large mounds of the **red wood ant**, made of needles and twigs, which can grow over a metre high. Wood ants are protected in Switzerland, because they eat many pest insects and spread plant seeds. The black garden ant often also occurs in gardens and on terraces.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large community of animals of the same species that lives together and shares the work.
An infertile female ant that looks for food, builds and looks after the brood.
Sweet juice that aphids give off and that ants like to eat.
A sharp liquid with which some ants defend themselves against enemies.
A resting stage in which the larva transforms into a finished ant.

gewusst: Researchers estimate that around 20 quadrillion ants live on Earth, which is over two million per human.
Some birds deliberately sit on anthills so that the formic acid drives parasites out of their feathers.
Ants have existed for over 100 million years, so they were already alive in the time of the dinosaurs.

teile.einleitung: Macaws are large, brightly coloured parrots from Central and South America with long tails and powerful beaks. They include the hyacinth macaw, the largest flying parrot in the world. With their loud calls and bright colours they are among the best-known birds of the rainforest.
wichtigste: Macaws are long-tailed parrots of the New World and belong to the tribe Arini.
Six genera are usually counted as macaws.
Typical is bare or hardly feathered facial skin.
Like all parrots, they have two toes pointing forwards and two pointing backwards.
In the species of the genus Ara, males and females look almost the same.
The hyacinth macaw is the largest flying parrot in the world.
Many macaw species are threatened by deforestation and the animal trade.

abschnitte.text: Macaws have colourful plumage in red, blue, yellow or green and a long, pointed tail. A typical feature is the bare or hardly feathered **facial skin** around the eyes. Their strong, curved beak can crack even hard nuts. The toes are arranged in **pairs**: two point forwards and two point backwards. In the species of the genus Ara, both sexes look almost the same.

Macaws live from Mexico to Argentina. Most species live in **tropical rainforests**, some also in savannas and palm groves. In Peru and Brazil, dozens of macaws often gather at clay walls on river banks and eat soil there. The minerals in the soil probably help them to neutralise poisons from unripe fruit.

Macaws are counted in the **tribe Arini**, the long-tailed New World parrots within the true parrots. Usually six genera are distinguished, including Ara, Anodorhynchus and Cyanopsitta. Well-known species are the scarlet macaw, the blue-and-yellow macaw and the red-and-green macaw. The name “Ara” comes from an Indigenous language of South America and imitates the call of the birds.

The **hyacinth macaw** from the genus Anodorhynchus is the largest flying parrot in the world. It grows to around 1 metre long and can weigh up to about 1.7 kilograms. Its plumage is cobalt blue, and only a ring around the eye and a strip of skin under the beak glow yellow. Only the flightless **kakapo** from New Zealand is heavier. The hyacinth macaw lives mainly in the Pantanal in Brazil and eats hard palm nuts.

Macaws mostly live in pairs, which often stay together for life. They nest in **tree holes** or rock crevices and usually lay two to three eggs. Several pairs often join together in flocks and fly over the forest calling loudly. Macaws can live to a great age, sometimes more than 50 years in human care.

Many macaw species are threatened by the clearing of forests and the illegal **animal trade**. Around the year 2000 the Spix's macaw was considered extinct in the wild. Thanks to breeding programmes, Spix's macaws could be released again in Brazil from 2022. International trade in macaws is strictly regulated by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES, also called the Washington Convention).

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird with a curved beak and gripping feet that can often imitate sounds.
A group of closely related genera in the classification of living things.
A group of very closely related species.
Two toes pointing forwards and two pointing backwards, as in all parrots.

gewusst: Macaws use their foot like a hand and hold food to their beak with it.
The Spix's macaw became known around the world through the animated film “Rio”.
The beak of a hyacinth macaw is so strong that it can crack coconuts.

teile.einleitung: The Basenji is a small, slim hunting dog from Central Africa that has a special feature: it does not bark. It is regarded as one of the oldest breeds of dog still in existence. With its wrinkled forehead and curled tail it looks quite unmistakable.
wichtigste: The Basenji comes from the Congo Basin in Central Africa.
It is regarded as one of the oldest breeds of dog still in existence.
Instead of barking, it makes yodelling and howling sounds.
Typical are the forehead wrinkles and the tightly curled tail.
It is about 40 to 43 centimetres tall and weighs about 10 to 11 kilograms.
It cleans itself as thoroughly as a cat.

abschnitte.text: The Basenji is a small, light dog with short, shiny fur. Common colours are red and white, black and white or tricolour. It has upright, pointed ears and a wrinkled forehead that gives it a thoughtful expression. Its tail is tightly **curled** over its back. It moves elegantly and quickly like a small antelope.

The Basenji comes from the forests in the area of the **Congo** in Central Africa. There the dogs helped people to hunt and drove game into nets. Genetic studies show that the Basenji, like the Saluki, is one of the **most ancient breeds of dog**. In the 1930s Basenjis were brought to England and bred further there. From there the breed spread to many countries.

abschnitte.titel: The dog that does not bark
abschnitte.text: A Basenji cannot bark properly because of the shape of its larynx. Instead it makes yodelling, singing sounds that some call a **barroo**. It can certainly growl, whine and howl, though. So it is not entirely silent. For people who do not want a yapping dog, this is still an advantage.

Basenjis are clever, curious and very independent. They have a strong **hunting instinct** and sometimes simply run off when they pick up a scent. They therefore need patient and consistent training. Because they have a lot of energy, they need long walks and exercise every day. They like to clean themselves and hardly smell of dog.

abschnitte.titel: A dog of the primitive type
abschnitte.text: In the Basenji some features of the wolf are still preserved. The females come into season only once a year, while most other breeds of dog do so twice. The international dog organisation **FCI** places it in the group of Spitz and primitive-type dogs. In Switzerland, too, there are breeders and fans of this rare breed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of dogs with the same appearance and similar nature that is deliberately bred.
Dogs that are still especially similar to the early domestic dogs.
The inborn urge to chase animals.
The worldwide umbrella organisation of dog breeders that lays down breeds.

gewusst: The name Basenji comes from a Bantu language and is often translated as “little wild thing” or “bush dog”.
In ancient Egyptian pictures you can see dogs that look very much like the Basenji.
Basenjis sometimes climb skilfully over fences.

teile.einleitung: The Alpine marmot is a rodent that lives high in the mountains in burrows it digs itself. It is known for its loud warning whistle and its long hibernation. In the Swiss Alps you can often watch it on sunny rocks in summer.
wichtigste: The Alpine marmot lives mainly in the Alps and in neighbouring mountain ranges.
It belongs to the rodents and is related to squirrels.
Marmots live in family colonies with several animals.
They dig living burrows, escape burrows and winter burrows.
In winter they hibernate for a long time.
During this, their heart beats much more slowly than usual.
In danger they warn each other with a shrill whistle.
A marmot mother usually has two to four young.

abschnitte.text: The Alpine marmot is a plump rodent with greyish-brown fur. It grows to about 50 centimetres long, plus a short, bushy tail. With its strong claws it can dig well. Its large, orange **incisors** keep growing throughout its life.
