Alpine marmots live mainly in the Alps and neighbouring mountain ranges, usually between about 1,300 and 2,700 metres. They like alpine pastures and meadows above the tree line. For their burrows they prefer loose but stable soil on **sunny slopes**. In Switzerland they are widespread throughout the Alps.

A marmot digs different kinds of burrows. In the **living burrow** the family lives in summer, and in small **escape burrows** it hides quickly when in danger. The **winter burrow** lies deeper in the ground so that it does not freeze there. It lines the sleeping chamber with dry grass.

In winter, marmots find hardly any food, so they **hibernate** from about October to April. The whole family snuggles tightly together for this. Their heart then beats much more slowly than usual, and their body temperature falls sharply. In this way they save energy and live off the fat that they ate up over the summer.

Marmots live in **family colonies** with several animals, often a steady pair with their young of the last few years. In early summer, the mother usually has two to four young. In sunshine the animals like to warm themselves sitting upright on rocks. Mostly they stroll about at a leisurely pace on four legs.

The greatest enemies are **golden eagles** and foxes. If a marmot discovers a danger, it lets out a shrill whistle, and all run to their burrows. When walkers approach, marmots watch attentively and flee only when you come too close. Anyone who stays quiet and keeps their distance can therefore observe them well.

begriffe.erklaerung: A deep sleep over the winter in which the body almost completely shuts down.
A mammal with incisors that keep growing, like a mouse or beaver.
A group of animals that lives together in an area.
An underground living cave with tunnels.

gewusst: During hibernation, a marmot loses a large part of its body weight.
The whistle is made not with the lips but in the larynx.
Marmots spend up to half a year in hibernation.

teile.einleitung: Aquaculture means deliberately raising fish, shellfish, crustaceans or algae in tanks, ponds or net pens. You can think of it as farming under water. Today about half of all fish eaten around the world already come from such farms.
wichtigste: Aquaculture is the farming of water animals and water plants.
Farmed species include salmon, trout, carp, prawns and mussels.
Perch are raised not only in lakes but also in fish farms with recirculating water systems.
Worldwide, about half of the fish eaten now come from aquaculture.
China is by far the biggest producer.
Aquaculture can relieve the pressure on the seas, but it also brings environmental problems.
Quality labels help shoppers to recognise responsibly farmed fish.

abschnitte.text: In **aquaculture**, animals and plants that live in water are fed and looked after by people. The word comes from the Latin “aqua” for water and “cultura” for cultivation. There are farms in fresh water, for example for trout and carp, and in the sea, for example for salmon and mussels. Algae are also grown in large quantities.

There are different kinds of fish farm. In **ponds**, carp grow up almost as they do in nature. In the sea, salmon swim in large **net pens** off the coast, for example in Norway. In closed **recirculating systems** the water is cleaned and used again and again, so that hardly any fresh water is needed.

In Switzerland mainly **trout** are farmed, often in facilities beside cool, clean streams. Perch are raised not only in lakes but also in fish farms with recirculating water systems. In the Tropenhaus Frutigen in the Bernese Oberland, sturgeon live in water that comes out warm from the Lötschberg Base Tunnel, and caviar is obtained from their eggs. Even so, most of the fish eaten in Switzerland come from abroad.

Because many seas are overfished, aquaculture is becoming more and more important. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), around 2022 for the first time more water animals were farmed than caught. **China** produces more than half of all farmed fish in the world. India, Indonesia, Vietnam and Norway are also important countries.

When very many fish live in a small space, diseases and parasites can spread quickly. Medicines are then sometimes used, and these get into the water. For prawn farms, large areas of **mangrove forest** were cut down in Asia. Quality labels such as ASC or organic show that stricter rules for the environment and animal welfare apply to a farm.

begriffe.erklaerung: The farming of fish, shellfish, crustaceans or algae by people.
A fish farm in which the water is cleaned and used again and again.
A large net cage in the sea or a lake in which fish are kept.
When more fish are caught than can grow back.

gewusst: More than 2,000 years ago the Chinese were already keeping carp in ponds.
In the Middle Ages, monasteries in Europe built fish ponds so that they could eat fish during Lent.
Part of the feed for farmed salmon consists of fishmeal, which is made from wild-caught fish.

teile.einleitung: The Asiatic lion is a population of lions that today lives only in the west of India. In the past lions also roamed through the Near East and even south-eastern Europe. Today India is the only country outside Africa where there are still wild lions.
wichtigste: In India there is still a small population of lions outside Africa.
The lions live in the state of Gujarat around Gir National Park.
In a count in 2025 about 890 Asiatic lions were counted.
Around 1900 there were only a very few left, perhaps about 20 animals.
Asiatic lions have a smaller mane and a fold of skin along the belly.
Strict protection has allowed the population to recover.
Zurich Zoo keeps Asiatic lions.

abschnitte.text: Asiatic lions are a little smaller than many African lions. The males usually have a shorter, looser **mane**, so that their ears remain clearly visible. A lengthways fold of skin on the belly is typical. A male weighs about 160 to 190 kilograms, a female considerably less.

In the past lions lived from Greece through Turkey and the Near East to India. Through hunting they disappeared in most countries. Today they live only in the state of **Gujarat** in the west of India, around **Gir National Park**. In the count of 2025 there were about 890 animals, after about 670 in 2020.

Asiatic lions live in prides that are usually smaller than in Africa. Often females live together with their young, while the males form groups of their own and join them only for mating. They hunt mainly deer such as the **chital** and the sambar, as well as wild boar. Sometimes they also kill cattle belonging to the herders who live in the area.

Around 1900 only a very few lions were left, estimates speak of about 20 animals. The Nawab of Junagadh, to whom the area belonged, put them under protection. In 1965 the Gir protected area was founded. Because all the lions live in one region, however, an epidemic could be dangerous, and so settling them at a second place is being discussed.

In India the lion is an important **symbol**. The national emblem of India shows the Lion Capital of the emperor Ashoka with four lions. In Europe, Asiatic lions are kept in zoos in a **breeding programme**. In Switzerland they live in Zurich Zoo in a facility modelled on the Gir forest.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the animals of a species that live together in a certain area.
A group of lions that lives and hunts together.
A large protected area for nature and animals.
The long hair on the head and neck of male lions.

gewusst: In the Gir area, lions and herders with their cattle have lived close to each other for a long time.
In ancient times there were also lions in Greece.
Genetically, the Indian lions are closely related to the lions of West and Central Africa.

teile.einleitung: The bearded vulture is one of the largest birds of the Alps and a real specialist: it eats almost only bones. For a long time it was wiped out in the Alps. Thanks to a large protection project it now soars over the Swiss mountains again.
wichtigste: The bearded vulture has a wingspan of about 2.5 to 2.9 metres.
An adult bearded vulture weighs about five to seven kilograms.
It eats mostly bones and bone marrow.
Unlike many vultures it has a feathered head and a black beard of feathers under the beak.
In Switzerland the first bearded vultures were released in the Swiss National Park in 1991.
Male and female take turns to incubate the eggs, and do so in the middle of winter.
Besides the Alps it lives, for example, in the Pyrenees, in the Himalayas and in Ethiopia.

abschnitte.text: The bearded vulture is a mighty bird of prey with long, narrow wings and a wedge-shaped tail. Its head is feathered, unlike in many other **vultures**, which have a bare head. Under the beak grow black bristle feathers, the **beard**, which gives it its name. The breast and belly of adult birds are often coloured rusty red. This colour does not come from the feathers themselves, but from iron-rich mud in which the bird bathes.

The bearded vulture eats mostly **bones** and bone marrow, and compared with other vultures it is much more specialised in this. It uses the remains of dead chamois, ibex or sheep that other animals leave behind. Its stomach acid is extremely strong and can dissolve bones. Bones that are too big it drops from the air onto rocks until they break. Such rock slabs are called **bone forges**.

Bearded vultures live in high, rocky mountains with open pastures and steep rock faces. They are found in the Alps, the Pyrenees, on Corsica and Crete, in the Himalayas and in Ethiopia. When flying they glide for a long time without flapping their wings, using updrafts on the mountain slopes. In this way they save energy and can search huge areas for food. Because they remove carcass remains that would otherwise be left lying, they are important for the **ecosystem** of the mountains.

The bearded vulture builds its large nest in rock niches. It lays its eggs in winter, usually between December and February, so much earlier than most birds. The female lays one or two eggs, and male and female take turns to **incubate** them for about eight weeks. Usually only one chick survives. It hatches in spring, when through the snow many animals have died and there are plenty of bones.

In the past people wrongly believed that the bearded vulture stole lambs or even children, and called it the **lamb vulture** (“Lämmergeier”). That is why it was hunted and was wiped out in the Alps at the beginning of the 20th century. From 1986 an international **reintroduction project** began, and in 1991 the first young bearded vultures were released in the Swiss National Park. Since then several hundred animals have been released in the Alps. Today bearded vultures breed again in the Grisons, in the Valais and in other Alpine areas.

begriffe.erklaerung: The flesh and remains of dead animals.
Animals from a breeding programme are set free in the wild.
A rock slab onto which the bearded vulture drops bones so that they break.
Rising warm air in which birds glide upwards without flapping their wings.

gewusst: A bearded vulture can swallow bones that are as long as a forearm.
In breeding stations bearded vultures can live to be more than 40 years old.
Young bearded vultures are dark brown and only get their pale adult plumage after about five to seven years.

teile.einleitung: Lake Constance, in German the Bodensee, is one of the largest lakes in central Europe and lies between Switzerland, Germany and Austria. It is a habitat for many fish, mussels and hundreds of thousands of water birds. For whitefish, lake trout and other animals it is a very special home.
wichtigste: Lake Constance borders Switzerland, Germany and Austria.
It is about 536 square kilometres in size and up to 251 metres deep.
The Rhine flows through Lake Constance.
About 30 native species of fish live in the lake, including Blaufelchen and lake trout.
The lake is poorer in nutrients today than in the past, so less plankton grows.
That is why professional fishers today catch fewer whitefish than in the past.
In winter hundreds of thousands of water birds rest at the lake.

abschnitte.text: Lake Constance lies on the northern edge of the Alps. It is bordered by Switzerland with the cantons of **Thurgau** and St Gallen, by Germany and by Austria. It consists of the large **Upper Lake** (Obersee) and the smaller Lower Lake (Untersee). With around 536 square kilometres it is, after Lake Geneva and Lake Balaton, one of the largest lakes in central Europe. At its deepest point it measures 251 metres.

The **Alpine Rhine** flows into the lake at Bregenz and brings water from the mountains of the Grisons and Vorarlberg. At Stein am Rhein the Rhine flows out again as the High Rhine. The water of Lake Constance is so clean that it is used as **drinking water** for several million people. In the depths the water is only about 4 degrees cold all year round.

About 30 native species of fish live in Lake Constance. Best known is the **Blaufelchen**, the most important food fish of the professional fishers. Added to these are perch, pike, burbot, eel and the **lake trout**, which swims up into the rivers to spawn. Some species such as the Bodensee-Kilch have unfortunately died out.

In the 1950s to 1970s a lot of sewage and fertiliser got into the lake. Algae grew strongly, and oxygen was lacking in the depths. Thanks to **sewage treatment plants** the lake is clean again today and poor in nutrients. Because less plankton grows as a result, the whitefish also find less food, and catches have fallen sharply. In addition, introduced species such as the **stickleback** and the quagga mussel have spread.

abschnitte.titel: Birds and nature on the shore
abschnitte.text: Lake Constance is one of the most important areas for **water birds** in central Europe. In winter hundreds of thousands of ducks, grebes and coots from the north rest here. In reed beds and reed meadows such as in the Rhine delta rare bird species breed. Cormorants also fish in the lake, which fishers and conservationists often argue about.

Around Lake Constance lie towns such as Constance, Bregenz, Lindau, Friedrichshafen, Kreuzlingen and Romanshorn. Scheduled ships link the three countries. Well-known destinations are the flower island of **Mainau** and the monastery island of Reichenau, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In summer the lake is popular for swimming, sailing and fishing.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who earns their living by fishing.
Tiny plants and animals that drift in the water.
An animal or plant that has been brought by people into a new area.
A plant that cleans waste water before it gets into rivers and lakes.

gewusst: Between the three countries there is no precisely fixed border in the water of the Upper Lake.
Lake Constance is also called the “Swabian Sea” in popular speech.
In very cold winters Lake Constance can freeze over completely, which last happened in 1963.

teile.einleitung: The hobby is a slim, very fast falcon that catches its prey in flight. It hunts dragonflies, swallows and even swifts. In summer it also breeds in Switzerland, and it spends the winter in Africa.
wichtigste: The hobby is about as big as a pigeon, but much slimmer.
It has long, sickle-shaped wings and is an excellent flier.
Typical features are the dark moustache stripe and the rust-red “trousers” on the legs.
It catches dragonflies and other insects in flight and often eats them straight away in the air.
It also hunts small birds such as swallows in flight.
It is a migratory bird and spends the winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
It does not build its own nest but uses old nests of crows.

abschnitte.text: The hobby grows to about 30 to 36 centimetres long, and its wingspan is about 70 to 84 centimetres. The back is dark slate grey, and the pale breast has dark streaks lengthways. On the head it has a clear black **moustache stripe**. The feathers on the legs and under the tail are rust red. In flight, with its long, pointed wings, it is reminiscent of a large **swift**.

The hobby is an **aerial hunter**: it catches almost all its prey in the air. It grabs dragonflies and beetles with its talons and often eats them still in flight. For dragonflies it is one of the most important predators. In summer it also hunts fast birds such as barn swallows, house martins, skylarks and swifts. Occasionally it even catches bats at dusk.

Hobbies live in open landscapes with woodland edges, single groups of trees, waters and wetlands. They breed in old **crows' nests** high up in trees or on electricity pylons. Breeding starts late, usually in June. That way the young hatch just when many young, inexperienced swallows and many large insects are on the wing. The female usually lays two to three eggs.

The hobby is a **migratory bird** and returns from Africa only at the end of April or in May. In August and September it flies south again. It spends the winter in Africa south of the Sahara, where it feeds on termites and other insects. In doing so it covers thousands of kilometres every year. Its summer range extends from Europe far into Asia.

In Switzerland the hobby is a rather rare breeding bird. It lives mainly in the Central Plateau and at lower altitudes, often near lakes and rivers. You often see it when it hunts for **dragonflies** over water. Because it depends on many large insects, it suffers from the decline in insects. In Switzerland, like all birds of prey, it is **protected**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird of prey with pointed wings that usually flies very fast.
A dark stripe on the head below the eye that looks like a moustache.
A bird that flies back and forth every year between its breeding area and winter quarters.
An animal that catches its prey in flight.

gewusst: The hobby is so agile that it can even catch the lightning-fast swifts.
In German it gets its name “Baumfalke” (tree falcon) because it breeds in trees, not because it hunts in the forest.
Young hobbies often learn to hunt first with dragonflies.

teile.einleitung: Flat-backed millipedes are a large group of diplopods, that is, millipedes with two pairs of legs per body ring. Typical are the side extensions of the body, which look like flat plates. They live hidden in damp leaf litter and help to break down dead plants.
wichtigste: Flat-backed millipedes are diplopods with plate-like extensions on the sides of the body.
Their scientific name is Polydesmida.
With several thousand species they are the largest order of diplopods.
Flat-backed millipedes have no eyes.
Many species defend themselves with poisonous hydrogen cyanide.
They eat rotting plant parts and are important for the soil.

abschnitte.text: Flat-backed millipedes belong to the **diplopods**, a group of the millipedes. In diplopods almost every body ring carries two pairs of legs. The flat-backed millipedes form the order **Polydesmida** and, with several thousand species, are the largest group of diplopods. They occur on all continents except Antarctica.

Typical of flat-backed millipedes are the side extensions on the body rings, which stick out like flat plates or wings. These extensions are called **paranota** and make the back look flat and band-like. Adult animals usually have about 20 body rings. Flat-backed millipedes have no eyes and find their way with their antennae.

Flat-backed millipedes live in the damp **leaf litter**, under stones, bark and in rotting wood. There they eat rotting leaves and other plant material. In this way, like woodlice and earthworms, they help to form humus. They need moisture and avoid dry, sunny places.

Many flat-backed millipedes have small glands on their sides from which they release a smelly liquid when in danger. In many species this produces **hydrogen cyanide**, a strong poison that scares off ants, spiders and other enemies. The native species, however, are harmless to people. Even so, you should wash your hands after touching them.

Young flat-backed millipedes hatch from eggs with only a few body rings and three pairs of legs. With every **moult** new rings and legs are added. Some species build a small chamber of soil for moulting. In Central Europe and in Switzerland the **flattened flat-backed millipede** is a common species that grows to about two centimetres long.

begriffe.erklaerung: A millipede in which almost every body ring carries two pairs of legs.
Side, plate-like extensions on the back of flat-backed millipedes.
A very poisonous substance that some animals produce for defence.
A layer of fallen leaves on the forest floor.

gewusst: In Thailand there lives a bright pink flat-backed millipede that is called the dragon millipede.
No millipede really has a thousand legs, flat-backed millipedes usually have only about 30 pairs of legs.

teile.einleitung: Alpaca wool is the wool of the alpacas from the Andes of South America. It is often softer than sheep’s wool and contains no wool grease, lanolin. That is why it is considered especially pleasant on the skin.
wichtigste: Alpaca wool comes from alpacas, which are shorn once a year.
It is often softer than sheep’s wool.
Unlike sheep’s wool, it contains no lanolin.
It keeps very warm and is nevertheless light.
Alpaca wool comes in many natural colours.
Most alpaca wool comes from Peru.
Jumpers, hats, socks and blankets are made from it.

abschnitte.text: Alpaca wool is the shorn coat of alpacas. Experts also speak of **alpaca fibre**. One alpaca usually supplies a few kilograms of wool a year. The finest wool comes from the back and sides of the animal.

Alpaca wool is often softer than sheep’s wool and itches less. It contains no **lanolin**, the wool grease of sheep, so it does not have to be washed as thoroughly. In many fibres there are small air chambers that hold the warmth well. In this way an alpaca jumper is warm and yet light.

Alpacas come in over 20 natural shades, from white through beige, brown and grey to black. The wool can therefore often be processed without dyeing it. White wool, however, can also be easily **dyed** in bright colours. Especially sought after is the very fine wool of young animals, called baby alpaca.

The alpacas are **shorn** once a year, usually in spring or summer. After that the wool is sorted, washed and combed. In **spinning**, the fibres are twisted into a thread. People then knit or weave clothing and blankets from the yarn.

Even the Incas in South America valued alpaca wool for valuable fabrics. To this day, most alpaca wool comes from **Peru**. For many families in the Andean highlands it is an important source of income. In Switzerland, too, small businesses process the wool of their own alpacas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fine, long hair from which yarn is made.
A grease in sheep’s wool that makes the fleece water-repellent.
The cutting off of the wool with scissors or a shearing machine.
The twisting of fibres into a firm thread.

gewusst: The wool of the wild vicuña, a relative of the alpaca, is among the most expensive wools in the world.
In the ancient Inca empire, the finest fabrics could be worn only by people of high rank.
Suri alpacas have such long, smooth locks that their fur shines almost like silk.

teile.einleitung: Antarctica is the region around the South Pole, with the iciest continent on Earth. Almost everywhere lies a thick ice sheet, and it is colder than anywhere else in the world. Even so, penguins, seals and whales live on its coasts, for example most emperor penguins.
wichtigste: Antarctica is the continent around the South Pole.
At about 14 million square kilometres it is larger than Europe.
Around 98 per cent of its area is covered with ice.
The lowest temperature on Earth was measured here, minus 89.2 degrees.
Emperor penguins live almost only in Antarctica.
No one lives there permanently, only researchers in stations.
The Antarctic Treaty protects the continent for peace and research.

abschnitte.text: **Antarctica** includes the continent of Antarctica around the South Pole and the surrounding seas. The continent is about 14 million square kilometres in size, which is about 340 times as big as Switzerland. It is surrounded by the **Southern Ocean**. In winter the sea freezes all around, and the sea ice almost doubles the area. Antarctica should not be confused with the Arctic at the North Pole.

Around 98 per cent of Antarctica is covered by an **ice sheet**, which is more than four kilometres thick in places. About 70 per cent of the Earth's fresh water is locked in this ice. In 1983 minus 89.2 degrees was measured at the Russian Vostok station, the lowest air temperature ever recorded. Because it snows so little, the interior of Antarctica counts as a **cold desert**. If all the ice melted, sea level would rise by many metres.

On land it is too cold for almost all animals, so most live on the coasts and in the sea. The **emperor penguin**, at over a metre tall, is the largest penguin. It breeds in the middle of the Antarctic winter on the sea ice, and the male keeps the egg warm on his feet for about two months. Other residents are Adélie penguins, Weddell seals, leopard seals and whales. The basis of the food chain is **krill**, a small crustacean that lives in huge swarms.

abschnitte.titel: Discovery and the race to the Pole
abschnitte.text: Only in 1820 did sailors see the Antarctic continent for the first time. On 14 December 1911 the Norwegian **Roald Amundsen** was the first to reach the South Pole. The Briton Robert Falcon Scott arrived a good month later and died with his companions on the way back. The man from Basel, **Xavier Mertz**, also took part in an expedition and died in Antarctica in 1913. A glacier there bears his name.

Nobody lives in Antarctica permanently, but researchers work in about 70 research stations. In summer there are a few thousand people there, in winter only about a thousand. The **Antarctic Treaty** of 1959 lays down that the continent may only be used and explored peacefully, and Switzerland joined it in 1990. Mining is forbidden, and animals and plants are strictly protected. Drill cores from the ice reveal what the Earth's climate was like hundreds of thousands of years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very large piece of land, such as Africa, Europe or Antarctica.
A huge, thick layer of ice that covers a whole land.
Small, shrimp-like crustaceans that serve as food for many whales, seals and penguins.
A base where scientists live and carry out research.

gewusst: There are no polar bears in Antarctica, they only live in the Arctic at the North Pole.
At the South Pole the sun rises only once and sets only once a year.
Antarctica is the continent with the greatest average height, because of the thick ice.

teile.einleitung: The queen ant is the mother of a whole ant colony. She lays the eggs from which all the other ants hatch. Despite her name, however, she gives no orders, and she is fed and protected by the workers.
wichtigste: The queen lays the eggs in an ant colony.
Young queens have wings and mate on the nuptial flight.
After founding a new nest, the queen loses her wings.
She stores the sperm of the males for her whole life.
A queen can live for several years, in some species over 20 years.
Without a new queen, a colony cannot continue to exist.
Some species have only one queen, others many queens per nest.

abschnitte.text: The **queen** is the only female in the colony that lays eggs, and in some species there are several. She is usually clearly larger than the workers and has a thick abdomen. The queen does not rule like a monarch. She is more the mother of all the animals in the nest. The workers feed, clean and protect her so that she can lay as many eggs as possible.

Young queens and males have **wings**. On warm days in summer, they leave their nests at the same time in their thousands, which is called the **nuptial flight**. In the air or on the ground they mate. The males die soon afterwards. The fertilised queen stores the sperm in a small sperm sac and uses it for a lifetime.

After mating, the young queen looks for a place for her new nest. There she breaks off her wings or loses them, because she no longer needs them. She digs a small chamber and lays the first eggs. The first larvae she feeds alone, and for this she breaks down her now unnecessary **flight muscles**. Only when the first workers have hatched do they take over the search for food.

From **fertilised** eggs arise females, that is, workers or new queens. From **unfertilised** eggs arise males. Whether a female larva becomes a worker or a queen depends mainly on the food. A queen can lay hundreds of thousands of eggs in her life, and in army ants even millions per month. With scent substances she shows the workers that she is alive and healthy.

While workers often live only weeks to a few years, a queen can live for several years. A queen of the black garden ant lived almost 29 years in the laboratory. When the queen dies, in many species no animals lay fertilised eggs any more. Without a new queen, the colony therefore cannot continue to exist. In the **red wood ant** there are often many queens in one nest, so such colonies can become very old.

begriffe.erklaerung: The female that lays the eggs in the ant colony.
The flight in which young queens and males mate.
A small store in the queen’s body in which she keeps the sperm.
The beginning of a new ant colony by a young queen.

gewusst: In some species of ants, the queen lives much longer than almost all other insects.
Some queens enter foreign nests and let their workers raise them.
After the nuptial flight, you sometimes see discarded ant wings everywhere on pavements in summer.

teile.einleitung: The asp viper is a venomous snake that also occurs in Switzerland. Besides the adder, it is the only venomous snake in the country. It is shy, lives on sunny, stony slopes and bites only when it feels threatened.
wichtigste: The asp viper is one of the two venomous snakes of Switzerland.
The other venomous snake of Switzerland is the adder.
Typical is its slightly upturned snout tip.
It has vertical, slit-shaped pupils.
It lives on sunny, stony slopes in the Jura, the Alps and Ticino.
Its young are born alive.
It is protected in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The asp viper usually grows to 60 to 75 centimetres long and has a stocky body. Its colour varies a lot: grey, brown, reddish or almost black. On its back it has dark crossbands or spots. Typical are the slightly upturned **snout tip** and the **vertical pupil**, which is round in harmless native snakes.

The asp viper lives in south-western Europe, mainly in France, Italy and Switzerland. It likes warm, sunny places with stones, rocks, dry-stone walls and bushes. In Switzerland it occurs in the **Jura**, in the Valais, in the western Alps, in the Bernese Oberland and in **Ticino**. In the mountains it climbs to over 2,000 metres.

The asp viper hunts mainly **mice** and other small mammals, sometimes also lizards. It lies in wait for its prey and bites in a flash. The venom works quickly, after which it follows the animal by its scent trail with its tongue. Like all snakes, it swallows its prey whole.

Mating takes place in spring, after **hibernation**. The asp viper does not lay eggs, the young develop inside the mother's body. In late summer, usually 4 to 10 young snakes are born alive. At birth they are already about 20 centimetres long and already have venom.

The asp viper is shy and usually flees before you see it. Bites are rare and happen almost only when it is picked up or accidentally trodden on. A bite is painful and must be treated by a doctor, but deaths are extremely rare in Switzerland. After a bite you should stay calm, call the emergency number 144 or **Tox Info Suisse** on 145, and go to hospital.

In Switzerland all reptiles are protected, including the asp viper. Here it counts as endangered, because its habitats are becoming overgrown with bushes or built over. Dry-stone walls and open scree slopes are especially important for it. When walking in its area, sturdy shoes and long trousers make sense.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of venomous snakes with long, movable fangs.
The dark hole in the middle of the eye through which light enters.
Crawling animals with scaly skin such as snakes, lizards and tortoises.
A long period of rest in winter in which animals use hardly any energy.

gewusst: Fewer than ten species of snake live in Switzerland, but only two of them are venomous.
Snakes smell with their forked tongue.
Young asp vipers shed their skin for the first time soon after birth.

teile.einleitung: Bees cannot speak, but they still have a language: they dance. With the bee dance, forager bees show their sisters where there is food. This dance language was decoded by the researcher Karl von Frisch.
wichtigste: With the bee dance, bees show other bees the way to food.
The round dance shows a food source very close by.
With the waggle dance, bees show food sources that are far away.
The waggle dance reveals the direction and distance of the food.
Bees find the way to flowers by scents and by the sun.
They find their way back to the hive with the help of the sun and landmarks.
The researcher Karl von Frisch received the Nobel Prize in 1973 for decoding it.

abschnitte.text: **Bee language** means the way honey bees pass information to each other. Most important are dances on the combs, and in addition there are scents, touches and vibrations. A forager bee that has found a lot of nectar returns to the hive and dances. The other bees follow her, feel her with their antennae and smell the scent of the flowers. After that they fly off themselves.

If the food is near the hive, say less than 50 to 100 metres away, the bee dances the **round dance**. She runs small circles, alternately to the left and to the right. The round dance says only: here nearby there is food. The others do not learn the direction. They find the flowers with the help of the scent that the dancer has brought with her.

For food sources that are far away, the bee dances the **waggle dance**. She runs a stretch straight ahead and wiggles her abdomen vigorously. Then she returns in a curve and begins again, so that a kind of figure of eight arises. The angle of the straight stretch to the vertical on the comb corresponds to the angle between the food source and the **sun**. The longer the bee waggles, the further away the food is.

abschnitte.titel: Finding the way on the move
abschnitte.text: Bees use the sun as a compass, even when clouds partly cover it. This is because they see **polarised light**, which humans cannot perceive. In addition they remember landmarks such as trees, houses or woodland edges. Near the flowers, colours and scents help. Many flowers also have patterns in ultraviolet light that show the bees the way to the nectar.

The Austrian researcher **Karl von Frisch** studied the behaviour of bees for decades. He put out little dishes of food at different distances and watched the dances in glass boxes. In the 1940s he decoded the meaning of the waggle dance. In 1973 he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it together with Konrad Lorenz and Nikolaas Tinbergen. Later researchers also confirmed his results with small robot bees.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bee dance in a circle that shows food near the hive.
A dance in the shape of a figure of eight that reveals the direction and distance of a food source.
Light that vibrates in a certain direction, by which bees can recognise the position of the sun.

gewusst: Bees dance in the dark hive, and the others feel the dance above all through touch and vibration.
Bees in different countries have slightly different dance “dialects”.
When swarming too, scout bees use the waggle dance to show where a good new home lies.

t85todg.t: Bambi, a Life in the Woods

teile.einleitung: “Bambi, a Life in the Woods” is an animal novel by the Austrian writer Felix Salten from 1923. It tells of the life of a young roe deer buck in the forest, from childhood to adulthood. Through Walt Disney's animated film, Bambi became world famous.
wichtigste: Bambi is a book by Felix Salten that appeared in 1923.
The main character in the book is originally a roe deer.
The story shows the life of a young roe buck in the forest with all its dangers.
In the book, man appears as the greatest threat to the animals.
In 1942 Walt Disney brought out a famous animated film.
In the Disney film the roe deer became an American white-tailed deer.
Felix Salten spent his last years in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: The novel **Bambi** appeared as a book in Vienna in 1923, after it had already been printed in a newspaper. The author **Felix Salten** was actually called Siegmund Salzmann and was a well-known Viennese journalist and writer. The book was quickly translated into many languages. It is regarded as one of the best-known animal novels in the world.

Bambi is a young **roe buck** who is born in a clearing in the forest. He learns from his mother what dangers there are and how to survive in the forest. In time he meets other animals, loses his mother to a hunter and has to become independent. An old, wise stag, the old Prince, shows him how to live alone and carefully.

Salten describes the forest very exactly and lets the animals talk to one another. Man is called only **He** by the animals and appears as a dangerous hunter. The book is therefore not only a children's story, but also a serious tale about life and death in nature. Many readers also understand it as a call to respect animals and nature.

In 1942 the animated film **Bambi** by Walt Disney came to the cinemas. Because audiences in the USA did not know European roe deer, Bambi became a **white-tailed deer** in the film. The film added funny supporting characters such as the rabbit Thumper and made the story more suitable for children. Since then many people think first of a fawn when they hear Bambi.

Felix Salten was of Jewish origin, and the National Socialists banned his books. In 1938 he fled from Vienna and moved with his wife to **Switzerland**. He lived in Zurich until his death in 1945. There he wrote more animal books, for example a sequel with the title Bambi's Children.

begriffe.erklaerung: A longer story in which animals are the main characters.
A small species of deer in Europe, the male is called a roe buck.
An American species of deer with a white underside to its tail.
A film made of many drawn pictures that are shown quickly one after another.

gewusst: The name Bambi probably goes back to the Italian word bambino for child.
In the German-speaking world the Bambi is also a well-known media award in the form of a golden roe deer.
Felix Salten also wrote the book “Perri, the Youth of a Squirrel”, which was also filmed by Disney.

teile.einleitung: The mountain tapir is the smallest species of tapir and lives high up in the Andes of South America. With its thick, woolly fur it is perfectly adapted to the cold in the mountains. Like all tapirs, it has a flexible, trunk-like nose.
wichtigste: The mountain tapir is the smallest of the tapir species.
It lives in the Andes of Colombia, Ecuador and northern Peru.
It has thick, woolly, dark fur.
Its upper lip is extended into a short trunk.
It is a plant eater and spreads seeds.
The mountain tapir is highly endangered.

abschnitte.text: The mountain tapir grows to about 1.8 metres long and around 80 centimetres high at the shoulder. That makes it the smallest of the tapir species. Its thick, **woolly fur** is blackish brown and protects it from the cold. Typical are the white edges on the lips and often on the ears too. With its short **trunk** it can grasp leaves and pick up smells.

The mountain tapir lives in the **Andes** of Colombia, Ecuador and the north of Peru. It is found in mountain forests and in the páramo, a damp high grassland, usually between about 2,000 and 4,500 metres above sea level. There it is often cold, misty and wet. It likes to stay near water and can swim well. It is the only tapir that lives so high in the mountains.

Mountain tapirs eat leaves, grasses, ferns, shoots and fruit. Because they eat seeds and pass them out again in other places, they help to spread the plants. That is why they are also called the **gardeners of the Andes**. They usually live alone and are active mainly at dusk and at night. They travel through their area along fixed paths.

The gestation lasts a very long time, about 13 months. Usually a single young is born. It has striped and spotted fur, which **camouflages** it well in the undergrowth. After a few months the stripes disappear. The young stays with its mother for about a year or longer.

Tapirs belong to the **odd-toed ungulates** and are therefore related to horses and rhinoceroses. There are only a few species of tapir, three live in Central and South America and one in South-East Asia. The mountain tapir is **highly endangered**, and there are probably only a few thousand animals left. It is hunted, and its habitat is turned into pastures and fields. Protected areas in the Andes are meant to save it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant-eating mammal with a short trunk, related to the horse and the rhinoceros.
Hoofed animals with an odd number of weight-bearing toes, for example horses.
Cold, damp grassland high in the Andes.
The longest mountain range in the world, along the west coast of South America.

gewusst: Tapirs have four toes on the front feet and only three on the hind feet.
Tapirs have existed for many millions of years, which is why they are also called living fossils.
The mountain tapir is also called the woolly tapir.

teile.einleitung: Autotomy means that an animal voluntarily throws off a part of its body in order to save itself. It is best known in lizards, which lose their tail when a predator grabs it. Often the lost part grows back afterwards.
wichtigste: Autotomy is the self-shedding of a body part for protection.
Lizards such as the sand lizard shed their tail when attacked and flee.
The slow worm can also lose its tail when attacked by a predator.
The shed tail goes on wriggling and distracts the enemy.
The regrown tail is called a regenerate and is usually shorter and without full bones.
Crabs, spiders and harvestmen can also shed legs.

abschnitte.text: The word **autotomy** comes from Greek and means roughly self-separation. The animal deliberately separates a body part, usually a tail or a leg. This happens when an enemy grabs the animal by this body part. In this way the animal can escape, even if it loses something for it.

In many lizards the tail vertebrae have a built-in **breaking point**, that is, a weak spot where they break easily. When a predator holds the tail fast, certain muscles contract and the tail comes away. Blood vessels close at once, so the animal hardly bleeds. The shed tail twitches for a while and so distracts the attacker.

After shedding, a new tail grows back in lizards, which is called **regeneration**. The new part is called a **regenerate** and is usually shorter and a different colour. It no longer contains real vertebrae, but only a tube of cartilage. In the slow worm often only a short, blunt stub grows back.

In Switzerland you can watch autotomy in the **sand lizard**, the wall lizard and the common lizard. The slow worm, a legless lizard, can also lose its tail when it is grabbed by a cat or a bird, for example. That is why you should never touch lizards by the tail. Harvestmen in the garden like to shed a leg when in danger.

Autotomy saves lives in many cases, but it also has disadvantages. Lizards store **fat reserves** in the tail, which are lost when it is shed. Without a tail they keep their balance less well and are often at a disadvantage when looking for a partner. In addition, regrowing costs a lot of energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The independent shedding of a body part in order to escape.
A prepared weak spot where something breaks off easily.
The regrowing of lost body parts.
The regrown body part, for example a new lizard tail.

gewusst: Some geckos can shed their tail several times in their lives and grow a new one.
Starfish can shed arms, and in some species a whole new starfish grows from a single arm.
A shed lizard tail can go on wriggling for several minutes.

teile.einleitung: A worker is a female honeybee who does all the jobs that need doing in the bee colony. She cleans, feeds, builds, guards and collects nectar and pollen. Without the thousands of hard-working workers a bee colony could not survive.
wichtigste: Workers are female bees who normally do not lay eggs themselves.
Most of the bees in a colony are workers.
They do all the jobs in the hive and outside.
Depending on her age, a worker takes on several different tasks.
In summer a worker lives for only about 4 to 6 weeks.
Winter bees, on the other hand, live for several months.
With the waggle dance, foragers show other bees good sources of food.

abschnitte.text: A bee colony consists of one **queen**, a few hundred drones and many thousands of workers. In summer a strong colony often has 30,000 to 50,000 bees. Workers are females whose ovaries are not fully developed. They are a little smaller than the queen and the male **drones**.

In the course of her life a worker has several tasks, a different one depending on her age. Young bees first clean the honeycomb cells, then as **nurse bees** they feed the larvae. Later they build new combs with wax from their wax glands and turn nectar into honey. Only in the last weeks of their lives do they fly out as **foragers**. Older bees that become too old to fly still help in the hive as guards or cleaners.

Foragers fly up to several kilometres to visit flowers. They carry the sweet nectar to the hive in their honey stomach. They carry the pollen as little balls, called **pollen baskets**, on their hind legs. In doing so they pollinate many plants, which is very important for fruit and vegetables.

When a forager has found a good source of food, she dances the **waggle dance** on the comb in the hive. The direction of the dance shows the direction of the food source in relation to the sun. The length of the waggling tells how far away it is. This bee language was decoded by the researcher Karl von Frisch, who received the Nobel Prize for it in 1973.

In summer the bees work so hard that they live for only about 4 to 6 weeks. In autumn, on the other hand, **winter bees** hatch, which live for several months. In winter they form a dense cluster and warm the queen by shivering their flight muscles. If a worker stings a person, her barbed sting stays stuck in the skin and she dies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female bee that works in the colony and normally does not lay eggs.
A male honeybee.
A young worker that feeds the larvae.
A structure of six-sided wax cells in which brood, honey and pollen are stored.
A dance with which bees show each other the way to sources of food.

gewusst: For a 500 gram jar of honey, bees have to fly many thousands of kilometres.
A worker produces only about a teaspoon of honey in her whole life.
Whether an egg becomes a worker or a queen is decided by the food: a queen larva gets royal jelly for the whole of her larval life.

teile.einleitung: The boa constrictor, in German called Abgottschlange, is a large constrictor snake from Central and South America. It is not poisonous and kills its prey by coiling around it. Because of its beautiful markings it is also a well-known terrarium snake.
wichtigste: The boa constrictor belongs to the family of boas (Boidae).
Carl von Linné described it in 1758 as Boa constrictor.
“Constrictor” means squeezer or strangler.
It is not poisonous and kills its prey by coiling around it.
It gives birth to live young, on average about 25.
It lives in Central and South America.
The German name comes from its role in religious cults.

abschnitte.text: The boa constrictor belongs to the family of **boas** (Boidae). The Swedish naturalist **Carl von Linné** described it scientifically in 1758 as Boa constrictor. It usually grows 2 to 3 metres long, large females somewhat more. Its body is strong and muscular. On a light brown background it has dark saddle-shaped patches that often turn reddish towards the tail.

The word **boa** comes from Latin and meant a large snake. In the Middle Ages the name was popularly linked with the Greek word bous, the ox. People told each other that such snakes sucked cows dry. The species name constrictor means squeezer or strangler. The German name Abgottschlange recalls that it was worshipped in religious cults.

The boa constrictor lives in **Central and South America**, from Mexico to Argentina. It occurs in rainforests, dry forests, savannas and even near villages. Young animals often climb into trees, while older ones stay more on the ground. It is usually active at dusk and at night.

The boa constrictor is **not poisonous**. It lies in wait for its prey, grabs it with its teeth and coils its body around it. A study from 2015 showed that the prey dies above all of **circulatory arrest**, because the blood can no longer flow. The snake senses when the heart no longer beats and then lets go. With its backward-curved teeth it holds the prey fast and pushes it down while swallowing. It eats rodents, birds, lizards and small mammals.

The boa constrictor does not lay eggs, but gives birth to **live young**. A female has about 10 to 65 young per litter, on average about 25. At birth the young are already around 40 to 50 centimetres long. They have to look after themselves at once.

Boa constrictors are often kept in **terrariums** and shown in zoos. In Switzerland strict animal welfare rules apply to keeping giant snakes, for example on the size of the terrarium. In their homeland they are useful because they eat rats and mice. For people they are generally not dangerous.

begriffe.erklaerung: A snake that kills its prey by coiling around it.
Without poison, the animal cannot poison by a bite.
A glass container in which reptiles are kept.
Broad patches across the back that look like a saddle.

gewusst: The boa constrictor is one of the few animals whose scientific name is also used in everyday speech.
After a big meal a boa often does not have to eat for weeks.
Like all snakes the boa smells with its forked tongue.

teile.einleitung: Leafcutter ants are ants from the Americas that cut leaves into pieces and carry them into their nest. They do not eat the leaves themselves, though. Instead they grow a fungus on them, which they feed on, like real little farmers.
wichtigste: Leafcutter ants grow a fungus as food on cut leaves.
The most important cultivated fungus is called Leucoagaricus gongylophorus.
They belong to the subfamily of myrmicine ants (Myrmicinae) and to the tribe Attini.
The two genera are called Atta and Acromyrmex.
An Atta colony has only a single queen, but often several million workers.
They live from the south of the USA to Argentina.

abschnitte.text: Leafcutter ants belong to the subfamily of **myrmicine ants** (Myrmicinae). Together with all the other fungus-growing ants they form the tribe **Attini**. There are two genera: Atta with just under 20 species and Acromyrmex. You can tell them apart by the spines on the back. Atta workers have three pairs of spines on the back, Acromyrmex workers four pairs.

Leafcutter ants live only in the Americas. Their range extends from the south of the USA to Argentina. They are most common in tropical rainforests and savannas of Central and South America. One species even lives in Texas and is therefore called **Atta texana**.

With their sharp jaws the ants cut pieces out of leaves and carry them over their heads into the nest. There they chew the leaves into a pulp on which a fungus grows. The fungus is called **Leucoagaricus gongylophorus**. It forms small, swollen and nutrient-rich tips, the **gongylidia**. The ants eat these and also feed their larvae with them.

A colony of the genus Atta has only a single **queen**. She lays eggs and in the course of her life can produce up to around 150 million workers. At the same time several million workers live in a large colony. The workers are of different sizes and have different jobs: large soldiers defend the nest, small ones tend the fungus. The underground nests can reach many metres deep and have hundreds of chambers.

Leafcutter ants are among the most important plant eaters in the tropics of the Americas. They loosen the soil and bring nutrients into the earth. For farmers, though, they can become a problem, because in one night they strip whole trees or fields bare. In some zoos and tropical houses you can watch their long **ant trails**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Nutrient-rich fungus tips that serve the ants as food.
The group of all ants that grow fungi.
An ant society with a queen and workers.
Two living things living together in a way that benefits both.

gewusst: Leafcutter ants have practised agriculture for millions of years, so much longer than humans.
An ant can carry a piece of leaf that weighs many times its own weight.
A young queen takes a small piece of fungus in her mouth with her when she founds a new nest.

teile.einleitung: The great spotted woodpecker is the most common woodpecker in Switzerland and in the whole of Europe. With its strong bill it hacks holes in trees, and in spring you can hear it drumming loudly. Its black and white plumage with the red patch under the tail makes it easy to recognise.
wichtigste: The great spotted woodpecker is the most common species of woodpecker in Europe.
It has black and white plumage and red under-tail feathers.
It hacks its nest hole itself into a tree trunk.
It defends its territory by drumming and threat displays.
In summer it eats mainly insects and their larvae, in winter many seeds.
Male and female take turns to incubate the eggs for about 10 to 12 days.
Its stiff tail serves it as a support when climbing.

abschnitte.text: The great spotted woodpecker is about 22 to 26 centimetres long, about as big as a blackbird. It has a black back with large white patches on the shoulders and a pale belly. Under the tail it gleams **red**, and the male additionally has a red patch on the back of the head. Young great spotted woodpeckers wear a red cap on the crown. Much smaller and rarer is its relative, the **lesser spotted woodpecker**, which is only about sparrow-sized.

The great spotted woodpecker moves up the trunk in hops and props itself up with its stiff **support tail**. On the feet two toes point forwards and two backwards, so it can cling on well. Its tongue is very long and has barbs at the tip, with which it pulls larvae out of tunnels in the wood. A specially built skull protects its brain when hammering.

In summer the great spotted woodpecker eats mainly **insects** and their larvae, which it finds under the bark or in the wood. In winter it feeds a lot on seeds from pine and spruce cones and on nuts. For this it wedges a cone in a fork of a branch or a crack in the bark and hacks the seeds out, and such a place is called a **woodpecker anvil**. Sometimes it also robs eggs or young from the nests of other birds and likes to come to bird feeders in winter.

In late winter and spring the great spotted woodpecker drums with very fast strokes of its bill on dry branches. With this it defends its **territory** and attracts a partner, and in addition it uses threat displays against intruders. In towns it sometimes drums on tin roofs or aerials, because these sound especially loud. Its call is a short, sharp “kix”.

The great spotted woodpecker builds its nest in a **hole** it has hacked itself in a tree trunk, often in rotten wood. The female usually lays 4 to 7 white eggs, which male and female take turns to incubate for around 10 to 12 days. The young then stay about three weeks in the hole and call loudly for food. Old woodpecker holes are later important homes for tits, starlings, bats and edible dormice.

begriffe.erklaerung: Stiff tail feathers on which a woodpecker props itself when climbing a tree.
A fork of a branch or a crack in which the woodpecker wedges cones to hack out the seeds.
An area that an animal defends against others of its species.
Animals that later move into an abandoned woodpecker hole.

gewusst: A great spotted woodpecker can drum on a branch more than ten times a second.
The tongue of the great spotted woodpecker is so long that it is stored in a loop around the skull.
Many animals, from tits to bats, live in old great spotted woodpecker holes.

teile.einleitung: The preen gland is a small gland on the back of most birds, directly above the tail. It produces an oily fat that the birds spread over their feathers with their bills. In this way the feathers stay supple and waterproof, and raindrops simply roll off.
wichtigste: The preen gland sits at the rump, that is the lower back above the tail.
It forms an oily secretion that contains fat and wax.
Birds spread this fat through the plumage with their bills when preening.
As a result raindrops simply roll off the plumage of a goose.
Water birds such as ducks and geese have especially large preen glands.
Some birds such as ostriches and emus have no preen gland.

abschnitte.text: The **preen gland** is the only large skin gland of birds, and experts also call it the glandula uropygialis. It lies under the skin at the **rump**, often hidden under a small tuft of feathers. Mammals have many sweat and sebaceous glands in the skin, birds by contrast almost none. The preen gland therefore takes on an important job in the care of the feathers.

When preening, the bird presses on the gland with its bill and picks up the oily **secretion**. Then it draws each feather singly through its bill and spreads the fat on it. Sometimes it also rubs its head on the gland, because it cannot reach its own head with its bill. This preening takes a long time every day in many birds.

The fat makes the feathers supple so that they do not become brittle and break. Together with the special structure of the feathers it makes sure that **water** rolls off. In a goose or duck a layer of air stays under the plumage, which keeps it warm and gives buoyancy when swimming. That is why ducks hardly feel cold even in ice-cold water.

Water birds such as ducks, geese and cormorants usually have large preen glands. Ostriches, emus, rheas and some pigeons and parrots, by contrast, have none or only a tiny gland. These birds care for their plumage with **powder down**, which breaks down into a fine dust. In the hoopoe the secretion of the females smells very unpleasant during the breeding season and so protects the nest.

When water birds get caught in an **oil spill**, their feathers stick together and lose their protective effect. The animals then get cold or can no longer swim. Helpers therefore carefully wash oiled birds with washing-up liquid. After that the birds have to grease their plumage again with the preen gland before they can be released.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the body that makes and gives off a substance, for example fat, sweat or saliva.
The rear part of a bird's back directly above the tail.
A substance that a gland gives off.
Special feathers that break down into fine dust and care for the plumage.

gewusst: The expression “like water off a duck's back” describes exactly the effect of the preen gland.
In the hoopoe the secretion of the preen gland stinks so strongly during the breeding season that it scares off enemies.
A bird cannot reach its own head with its bill, so it rubs it directly on the gland.

teile.einleitung: Species extinction means that species of animals and plants disappear from the Earth for ever. This has always happened, but today species are dying out much faster than before because of the influence of humans. Experts therefore speak of one of the greatest challenges of our time.
wichtigste: When an animal species disappears from the whole world, it is called extinction.
When a species is destroyed by humans, it is called extermination.
In the history of the Earth there were five great mass extinctions.
Today species are dying out much faster than they naturally would.
The most important cause is the destruction of habitats.
According to a world report from 2019, about a million species are threatened with extinction.
An extinct species never comes back.

abschnitte.text: A species counts as **extinct** when not a single living individual of that species exists any more. If it is deliberately destroyed by humans, this is called **extermination**. Species extinction is actually a natural process, because almost all species that have ever lived have died out. The problem, though, is that today it is happening much faster than normal.

In the history of the Earth there were five great **mass extinctions**, in which very many species disappeared in a short time. The biggest happened about 252 million years ago at the end of the Permian, when probably more than three quarters of all species died out. The best known was 66 million years ago, when a giant asteroid hit the Earth. Then the dinosaurs disappeared, with the exception of the birds.

The most important cause is the destruction of **habitats**, for example when rainforests are cut down or bogs are drained. Added to this are overfishing, hunting and poaching. Environmental poisons, climate change and introduced animals and plants that push out native species are also dangerous. The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, **IPBES**, estimated in 2019 that about a million species are threatened with extinction.

The **dodo**, a flightless bird from the island of Mauritius, was wiped out in the 17th century. The passenger pigeon was once one of the commonest birds in North America, but the last one died in 1914 in a zoo in Cincinnati. The thylacine from Tasmania disappeared in the 1930s. Many other species die out unnoticed before they have even been discovered.

In Switzerland, too, about a third of the animal and plant species studied are endangered. Bear, wolf, lynx and ibex had at times disappeared from here altogether. Some have returned or have been reintroduced. Especially threatened today are species of wetlands, dry meadows and many **insects**.

Every species has its job in the **ecosystem**, the interplay of all living things. Bees and other insects, for example, pollinate our fruit trees. If too many species disappear, the whole web of living things can start to wobble. Protected areas, nature-friendly farming and climate protection help to slow down species extinction.

begriffe.erklaerung: When not a single living individual of a species exists any more.
Extinction of a species that was caused by humans.
A time in which very many species die out in a short period.
The variety of all living things and habitats on Earth.

gewusst: It is estimated that more than 99 per cent of all species that ever lived on Earth have died out.
The last passenger pigeon was called Martha.
Some experts say that we are right now in the sixth mass extinction in the history of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Beeswax is a natural building material that honey bees make themselves. They build their combs out of wax. People too have used beeswax for thousands of years, for example for candles and ointments.
wichtigste: Bees build their combs out of wax.
The wax forms in glands on the abdomen of young workers.
It is sweated out in the form of tiny, transparent flakes.
To produce wax, bees need a lot of honey as energy.
Beeswax melts at about 62 to 65 degrees.
People use it for candles, cosmetics, ointments and wax wraps.
Fresh wax is almost white and only turns yellowish through pollen and propolis.

abschnitte.text: **Beeswax** is a substance that honey bees make in their bodies. It is solid, but can be kneaded and shaped well when warm. Bees build their **combs** from it and close the honey cells with it. Beeswax repels water and smells slightly of honey. It consists of many different fatty substances.

Workers have four pairs of **wax glands** on the underside of the abdomen. These are especially active when the bees are about two to three weeks old. The glands secrete tiny, transparent wax flakes. The bees take them with their legs, chew them soft and attach them to the comb. For one kilogram of wax the bees have to eat several kilograms of honey.

Freshly secreted wax is almost white. Only with time does it turn yellow to brownish through pollen and **propolis**. Old brood combs even become dark brown. Beeswax melts at about 62 to 65 degrees and is solid at room temperature. In the warm hive, however, it stays just soft enough for the bees to build with it.

Even the ancient Egyptians used beeswax, for example for candles and for embalming. Today it is made into **beeswax candles**, lip balm, ointments and creams. Cloths soaked in wax, the wax wraps, replace cling film in the kitchen. Furniture and wooden floors are cared for with wax. As a food additive beeswax carries the number E 901 and coats some sweets, for example.

Beekeepers melt down old combs and clean the wax. From it new **foundations** are pressed, which they give back to the bees. In this way a cycle arises, and the bees save energy. In Switzerland many beekeepers take care to use their own wax so that no harmful substances from foreign wax get into the hive.

begriffe.erklaerung: Small glands on the abdomen of workers from which wax emerges.
Tiny, thin wax scales from which bees build their combs.
A resin that bees collect and that colours the wax yellowish.

gewusst: For one kilogram of wax over a million tiny wax flakes are needed.
Beeswax candles smell slightly of honey when they burn.

teile.einleitung: Avermectins are active substances against worms and other parasites that originally come from a soil bacterium. They help millions of people and animals, but can also harm useful insects such as dung beetles. Their discovery was honoured with the Nobel Prize.
wichtigste: Avermectins are substances against parasites such as worms, mites and lice.
They were obtained from the soil bacterium Streptomyces avermitilis.
The best-known active substance in this group is ivermectin.
Satoshi Ōmura and William C. Campbell received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2015 for the discovery.
In veterinary medicine, grazing animals such as cattle, sheep and horses are wormed with them.
Residues in the dung of treated animals can harm dung beetles and their larvae.

abschnitte.text: The Japanese researcher **Satoshi Ōmura** collected soil samples in the 1970s in order to find new bacteria. In a sample from Japan he discovered a bacterium that was later called **Streptomyces avermitilis**. The American William C. Campbell found out that substances from this bacterium kill worms in animals. These substances were called avermectins.

Avermectins attack the nerves and muscles of invertebrates such as worms, mites and insects. The parasites are paralysed as a result and die. In mammals and people they work much more weakly in the usual amounts, because these nerve sites are built differently and are protected by the **blood-brain barrier**. That is why they can be used as a medicine.

From the avermectins the active substance **ivermectin** was developed. It is used mainly in Africa and South America against river blindness, a disease caused by tiny threadworms that can make people blind. Since 1987 a pharmaceutical company has been giving the medicine away in large amounts for this disease. For this achievement Ōmura and Campbell received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine in 2015.

In farming, cattle, sheep, goats and horses are wormed with avermectins. They also help against mites, lice and warble flies. In dogs and cats related substances are used against parasites. Part of the active substance, however, is excreted again unchanged in the **droppings**.

In the dung of treated animals, residues of the products often remain for days or weeks. Dung beetles, dung flies and their larvae, which live in cowpats, can be harmed or die as a result. Then the **cowpats** are broken down more slowly and the pasture stays dirty for longer. Experts therefore recommend treating animals only when necessary and not all at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that lives on or in another living thing and harms it.
The best-known medicine in the group of the avermectins.
A tropical disease caused by threadworms that can lead to blindness.
Freeing an animal of worms with a medicine.

gewusst: A teaspoon of garden soil contains millions of bacteria, and from one of them came a Nobel Prize medicine.
The soil sample with the famous bacterium came from near a golf course in Japan.

teile.einleitung: Alpacas are fluffy animals from the Andes of South America that are related to camels. They are kept mainly for their soft wool. In Switzerland, too, you see alpacas on pastures more and more often.
wichtigste: Alpacas originally come from the Andes of South America.
They are mammals and belong to the camels, but have no humps.
An adult alpaca weighs about 50 to 80 kilograms.
Alpacas live to be about 15 to 20 years old.
A young alpaca is called a cria.
They are smaller than llamas and have shorter ears.
When they feel threatened or annoyed, they spit.
When they are content, they hum softly.

abschnitte.text: Alpacas have a long neck, a small head and thick, soft fur. They are smaller than **llamas** and have shorter, pointed ears. An adult animal weighs about 50 to 80 kilograms. Their fur comes in many colours, from white through brown to black.

Alpacas come from the **Andes** in South America, above all from Peru, Bolivia and Chile. There they live in the highlands at 3,500 to 5,000 metres. They were bred several thousand years ago from the wild **vicuña**. The Incas used their wool for valuable fabrics.

Like camels and llamas, alpacas belong to the **tylopods** (the “pad-footed” animals). On each foot they have two toes with soft sole pads instead of hard hooves. These pads spare the ground and the turf. That is why alpacas are well suited to delicate pastures, including in the mountains.

Alpacas are **herd animals** and must never be kept alone. When they are content, they hum softly. If they feel threatened or annoyed, they spit, though mostly at each other and not at people. They deposit their dung together at a few fixed places, which makes cleaning up easy.
A female alpaca carries her young for about eleven months. Usually only one young is born, called a **cria**. It can stand and walk after a short time. Alpacas live to be about 15 to 20 years old.

In Switzerland today, many farms and families keep alpacas. Once a year, in spring or summer, they are **shorn** so that they do not get too hot in the warm weather. Jumpers, hats and blankets are made from the wool. Alpaca walks are also popular, in which you lead the animals on a lead.

begriffe.erklaerung: The word for a young alpaca.
A group of animals with soft foot pads, to which camels, llamas and alpacas belong.
The wild animal from the Andes from which the alpaca descends.
An animal that has to live in a group with others of its kind.

gewusst: Alpacas have no incisors at the front of the upper jaw, but a hard dental pad.
There are two types of alpaca: the fluffy Huacaya and the Suri with long, smooth locks.
Alpaca wool comes in over 20 natural shades.

teile.einleitung: The African wild dog, also called the painted dog, is a predator with a brightly patched coat. It lives in packs and is one of the most successful hunters in Africa. Sadly, it is highly endangered today.
wichtigste: The African wild dog is also called the painted dog.
It is a meat eater and usually hunts in a pack.
Wild dogs are very enduring runners.
They mostly hunt in the early morning and late afternoon.
Normally only the highest-ranking pair has offspring.
Other pack members help to raise the pups.
The wild dog is highly endangered through loss of habitat and persecution.

abschnitte.text: The wild dog has a coat with black, yellow, brown and white patches. Every animal has its own **pattern of patches**, like a fingerprint. Striking are the large, round ears and the white tip of the tail. It weighs about 20 to 30 kilograms and, in spite of its name, is not related to hyenas.

African wild dogs live in savannas and open woodland south of the Sahara. Larger populations exist, for example, in Botswana, Tanzania and Zimbabwe. Their **ranges** are very large, often several hundred square kilometres. They therefore need a lot of undisturbed space.

Wild dogs hunt together in a **pack**, mostly in the early morning and late afternoon. They are very enduring runners and often pursue antelopes such as impalas over several kilometres. A large share of their hunts succeed, more than in lions. As meat eaters, they keep the numbers of their prey in balance.

A pack often numbers about 10 animals, sometimes clearly more. Normally only the highest-ranking pair has young, often many pups at once. The other pack members help with raising them and bring up food for the pups and for sick animals. Among themselves, wild dogs communicate with sounds such as **twittering** and whimpering.

The greatest danger is the **loss of habitat**, because fields and settlements are growing. In the past, wild dogs were often killed because they were seen as a danger to livestock. On roads, many are run over by vehicles. They can also catch diseases such as rabies or distemper from domestic dogs.

Today probably only a few thousand wild dogs live in the wild. The International Union for Conservation of Nature classes the species as **endangered**. Protected areas, vaccinations of domestic dogs and help for livestock keepers are meant to protect the animals. Zoos also take part with breeding programmes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of dogs or wolves that lives and hunts together.
An animal that feeds mainly on other animals.
The area in which an animal or a group roams.
A young dog.

gewusst: Researchers have observed that wild dogs vote with sneezes before setting off on a hunt.
The scientific name Lycaon pictus means roughly painted wolf.
Unlike domestic dogs, wild dogs have only four toes on their front feet.

teile.einleitung: Dormice are a family of small, nocturnal rodents with big eyes and often a bushy tail. Best known is the edible dormouse, which in German is also called Bilch in everyday speech. Dormice are true masters of hibernation.
wichtigste: Dormice are a family of rodents, in German they are also called Schläfer, meaning sleepers.
The edible dormouse belongs to the dormice and is also called Bilch in German.
In Switzerland there live, among others, the edible dormouse, the hazel dormouse and the garden dormouse.
Dormice are nocturnal and climb very skilfully.
They hibernate for a long time, the edible dormouse often for seven months or more.
Dormice eat fruit, nuts, seeds, buds and also insects.
Many dormice can slip off the skin of their tail when in danger.

abschnitte.text: **Dormice** look a little like a cross between a mouse and a squirrel. They have big, dark eyes, roundish ears and soft fur. The tail is long and bushy in most species. The **edible dormouse**, at about 15 cm body length plus tail, is the largest dormouse in Switzerland. The hazel dormouse is much smaller and has orange-brown fur.

Worldwide there are about 30 species of dormouse in Europe, Asia and Africa. In Switzerland the edible dormouse, the **hazel dormouse** and the **garden dormouse** occur. The garden dormouse has a black face mask reminiscent of a robber. The edible dormouse and the hazel dormouse live mainly in deciduous forests and hedges. The garden dormouse is also found in the mountains up to above the tree line.

Dormice are **nocturnal** and spend the day in tree holes, nest boxes or nests. With their feet they climb skilfully in trees and bushes. They eat beechnuts, hazelnuts, fruit, buds and insects. In autumn they fatten themselves up with a thick layer of fat. Sometimes edible dormice move into attics and huts and make noise at night.

Dormice hibernate for an especially long time. The edible dormouse often sleeps from September or October until May, that is about seven months, which is where its German name Siebenschläfer, “seven sleeper”, comes from. In this time its body temperature drops to a few degrees, and the heart beats only very slowly. It usually hibernates in a hole in the ground. In bad beech mast years edible dormice often have no young at all.

The ancient Romans kept edible dormice in clay vessels, fattened them with nuts and ate them as a delicacy. Today dormice are protected in Europe. The hazel dormouse needs varied hedges and woodland edges with hazel bushes, which have vanished in many places. Anyone who promotes nest boxes and **hedges** helps the little climbers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small rodent from the family of sleepers, for example the edible dormouse.
A long resting state in winter in which body temperature and heartbeat drop sharply.
Animals that are out and about at night and sleep during the day.

gewusst: The edible dormouse is called Siebenschläfer in German, meaning “seven sleeper”, because it spends about seven months in hibernation.
When in danger, a dormouse can slip off the skin of its tail and so escape from an enemy.

teile.einleitung: Scarab beetles, in German called leaf-horn beetles, are a huge beetle family with many well-known members such as the cockchafer, the rose chafer and the rhinoceros beetle. Their feature is antennae that end in a club of movable little plates. That is where their German name comes from too.
wichtigste: Scarab beetles are a large family of beetles with several tens of thousands of species.
Their antennae end in a club of plates that can be spread like a fan.
With these antennae they smell food and partners.
The cockchafer belongs to the scarab beetles.
Rose chafers, rhinoceros beetles and dung beetles are also scarab beetles.
Their larvae are called grubs and are thick and curved into a C shape.
Dung beetles, too, are counted among the scarab beetles in the wider sense.

abschnitte.text: Scarab beetles usually have a strong, stocky body. Their typical feature is the **antennae**: they end in a club of several flat little plates, the **lamellae**. The beetles can spread these like a small fan. In this way they pick up smells especially well. Many species gleam metallic green, golden or bronze.

The **cockchafer** is the best-known scarab beetle in Switzerland. The rose chafer likes to sit on flowers in summer. Males of the rhinoceros beetle carry a horn on the head. The dung beetle shapes balls of dung and rolls them away. Among the giants are the African goliath beetle and the South American Hercules beetle, one of the longest beetles in the world.

The larvae of scarab beetles are called **grubs**. They are whitish, thick and usually curved into a C shape. Depending on the species they live in the soil, in dung, compost or rotting wood. Cockchafer grubs eat roots and in Switzerland usually live in the soil for three years. After that they pupate, and in spring the adult beetles hatch.

Cockchafers fly in large numbers in Switzerland every three years, in the so-called **flight years**. Depending on the region there are different flight years, for example the Basel, the Bern and the Uri flight year. In the past there were so many cockchafers that schoolchildren had to collect them. Grubs can badly damage meadows and fruit trees. Today farmers sometimes use a fungus as a natural opponent.
