Many scarab beetles and the related dung beetles feed on animal dung. They bury it in the soil and lay their eggs in it. In this way they bring nutrients into the earth and loosen the soil. On cattle pastures they help cow pats to disappear quickly. The ancient Egyptians revered the **sacred scarab** as a symbol of the sun.

begriffe.erklaerung: Flat, movable little plates at the end of the antennae of scarab beetles.
The thick, C-shaped larva of scarab beetles such as the cockchafer.
A year in which especially many cockchafers hatch in a region.
Another name for the dung beetle, a sacred animal in ancient Egypt.

gewusst: Before taking off, a cockchafer pumps air into its body, which is called “Zählen” (counting) in German.
Dung beetles can find their way at night by the Milky Way.

teile.einleitung: The blue shark is a slim shark that lives in the open sea. As its name reveals, its back is bright blue. It is one of the sharks that make the longest journeys through the oceans.
wichtigste: The blue shark has a bright blue back and a white belly.
It lives in the open sea in almost all warm and temperate oceans.
Blue sharks travel very long distances, sometimes across the Atlantic.
They eat mainly squid and small fish.
Blue sharks give birth to live young, often dozens at once.
Every year very many blue sharks are caught, which is why they are considered threatened.

abschnitte.text: The blue shark has a long, slim body and a pointed snout. Its back is strongly **blue**, the sides paler and the belly white. This colouring camouflages it in the water from above and from below. Striking are its very long, narrow **pectoral fins**. Blue sharks usually grow 2 to 3 metres long, rarely almost 4 metres.

Blue sharks live in the **open sea**, far from the coasts. They are found in almost all tropical and temperate oceans, including the Mediterranean. They travel huge distances, following ocean currents and their prey. Tagged animals have crossed the whole Atlantic between America and Europe.

Blue sharks eat mainly **squid** and small shoaling fish such as herring and mackerel. Sometimes they also eat dead whales or seabirds. They have teeth with saw-like serrations with which they hold their prey well. They often hunt at night, when squid come up from the depths.

The blue shark does not lay eggs, but gives birth to **live young**. The young grow up in the mother's body and are nourished through a kind of placenta. After about 9 to 12 months usually 25 to 50 young are born, sometimes even over 100. At birth the young are about 40 centimetres long and are independent at once.

Blue sharks are the sharks that are caught most often worldwide. Many end up as **bycatch** in the nets and on the lines of fishers who actually want to catch tuna or swordfish. Their fins are sold above all in Asia for shark fin soup. That is why the blue shark is considered threatened and is now protected by international trade rules. For people it is only rarely dangerous, and attacks hardly ever happen.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fins at the side behind the head of a fish.
Animals that get caught in the fishing net unintentionally.
The open sea far from the coasts.
Colours that make an animal hard to see in its surroundings.

gewusst: Blue sharks are among the farthest-travelling sharks in the world.
A female blue shark can give birth to over 100 young at once.
When a blue shark dies, its skin quickly loses the bright blue colour.

teile.einleitung: Nurse sharks are easy-going sharks that often lie quietly on the seabed during the day. They only become active at night, when they go hunting. They are usually harmless to people as long as they are left alone.
wichtigste: Nurse sharks form a family of their own with only a few species.
During the day they often lie quietly on the seabed, sometimes in groups.
At night they hunt fish, crabs, squid and mussels.
They suck in their prey with their mouth like a vacuum cleaner.
They have two barbels on their snout for feeling their way around.
The Atlantic nurse shark grows to about three metres long.
Nurse sharks give birth to live young.

abschnitte.text: Nurse sharks have a strong, brown body with a broad head and small eyes. Their mouth sits right at the front, and in front of it hang two fleshy **barbels** that they use to feel along the seabed. The two dorsal fins sit far back. The **Atlantic nurse shark** usually grows to about two to three metres long, occasionally a little larger. Their skin feels rough like sandpaper.

Nurse sharks live in warm, shallow coastal waters, often in **coral reefs**, lagoons and seagrass meadows. The Atlantic nurse shark is found on both sides of the Atlantic and in the eastern Pacific, for example in the Caribbean and off Florida. The tawny nurse shark lives in the Indian and Pacific Oceans. During the day they rest in caves or under rock ledges. Often several animals lie close beside or even on top of one another.

Nurse sharks are **nocturnal**. In the dark they slowly search the seabed. They eat fish, crabs, squid, sea urchins and mussels. With their strong gill muscles they create a powerful suction and simply **suck** their prey in. They can even pull snails out of their shells this way.

Many sharks have to keep swimming all the time so that water flows over their gills. Nurse sharks, however, can actively pump water through their mouth and **gills**. That is why they can lie motionless on the bottom for hours. Small openings behind the eyes, called **spiracles**, also help them to breathe. This saves them a lot of energy.

Nurse sharks are **live-bearing**: the eggs develop inside the mother's body. A female gives birth to about 20 to 30 young, which are already a good 25 centimetres long. Nurse sharks are usually harmless to people. But if they are disturbed or pulled by the tail, they can bite hard and do not let go quickly. Because they are calm, they can also be seen in large show aquariums.

begriffe.erklaerung: Feeler-like threads of skin near the mouth that a fish can use to feel and taste.
An animal that is mostly awake at night and looks for food then.
The breathing organs of fish, which take oxygen from the water.
A small opening behind the eye of many sharks and rays through which water can flow in.

gewusst: Nurse sharks can suck in their prey faster than the eye can follow.
A nurse shark can lie still and breathe at the same time, which many other sharks cannot do.

teile.einleitung: Bisons are large, strong wild oxen with a hump and a shaggy mane. Today there are two species: the American bison in North America and the wisent in Europe. Both were almost extinct and were saved by humans.
wichtigste: Bisons are mammals and belong to the bovid family (Bovidae).
Today there are two species: the American bison and the wisent.
Bisons have horns on the sides of the head that are not renewed every year.
They are plant eaters and ruminants that live in herds.
Both species were almost wiped out and were saved by protection programmes.
The wisent is the heaviest land animal in Europe.
In the Ice Age the steppe bison lived in Europe, including Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Bisons** have a massive body, a high hump on the shoulders and a broad head. Males and females carry short, curved **horns**. Unlike deer antlers, horns are not shed every year, they grow all life long. They consist of a bony core with a sheath of horn. The fur is dark brown, long and shaggy at the front.

The **American bison** lives in North America on prairies and in forests. The **wisent** is the European bison and lives in forests, above all in Poland, Belarus and other eastern European countries. The wisent has longer legs and a less mighty head than the American bison. A wisent bull can weigh around 900 kg. Both species can breed with each other, so closely are they related.

Bisons are **ruminants** and eat grasses, herbs, leaves and bark. They live in herds of cows and calves, while older bulls often roam alone. In the mating season the bulls fight over the females with head butts. The cows usually give birth to one calf a year. Bisons can live to be about 20 years old or more.

Both species of bison almost became extinct. The American bison was almost completely shot in the 19th century. The last free-living wisent was killed in the 1920s, and only a few dozen animals survived in zoos. Through **breeding programmes** and release into the wild, there are again thousands of animals of both species today. The wisent has lived free again since 1952 in Poland's Białowieża Forest.

In the Ice Age the **steppe bison** roamed across Europe, including the area of present-day Switzerland. Cave painters showed it, for example, in the cave of Altamira in Spain. Wisents lived in central Europe until the Middle Ages. Today you can see wisents in Swiss animal parks. Since 2022 a small herd of wisents has also lived in a large forest enclosure in Thal in the canton of Solothurn, to test whether wisents could live in Switzerland again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The European bison, a large wild ox of the forests.
An animal family with horns that are not shed, for example cattle, sheep, goats and bison.
An extinct bison of the Ice Age that also lived in Europe.
Animals from breeding or a zoo are set free in nature.

gewusst: All of today's wisents descend from only twelve zoo animals.
Despite their weight, bisons are fast runners and good swimmers.

teile.einleitung: The American bison is the largest land animal in North America. In the past, huge herds with millions of animals roamed across the prairie. In the 19th century it was almost wiped out, but today there are many bison again.
wichtigste: The bison is the largest land mammal in North America.
A bison bull can weigh around one tonne.
Bison eat mainly grass and herbs.
In the past, many millions of bison lived on the prairie.
Around 1890, only a few hundred wild animals were left.
Prairie peoples such as the Lakota traditionally hunted bison.
It is often wrongly called a buffalo.

abschnitte.text: The **American bison** (Bison bison) is a wild bovine with a mighty head and a high hump on the shoulders. A fully grown bull can weigh around one tonne and stand almost two metres tall at the shoulder. Head, neck and front legs carry long, dark brown fur, which is especially dense in winter. Both sexes have short, curved horns. Despite their size, bison can run very fast, about 55 kilometres per hour.

The great herds lived mainly on the **prairie**, a wide grassland in the middle of North America. Bison eat mainly grass and herbs, and in winter they scrape the snow away with their heads. By grazing, they keep areas open and create habitat for other animals and plants. They like to roll in dust or sand to get rid of parasites and to care for the skin. The hollows that arise in this way are called **wallows**.

Bison live in herds, cows and calves together, older bulls often alone or in small groups. Most calves are born in spring. Their fur is at first reddish to light brown, and only after a few months does it become dark. The most important natural enemy is the **wolf**. When wolves attack, the herd often stands protectively around the calves.

For the **Plains Indians**, for example the Lakota, Cheyenne and Comanche, the bison was vital. They used almost everything from the animal: meat as food, hide for clothing and tents, bones for tools and sinews as thread. The bison also played an important role in their stories and ceremonies. With the wiping out of the bison, these peoples lost their livelihood.

Before the arrival of the Europeans, probably tens of millions of bison lived in North America. In the 19th century they were shot in huge numbers for hides, tongues and for sport, and often the carcasses were simply left lying. Around 1890, only a few hundred wild animals were left. A few people saved the last herds, and one of them survived in **Yellowstone National Park**. Today there are several hundred thousand bison again, though most of them on farms.

In 2016 the bison was declared the **national mammal** of the USA. A distinction is made between the plains bison and the larger wood bison, which lives in Canada. In Europe a close relative lives, the **wisent**. In Switzerland, an experiment has been running for some years in the Solothurn Jura to keep wisent in a large forest enclosure. Bison in national parks are not tame animals, and visitors have to keep a great distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wide, flat grassland in North America.
A male bovine, so also a male bison.
The European relative of the bison.
A group of animals that lives together and roams about.

gewusst: True buffalo, such as the water buffalo, live in Asia and Africa, not in America.
In Yellowstone National Park, people are injured every year because they get too close to bison.
A bison can jump almost two metres high from a standing start.

teile.einleitung: The lesser stag beetle is a black beetle that is closely related to the famous stag beetle. It is much smaller and has no antler-like mandibles, but it is considerably more common. You often find it on rotting wood in woods, parks and gardens.
wichtigste: The lesser stag beetle is closely related to the stag beetle and belongs to the stag beetle family.
Its scientific name is Dorcus parallelipipedus.
It is usually about 2 to 3 centimetres long and matt black.
The males have only short, strong mandibles and no large antlers.
Its larvae develop for several years in rotting hardwood.
In Switzerland it is quite widespread at lower altitudes.

abschnitte.text: The lesser stag beetle, in Latin **Dorcus parallelipipedus**, belongs to the family of **stag beetles**. The large stag beetle is therefore its close relative. Unlike in the stag beetle, however, the mandibles of the males are not lengthened into antlers. You can recognise males by their broader head and the somewhat larger jaws.

The lesser stag beetle usually grows to about 2 to 3 centimetres long. Its body is matt black and looks like a flat, oblong block. The Latin name also points to this, as it recalls a **cuboid**. The antennae are bent and end in a small club made of little plates.

Lesser stag beetles live in deciduous woods, parks, orchards and gardens with old trees. They need **dead wood**, that is, dead, rotting wood from trees such as beech, oak, willow or fruit trees. The adult beetles are about from May to September, mainly at dusk and in the night. During the day they hide under bark or in cracks in the wood.

The female lays her eggs in rotting wood, often in tree stumps on the ground. The white, curved **larvae** eat their way through the decaying wood for two to three years. After that they pupate, and the finished beetle hatches. The adult beetles can overwinter and sometimes live for more than a year.

Lesser stag beetles help to break down dead wood and turn it into soil. This makes them important members of the forest **cycle**. In Switzerland the lesser stag beetle is still quite common, while the stag beetle has become rare. Anyone who leaves old tree stumps and woodpiles lying in the garden creates habitat for these beetles.

begriffe.erklaerung: The beetle family to which the stag beetle and the lesser stag beetle belong.
Dead wood that serves many animals as food and shelter.
The young form of an insect, which looks quite different from the adult animal.
The chewing tools of beetles, lengthened into antlers in the male stag beetle.

gewusst: Because of its size and colour, the lesser stag beetle is often mistaken for a female stag beetle.
Its larvae often live longer than the finished beetle.

teile.einleitung: The slow worm looks like a small snake, but is a lizard without legs. In Switzerland it is often found in gardens, at woodland edges and on meadows. It is not blind, by the way: it even has eyelids and can blink.
wichtigste: The slow worm is a legless lizard and not a snake.
It grows to about 40 to 50 centimetres long.
You recognise it by the eyelids with which it can blink.
It eats mainly slugs and earthworms.
When in danger it can shed its tail.
The young are independent from the start.
It is harmless and protected in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The slow worm belongs to the **anguid lizards**, a family of lizards. Its ancestors had legs, and today only remains of the shoulder and pelvic girdles are left in the body. Unlike snakes it has movable **eyelids** and can blink. It also has a long tail that makes up about half of the body length. Fully grown it usually reaches 40 to 50 centimetres in length.

The slow worm is usually brownish to grey and often gleams metallic, almost like copper or bronze. Its scales are smooth, and beneath them lie small bony plates. Males are often more uniform in colour, while females have dark sides and a dark **stripe down the back**. The young are silvery or golden with a dark stripe down the back.

Slow worms eat mainly **slugs**, earthworms and insect larvae. They flick their tongues to pick up smells. Their teeth are small and curved slightly backwards so that slippery prey does not escape. They swallow the prey whole or in large pieces. Gardeners are glad to have them, because they eat many slugs.

Slow worms are out and about mainly at dusk and after rain. They spend the winter in **winter dormancy** in holes in the ground or under leaves, often in groups. In spring they bask first to warm up. If a slow worm is picked up, it writhes and can shed its tail. The tail keeps wriggling and distracts the enemy, but grows back only as a short stump.

Mating takes place in spring. In late summer the female usually gives birth to about 8 to 12 young. At birth the young are still in a thin egg membrane, from which they hatch at once. The mother does not look after them, and the young are **independent** from the start.

The slow worm is one of the most common **reptiles** in Switzerland. It lives from the lowlands up into the mountains at over 2,000 metres. Like all native reptiles it is protected. Dangers are cars, mowers, robot lawnmowers and house cats. Anyone who leaves piles of stones, piles of leaves and wild corners in the garden offers it a home.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reptile with scales, usually with four legs, such as a wall lizard or a gecko.
A cold-blooded animal with scaly skin, for example a snake or a lizard.
A resting time in winter in which the animal is hardly active.
The ability to shed the tail when in danger.

gewusst: Slow worms can become very old, and in captivity one reached over 50 years.
The German name Blindschleiche probably does not come from “blind”, but from an old word for “dazzling” or “shiny”.
A slow worm can only really shed its tail once, after that a stump remains.

teile.einleitung: The Border Collie is a herding dog from Great Britain and is regarded as one of the cleverest breeds of dog in the world. It helps shepherds to round up and steer flocks of sheep. With its stamina and love of work it is also a star in dog sports.
wichtigste: The Border Collie is a herding dog that helps to round up sheep.
The breed comes from the border country between England and Scotland.
It is regarded as one of the most intelligent breeds of dog.
It steers sheep with its fixed stare, the “eye”.
It is usually black and white, but there are many colours.
It needs a great deal of exercise and mental activity.

abschnitte.text: The Border Collie comes from the **border country** between England and Scotland. In English the border is called border, hence its name. There such dogs have helped the shepherds in the hills for centuries. For a long time it was bred only for its performance at work, not for its looks.

The Border Collie is medium-sized, and males grow to about 53 centimetres high. It usually weighs about 14 to 20 kilograms. The coat can be short or medium-long. Most often it is **black and white**, but there are also brown, red, grey or spotted animals. Its body is slim, athletic and agile.

The Border Collie steers sheep mainly with its **fixed stare**, the so-called eye. In doing so it creeps crouching round the flock without biting the animals. The shepherd gives it commands with whistles and calls, for example for left, right or stop. In this way a dog can drive a whole flock alone across wide pastures. In competitions, the **sheepdog trials**, dog and shepherd show their skill.

Border Collies learn very fast and can remember many words. They want to be kept busy constantly and like to work together with people. If they get too little to do, they get bored and sometimes herd children, bicycles or cars. That is why a Border Collie suits only people who have a lot of time and enjoy exercise.

In **dog sports** such as agility, obedience or frisbee, Border Collies are among the most successful dogs. They are also used as rescue dogs and search dogs. In Switzerland some Border Collies still work as herding dogs on sheep pastures and alps. They usually live to be about 12 to 15 years old.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dog that helps to steer animals such as sheep or cattle.
The fixed stare with which the Border Collie steers sheep.
A dog sport with an obstacle course of hurdles, tunnels and slalom.
A group of animals of one species with similar appearance and nature.

gewusst: A Border Collie called Chaser learned the names of over 1,000 toys.
In sheepdog trials Border Collies are judged mainly on their work, not on their looks.
Without sheep, some Border Collies start to herd ducks, hens or even children.

teile.einleitung: Adaptive radiation is the name for it when many new species arise in a short time from a single ancestral species. Each new species adapts to a different way of life. A lovely example exists right on our doorstep: the whitefish in the Swiss lakes.
wichtigste: In adaptive radiation, many new species arise from one ancestral species.
The new species adapt to different food and habitats.
The word radiation means a spreading out, like rays from one point.
Famous examples are Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos Islands.
In the Swiss lakes, so many different species of whitefish have arisen in this way.
Adaptive radiation often happens on islands or in newly formed lakes.
It helps us to understand how the diversity of species on Earth arose.

abschnitte.text: Adaptive radiation is a term from **evolution**, that is, the development of living things. Adaptive means adjusted, and radiation means spreading out. From one ancestral species, many new species develop in different directions, like rays from a lamp. Each new species uses its own **ecological niche**, that is, a particular way of living and feeding.

Often a species arrives in a new habitat where there is still little competition. This can be a new island or a lake after the Ice Age. The animals find many different sources of food there. Through **natural selection**, the animals that suit their food best survive, and with time separate species arise.

On the Galápagos Islands in the Pacific live around 15 species of finches, which all descend from one ancestral species. Their beaks are quite different: thick ones for cracking seeds, pointed ones for catching insects. The researcher **Charles Darwin** collected these birds in 1835 on his voyage with the ship Beagle. They later helped him to understand his idea of evolution.

After the last Ice Age, around 15,000 years ago, the large Swiss lakes formed anew. Whitefish that came into these lakes developed into many different species. Some live in open water and eat plankton, others search the bottom for small animals. In the lakes around the Alps, dozens of **whitefish species** are known today, which can often be told apart only by small differences.

In Lake Victoria in Africa, hundreds of species of **cichlids** have arisen, and in an astonishingly short time. In Hawaii there are many species of honeycreepers with quite different beaks. The marsupials in Australia have also split into many forms, from the kangaroo to the wombat. After the dinosaurs died out, the mammals spread in a similar way.

New species from an adaptive radiation are often delicate. If their habitat changes, they can disappear again. In some Swiss lakes, whitefish species died out when too much fertiliser got into the water in the 20th century. Clean water is therefore important for preserving this **diversity of species**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change and development of living things over many generations.
The original species from which new species emerge.
The special way of life of a species, for example what it eats and where it lives.
Living things that are better adapted survive more often and have more offspring.

gewusst: Some cichlid species in Lake Victoria probably arose only in the last 15,000 years or so.
Some whitefish species in Swiss lakes live in only a single lake in the whole world.
Darwin realised only after his voyage how important the finches were for his ideas.

teile.einleitung: A retriever is a dog that was bred to find things and bring them back carefully. This bringing back is called retrieving. Well-known retrievers are the Labrador Retriever and the Golden Retriever.
wichtigste: When a dog brings back a ball or a stick, this is called retrieving.
Retrievers are named after what they do: “retrieve” means to fetch back.
They were bred to fetch birds shot during a hunt.
They carry the game in a soft mouth without damaging it.
Many retrievers love water and like to swim.
The Labrador and the Golden Retriever are the best-known breeds.
Because of their friendly nature they often work as guide dogs for the blind.

abschnitte.text: The word **retrieving** in German, “Apportieren”, comes from the French “apporter”, which means to bring. The dog fetches an object and brings it back to its person. Many dogs do this quite naturally when playing with a ball or stick. In retrievers this joy is especially strong, because they were bred for it over many generations.

Most retrievers come from **Great Britain** and North America. Hunters needed dogs that would fetch shot ducks and other birds out of water or dense undergrowth. The dog has to wait patiently and must not eat the game. It carries it carefully back in a **soft mouth**.

In the international dog organisation FCI, the **retrievers** form a group of their own together with flushing dogs and water dogs. These include the Labrador Retriever, the Golden Retriever and the Flat-coated Retriever. Other breeds are the Chesapeake Bay Retriever, the Curly-coated Retriever and the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever. Labradors come in black, yellow and brown, while Golden Retrievers have long, golden fur.

Because retrievers are calm, friendly and eager to learn, many work as **guide dogs for the blind**. In Switzerland the guide dog school in Allschwil in the canton of Basel-Landschaft trains mainly Labradors. Retrievers also help as rescue dogs, therapy dogs or sniffer dogs at customs. Their good nose and their willingness to work together make them ideal for this.

Retrievers need plenty of exercise and things to do. Long walks, swimming and search games give them great pleasure. Instead of sticks, which dogs can hurt themselves on, balls or special cloth **dummies** are better. Because Labradors like to eat a lot, you should keep an eye on their weight.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fetching an object and bringing it back.
The English word for a dog that retrieves, it means roughly one who fetches back.
A small cloth bag that is thrown in training and brought back by the dog.
A specially trained dog that shows blind people the way safely.

gewusst: A well-trained retriever can carry a raw egg in its mouth without it breaking.
The Labrador Retriever has been one of the most popular family dogs in the world for years.
Labradors have a kind of webbing between the toes that helps when swimming.

teile.einleitung: The Atlantic ridley sea turtle, also called Kemp's ridley, is regarded as one of the smallest sea turtles in the world. It lives mainly in the Gulf of Mexico and is famous for its mass arrivals to lay eggs. At the same time it is one of the most threatened turtles of all.
wichtigste: The Atlantic ridley sea turtle is one of the smallest sea turtles.
Its scientific name is Lepidochelys kempii.
It lives mainly in the Gulf of Mexico and on the Atlantic coast of North America.
The females often come ashore in large groups at the same time to lay eggs.
Unlike most sea turtles, it mostly lays its eggs during the day.
The species is critically endangered and strictly protected.

abschnitte.text: The Atlantic ridley sea turtle is one of the smallest **sea turtles**. Its shell is only about 60 to 70 centimetres long and almost as wide as it is long. Adult animals usually weigh around 35 to 45 kilograms. In adult animals the upper shell is grey-green and the lower shell pale yellowish.

The species lives mainly in the **Gulf of Mexico**, but young animals also swim along the east coast of the USA far to the north. It likes to stay in shallow water with a sandy or muddy bottom. Occasionally young animals are carried by ocean currents as far as the coasts of Europe. Almost all females lay their eggs on beaches in the Mexican state of Tamaulipas.

This turtle's favourite food is **crabs**, which it cracks with its strong horny beak. It also eats mussels, snails, jellyfish and sometimes fish. It usually looks for its prey on the seabed. Its strong jaws are well made for breaking hard shells.

The females often come ashore in their hundreds at the same time to lay their eggs. This mass event is called an **arribada**, which is Spanish and means arrival. Each female digs a pit with her hind flippers and lays about 100 eggs in it. After about seven to eight weeks the young hatch and crawl straight to the sea.

In the past, tens of thousands of females came ashore on a single day at the main beach, Rancho Nuevo in Mexico. Through the collecting of eggs and through fishing nets in which the animals drowned, the population collapsed. Today the nests are guarded, and in many areas fishermen have to use nets with **escape openings** for turtles. The species still counts as critically endangered.

begriffe.erklaerung: A turtle that lives in the sea and has flippers instead of feet.
The mass arrival of many female turtles to lay eggs on the same beach.
A large bay of the sea between the USA, Mexico and Cuba.
The highest level of threat for animals that still live in the wild.

gewusst: The name Kemp's ridley recalls Richard Kemp, a fisherman from Florida who sent animals to researchers.
Whether an egg hatches into a male or a female depends on the temperature in the sand.

teile.einleitung: Poison dart frogs are small, brightly coloured frogs from the rainforests of Central and South America. Their colours warn enemies: many of them are poisonous. Some species are also called arrow poison frogs, because people used their poison for hunting darts.
wichtigste: Poison dart frogs live in the rainforests of Central and South America.
Most are only 1.5 to 5 centimetres in size.
Their striking colours warn predators of their poison.
The poison comes from their food, for example from ants and mites.
The golden poison frog is one of the most poisonous animals in the world.
The parents look after the tadpoles and carry them on their backs.

abschnitte.text: Poison dart frogs are very small frogs, and most species grow only 1.5 to 5 centimetres long. They gleam in red, yellow, blue, green or orange, often with black patterns. These garish colours are called **warning colours**. They show birds, snakes and other enemies: watch out, I am poisonous. Experts call this kind of protection **aposematism**.

Poison dart frogs live in the damp **rainforests** from Nicaragua to Brazil and Bolivia. Despite their name, which in German means tree climbers, many species live on the ground in the leaf litter. Others climb on trees and plants. They are active during the day, which is rather unusual for frogs. They need high humidity and warmth.

The poison sits in the skin of the frogs. They do not make it themselves, but take it in with their food, above all from ants, mites and small beetles. Frogs in zoos and terrariums that are given other food are therefore usually not poisonous. The most poisonous is the **golden poison frog** from Colombia, whose poison is called batrachotoxin. Indigenous peoples in Colombia smeared it on the tips of their **blowpipe darts**.

Poison dart frogs lay their eggs on land, usually in damp places under leaves. When the tadpoles hatch, they crawl onto the back of one parent. The father or the mother carries them to small bodies of water, for example into the leaf rosettes of **bromeliads**. In the strawberry poison frog the mother visits her tadpoles and puts unfertilised eggs down for them as food. This kind of care is rare in frogs.

Researchers study the frogs' poisons because new **medicines** may perhaps come from them, for example against pain. Many species are threatened by the clearing of the rainforest and by trade. The fungal disease chytridiomycosis also endangers them. They are bred in zoos and terrariums. In this way even rare species are kept for the future.

begriffe.erklaerung: A striking colour that warns enemies of poison or a bad taste.
The larva of a frog, which lives in water and breathes with gills.
A tropical plant in whose leaf rosette rainwater collects.
A long tube from which you shoot small darts by blowing.

gewusst: The poison of a single golden poison frog could kill several people.
Only three species of frog were actually used for poison darts.
Some tadpoles live in a tiny puddle of water that in a leaf cup is only as big as a spoonful.

teile.einleitung: A bioindicator is a living thing that tells us something about the state of the environment. Whether it is present in a place or missing, you can draw conclusions about the quality of the water, air or soil. Mayfly larvae in a stream show, for example, that the water is clean.
wichtigste: Bioindicators are species whose presence allows conclusions about environmental quality.
Mayfly, stonefly and caddisfly larvae indicate clean stream water.
Red midge larvae and tubifex worms also live in heavily polluted water.
Lichens on trees show how clean the air is.
Stinging nettles like to grow on soils with a lot of nitrogen.
Bioindicators show environmental quality over a longer time, not just a moment.
School classes too can determine water quality with stream animals.

abschnitte.text: The word **bioindicator** means “indicator of life”. What is meant are plants, animals, fungi or lichens that can only live under certain conditions. Some species need very clean water or very pure air. Others also tolerate pollution. Anyone who knows which species live in a place can therefore estimate what state the environment is in.

If you lift stones in a stream, you often find small creatures. **Mayfly larvae**, stonefly larvae and caddisfly larvae need a lot of oxygen and clean water. If you find them, the stream is usually in good condition. If almost only red midge larvae or tubifex worms live there, the water is probably polluted. In Switzerland experts from the cantons study streams in this way regularly.

**Lichens** are a community of fungus and alga. They take up water and substances directly from the air and are therefore very sensitive to air pollutants. Where the air was heavily polluted with sulphur dioxide, there used to be hardly any lichens on city trees. Since the air has become cleaner, many lichens have returned to the cities. They are still used today to monitor air quality.

Plants too reveal a lot about the **soil**. Stinging nettles and dandelions like to grow where there is a lot of nitrogen in the soil, for example from fertiliser. Heather and blueberries tend to indicate acidic soils poor in nutrients. Farmers and gardeners use such **indicator plants** to understand their soil better.

A chemical measurement shows only what the water is like at the moment of the sample. Living things, by contrast, live in a place for weeks or months. They therefore also show pollution that is already over. A well-known historical example is the **canary** in the mine: if it lost consciousness, the miners knew that dangerous gas was in the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that reveals something about the environment through its presence or absence.
A community of a fungus and an alga or a bacterium.
A plant that indicates certain properties of the soil.
How clean and healthy the water of a stream or lake is.

gewusst: Miners used to take canaries underground with them because they noticed poisonous gases sooner than humans.
Some lichens grow only a few millimetres a year and can become very old.

teile.einleitung: The Alpine newt is a small tailed amphibian that is common in Switzerland, from the lowlands high up into the Alps. In spring the male turns into a brilliant blue showpiece. For the rest of the year the Alpine newt lives hidden on land.
wichtigste: The Alpine newt is an amphibian and belongs to the tailed amphibians.
It occurs in the Alps up to over 2,500 metres above sea level.
Its belly is bright orange and without spots.
In spring it spawns in calm pools and small ponds.
In the water it has a tail flattened from the sides like a paddle.
It is active mainly at dusk and at night.
Its skin gives off slightly poisonous substances that protect it from enemies.

abschnitte.text: The Alpine newt grows to about 8 to 12 centimetres long, and the females are somewhat larger. Typical is its orange-red belly without spots. In spring the male has a blue back, a low yellowish **dorsal crest** with dark spots and on the sides a white band with black dots. In the water the tail is flattened from the sides and serves as a **paddle**. On land the skin is drier, rougher and less shiny.

The Alpine newt lives in central and eastern Europe, above all in forests and in hilly or mountainous areas. It probably gets its name because it is also common in mountain regions. In the Alps it is found up to over 2,500 metres above sea level. In Switzerland it is one of the most common **amphibian species**. During the day it hides on land under stones, wood or leaves.

Alpine newts eat small animals such as insect larvae, worms, snails and small crustaceans. In the water they also eat frogspawn and tadpoles. They hunt mainly at dusk and at night. As adults they breathe with their lungs and in addition through the **skin**. That is why their skin must always stay damp.

In spring the Alpine newts migrate to calm pools and small ponds. The male courts the female by waving his tail and then deposits a **packet of sperm**. The female takes it up with her cloaca, and so the eggs are fertilised inside the body. After that she wraps each egg singly in a leaf of a water plant. The larvae have tufts of gills on the outside and need about two to four months for the **metamorphosis** into a land animal.

Predators include fish, birds, snakes and large water beetles. The skin of the Alpine newt gives off slightly poisonous substances that put many predators off. Young Alpine newts become **sexually mature** only after about two to three years. The animals usually spend the winter on land in a frost-proof hiding place. In Switzerland all amphibians are protected, so Alpine newts must not be caught or taken away.

begriffe.erklaerung: An amphibian with a tail, for example a newt or a salamander.
A shared body opening for waste and reproduction.
The transformation of a larva into an adult animal.
Laying eggs in the water.

gewusst: In one spring an Alpine newt female can lay over a hundred eggs and wraps each one singly.
In some cold mountain lakes Alpine newts stay in the larval stage with gills all their lives and still reproduce.
An Alpine newt can live to be over ten years old.

teile.einleitung: Albatrosses are large seabirds that glide over the oceans for months without setting foot on land. The wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of all birds alive today. Many species of albatross are threatened today.
wichtigste: Albatrosses form the bird family Diomedeidae.
They belong to the order of tube-nosed seabirds (Procellariiformes).
Today around 20 species of albatross in four genera are distinguished.
With up to around 3.5 metres, the wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of all living birds.
Its scientific name is Diomedea exulans.
Albatrosses can live to a great age, often over 50 years.
Many species are threatened by fishing and plastic waste.

abschnitte.text: The albatrosses form the family **Diomedeidae** and belong to the order of **tube-nosed seabirds** (Procellariiformes). Today around 20 species in four genera are distinguished. Diomedea includes the great albatrosses such as the wandering albatross, and Phoebastria mainly the species of the North Pacific such as the Laysan albatross. The dark-coloured sooty albatrosses form the genus Phoebetria, and the smaller species of the genus Thalassarche are often called mollymawks in the Southern Hemisphere.

The name albatross probably goes back to the Spanish-Portuguese word **alcatraz**. Sailors used it in the past for various large seabirds. The naturalist Carl von Linné named the genus Diomedea after **Diomedes**, a figure from Greek legend. According to the legend, companions of Diomedes were turned into birds.

Albatrosses have very long, narrow wings. With them they use the wind over the waves so skilfully that they hardly have to flap their wings. This flying technique is called **dynamic soaring**. In this way they cover thousands of kilometres and sometimes even circle the whole of Antarctica.

On the beak sit tube-shaped nostrils, which give the order its name. With their good **sense of smell**, albatrosses find food on the open sea. They eat mainly squid, fish and krill from the surface of the water. Excess salt is got rid of through a **salt gland**, and the liquid drips from the beak.

Albatrosses breed in colonies on remote islands, above all in the Southern Ocean and the North Pacific. A pair often stays together for life and greets each other with a dance. There is only a single egg per breeding attempt, and raising the chick takes many months. In the wandering albatross, a pair therefore usually breeds only every two years.

Many species of albatross are considered threatened today. They get caught on the hooks of **longline fishing** and drown. They also swallow pieces of plastic that they take for food, and even feed them to their chicks. With simple measures, such as bird-scaring lines on fishing boats, many birds can be saved.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance from one wing tip to the other with the wings spread out.
An order of seabirds with tube-shaped nostrils on the beak.
A group of closely related species.
Fishing with lines many kilometres long and many baited hooks.

gewusst: A Laysan albatross called Wisdom on the Midway Islands was still laying eggs at over 70 years old.
After leaving the nest, young albatrosses often stay at sea for several years before they return to land for the first time.
The albatross plays an important role in a famous English poem about an old sailor.

teile.einleitung: The Asian tiger mosquito is a small, black-and-white striped mosquito that originally comes from South-East Asia. For some years now it has also been found in the south of Switzerland and is spreading further. It bites mainly during the day and can transmit diseases in warm countries.
wichtigste: You can best recognise the Asian tiger mosquito by its black-and-white stripes.
It originally comes from South and South-East Asia.
For some years now it has also been found in the south of Switzerland.
It was spread mainly with old car tyres and plants.
Unlike many native mosquitoes, it also bites during the day.
It can transmit diseases such as dengue fever or chikungunya.
Anyone who avoids standing water in the garden helps to fight it.

abschnitte.text: The Asian tiger mosquito is smaller than a centimetre and deep black. Its legs and body have striking **white stripes**, hence the name. A single white stripe along the back is also typical. Its scientific name is **Aedes albopictus**.

The tiger mosquito originally lives in the forests of South and South-East Asia. Through world trade its eggs reached many countries in old **car tyres** and ornamental plants. The eggs even survive drought for months. In Europe it was found first in Albania and then in Italy, from where it spread further.

In Switzerland the tiger mosquito was first discovered in 2003 in **Ticino**. By now it is widespread there and also occurs in parts of the Grisons. For some years it has also been found north of the Alps, for example in Basel and in the Zurich region. The cantons monitor its spread with special traps.

Only the females bite, because they need blood for the development of their eggs. The tiger mosquito is a **day-active** mosquito and often bites in the morning and in the late afternoon. It lays its eggs in small collections of water, for example in plant pot saucers, watering cans or rain barrels. After only about a week new mosquitoes can hatch from them.

In tropical countries the tiger mosquito transmits disease germs such as **dengue**, chikungunya or Zika. To do so it first has to bite a sick person, for example someone who caught the infection on a trip. In Italy and France there have already been a few outbreaks. In Switzerland the risk is so far low, but the authorities are watching the situation closely.

The best measure is to avoid **standing water** around the house. Saucers, buckets and toys should be emptied or turned over regularly. Rain barrels should be covered with a tight lid or net. Against bites, light-coloured long clothing and mosquito repellent help.

begriffe.erklaerung: An insect whose females suck blood.
A living thing that has been brought into a foreign area and spreads strongly there.
A disease from tropical countries that is spread by mosquitoes.
An animal that is mainly on the move during the day.

gewusst: Even a bottle cap filled with water is enough for the tiger mosquito as a nursery.
The tiger mosquito usually flies only a few hundred metres, but likes to travel as a stowaway in cars.
In Ticino, trials are being made with releasing sterile males so that the females have no offspring.

teile.einleitung: Species conservation means saving animals and plants from extinction. It includes laws, protected areas and breeding programmes in zoos. Some severely threatened species can today only be saved this way, because they have almost disappeared in the wild.
wichtigste: Species conservation aims to prevent animal and plant species from dying out.
Severely threatened species can sometimes only be saved in zoos or protected areas.
The Red List shows how badly a species is endangered.
The Washington Convention (CITES) regulates worldwide trade in endangered species.
The most important protection is preserving habitats.
In Switzerland the ibex, the beaver and the bearded vulture have been successfully reintroduced.
Each and every one of us can contribute to species conservation.

abschnitte.text: **Species conservation** means all the measures that are meant to preserve threatened animals and plants. This includes protecting habitats such as forests, bogs and rivers. Hunting and trade in rare species are also restricted or banned. The aim is for the species to be able to live in nature again in stable numbers.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature, **IUCN**, which has its seat in Gland in the canton of Vaud, publishes the worldwide **Red List**. In it, species are classed, for example, as vulnerable, endangered or critically endangered. Switzerland also has its own Red Lists for its animals and plants. They show where protection is especially urgent.

The **Washington Convention on endangered species**, CITES for short, was concluded in 1973. It regulates international trade in more than 40,000 species of animals and plants. Its secretariat is in Geneva. Anyone who brings, for example, ivory or protected corals into Switzerland as a souvenir is committing an offence.

When a species has almost disappeared in nature, **breeding programmes** in zoos help. Zoos exchange animals with each other so that the animals are not too closely related. The Przewalski's horse was extinct in the wild and was released again in Mongolia thanks to zoo animals. Zurich Zoo and Basel Zoo also take part in such programmes.

The **ibex** was wiped out in Switzerland in the 19th century. From 1906 young animals from Italy were brought to the Peter and Paul wildlife park in St Gallen and later released. Today about 18,000 ibex live in the Swiss Alps again. The beaver and the **bearded vulture**, which has been released in the National Park and elsewhere since 1991, have also returned.

Everyone can do something for species conservation in everyday life. A garden with native plants and wild corners helps insects, birds and hedgehogs. When shopping you can look for quality labels for sustainable fish and wood. You should also not buy souvenirs made from protected animals or plants.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of living things that can reproduce with one another.
A list that shows how badly animal and plant species are threatened.
The Washington Convention, which regulates trade in endangered species.
When animals are set free from human care into the wild.

gewusst: The first ibex for the reintroduction in Switzerland were secretly smuggled out of Italy.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), which publishes the Red List, has its headquarters in Switzerland.
The California condor survived only because in 1987 the last wild animals were caught and bred in zoos.

teile.einleitung: Mountain gorillas are large apes that live in the misty mountain forests of East Africa. There are only about a thousand of them left. Thanks to strict protection, however, their number has grown again in recent decades.
wichtigste: Mountain gorillas live in the Virunga volcanoes and in the Bwindi forest in Africa.
Their habitat lies in Rwanda, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Their fur is denser and longer than that of lowland gorillas, because it is colder in the mountains.
They eat plants, for example leaves, stems and bamboo.
A group is led by a large male, the silverback.
In a count in 2018 slightly over 1,000 mountain gorillas lived.
The researcher Dian Fossey made them world famous.

abschnitte.text: Mountain gorillas are a subspecies of the **eastern gorilla**. Fully grown males can be about 1.7 metres tall when standing upright and weigh around 200 kilograms. Females are much lighter. Their black fur is denser and longer than that of lowland gorillas, because it is cold and damp in the mountains. In older males the fur on the back turns silvery grey, which is why they are called **silverbacks**.

Mountain gorillas live in only two places in the world. One group lives in the **Virunga volcanoes** on the border of Rwanda, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The other lives in Bwindi National Park in Uganda. Their habitat usually lies between about 2,200 and 4,000 metres above sea level. There the forests are often wrapped in mist.

Mountain gorillas are almost pure **plant eaters**. They eat leaves, stems, roots, bark and occasionally fruit. Young bamboo shoots are the favourite food of some groups when they grow in the rainy season. A large male eats many kilograms of plants a day. Now and then they also eat ants or other small animals.

Mountain gorillas live in groups of often about 10 animals, though some are much larger. The silverback leads the group, settles arguments and protects it. When there is danger he rears up and drums on his chest with his hands. Every evening each gorilla builds itself a **sleeping nest** out of branches and leaves. After a gestation of about eight and a half months, a female usually has a single young, and only about every four years.

In the 1980s there were only about 250 mountain gorillas left in the Virunga mountains. The American researcher **Dian Fossey** lived with them for many years and fought against poaching. Her book “Gorillas in the Mist” was made into a film and became world famous. Today rangers protect the animals, and tourists pay a lot of money to visit them. This money helps with protection, but even so mountain gorillas are still considered **highly endangered**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Large apes without a tail such as gorillas, chimpanzees and orangutans.
An adult male gorilla with silvery grey fur on its back.
A group within an animal species that differs slightly from the others.
A person who guards animals and nature in a national park.

gewusst: No zoo in the world has mountain gorillas, you only see them in the wild.
Gorillas share a large part of their genes with us humans.
Every gorilla has a unique nose, by which researchers tell the animals apart.

teile.einleitung: The Bear Park Bern is a large, natural-style enclosure for brown bears on the bank of the Aare, directly below Bern's Old Town. It opened in 2009 and replaced the cramped old Bear Pit, which is still part of it. Here you can watch the heraldic animals of the city of Bern free of charge.
wichtigste: The Bear Park lies on the slope by the Aare at the Nydegg Bridge in Bern.
It opened on 25 October 2009.
The enclosure is about 6,000 square metres in size.
The old Bear Pit is linked with the park by a tunnel.
Brown bears have been kept in Bern for a long time.
The first residents were the bears Finn and Björk, who had twins in December 2009.
A visit to the Bear Park is free.

abschnitte.text: The Bear Park lies at the eastern end of the **Old Town of Bern** on the other side of the Nydegg Bridge. It stretches from the old Bear Pit down a steep slope to the bank of the **Aare**. From the paths above you have a lovely view of the bears and the Old Town. The Old Town of Bern is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The park is about **6,000 square metres** in size and so much bigger than the old pit. The bears have trees, rocks, caves, soil to dig in and a pool where they can bathe and snap at fish. A tunnel links the slope with the historic **Bear Pit**, which serves as an extra part of the enclosure. This way the animals can also retreat when they do not feel like having visitors.

In Bern, **brown bears** have been kept as living heraldic animals for centuries. At the opening in 2009 the bears **Finn** and **Björk** moved into the park. In December 2009 they had twins, who were named Berna and Ursina. Berna moved to a bear park in Bulgaria in 2013, and Ursina stayed in Bern.

The old Bear Pit from 1857 was cramped and walled in with stones. That no longer matched ideas of **keeping animals in a way suited to their species**. Bears want to climb, dig, swim and hide. That is why the city of Bern built the new park, in which the animals can behave much more naturally.

The Bear Park is open round the clock and a visit costs nothing. Feeding is forbidden, because the bears get a balanced diet from the keepers. In winter the bears go into **winter dormancy** in their dens and then often cannot be seen. The park is looked after by the **Dählhölzli Animal Park** in Bern.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large species of bear that lives in Europe, Asia and North America.
In the way that matches the natural needs of an animal.
The long winter sleep of bears in a den.
The longest river that flows entirely within Switzerland, it also flows through Bern.

gewusst: The opening of the Bear Park on 25 October 2009 was celebrated with a big public festival.
When the Aare floods, the bank at the lower part of the park can be flooded.

teile.einleitung: The aurochs was a huge wild bovine that once lived in large parts of Europe, Asia and North Africa. Our cows today are descended from it. It has been extinct for almost 400 years.
wichtigste: The aurochs, also called the “Ur”, was a wild bovine.
Our domestic cows are descended from the aurochs.
The scientific name is Bos primigenius.
Bulls reached a shoulder height of about 1.6 to 1.8 metres.
The last known animal died in 1627 in Poland.
Stone Age people painted aurochs on cave walls, for example at Lascaux in France.

abschnitte.text: The aurochs, also called the **Ur**, was much bigger than most cows today. The bulls had a shoulder height of about 1.6 to 1.8 metres and could weigh around a tonne. They were blackish brown with a pale stripe on the back, while the cows were smaller and reddish brown. Both had large **horns** that curved forwards.

Aurochs lived in open woodland, river meadows and damp grasslands. Their range stretched from Europe through the Near East to India and North Africa. They ate grasses, herbs, leaves and acorns. In Switzerland their bones have been found at many sites from the Stone Age, including in **pile-dwelling settlements**.

About 10,000 years ago people in the **Near East** began to tame aurochs. Over many generations this developed into domestic cattle. In India, too, one form of the aurochs was tamed, and from it came the zebu with its hump. The tamed cattle became smaller and calmer than their wild ancestors.

Through hunting and because forests were turned into fields and pastures, the aurochs disappeared little by little. At the end they lived only in a forest near **Jaktorów** in Poland, where they were protected by kings. In 1627 the last known cow died there. The aurochs is one of the first animals whose extinction was recorded exactly.

In the 1920s and 1930s the Heck brothers in Germany tried to breed aurochs again from domestic cattle. The result is called **Heck cattle**, but it resembles the Ur only in part. Today there are other breeding projects that cross cattle with the most primitive features possible. Some of these cattle are used in nature reserves to keep landscapes open.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another name for the aurochs.
Taming and breeding wild animals into domestic animals.
A breed of cattle that is meant to look like the aurochs.
Stone Age settlements on the shores of lakes, including in Switzerland.

gewusst: The Stone Age paintings in the cave of Lascaux show aurochs that are painted more than five metres long.
In the past, drinking horns for feasts were made from the horns of aurochs.
In the coat of arms of the canton of Uri you can see a bull's head, which is often linked with the Ur.

teile.einleitung: The Western European hedgehog is the species of hedgehog that lives here in Switzerland. With its thousands of spines and pointed snout it is one of the best-known wild animals in gardens. At night it goes looking for beetles, worms and slugs.
wichtigste: The Western European hedgehog is the hedgehog that lives in Switzerland.
It grows to about 20 to 30 centimetres and has thousands of spines.
It likes best to eat insects, worms and slugs.
In winter it hibernates for about 4 to 6 months.
Baby hedgehogs have soft, white spines at birth.
Bread and milk are unsuitable for hedgehogs.
With a hedgehog house and a bowl of water you can help it in the garden.

abschnitte.text: The Western European hedgehog grows to about 20 to 30 centimetres and usually weighs 800 to 1,500 grams. Its back is covered with about 6,000 to 8,000 **spines**, which are modified hairs. The chest is covered in brownish hair, which is where its German name Braunbrustigel, “brown-breasted hedgehog”, comes from. Its snout is long and pointed, and it has small, pointed teeth. When in danger it rolls itself up into a spiky ball.

The Western European hedgehog lives in western and central Europe, and also everywhere on the Swiss Central Plateau. It likes hedges, woodland edges, meadows, parks and **gardens**. Today in villages and towns there are often more hedgehogs than on intensively farmed fields. It climbs over small obstacles and needs gaps in fences to travel from garden to garden.

Hedgehogs are **nocturnal** and go looking for food at dusk. They like best to eat beetles, caterpillars, earthworms and slugs. They find their prey above all with their fine nose. Bread is hard for hedgehogs to digest, and milk does not agree with them. Anyone who wants to help puts out a shallow bowl of water.

In autumn the hedgehog fattens itself up with a thick layer of fat. From about November it **hibernates**, which lasts about 4 to 6 months. In this time its body temperature drops sharply, and its heart beats only a few times a minute. It sleeps in a nest of leaves under hedges, woodpiles or in a hedgehog house.

In summer the female usually gives birth to 4 to 5 young. The baby hedgehogs are blind and have soft, white **spines** so that the mother is not hurt at birth. After a few hours the first dark spines grow in. After about six weeks the young go their own ways.

In Switzerland the hedgehog is protected. Many hedgehogs die in **road traffic**, through robot lawnmowers, strimmers or in garden ponds with steep edges. Slug poison also harms them. With piles of leaves, hedges, a hedgehog house and open gaps in the fence you can help hedgehogs in the garden. Robot lawnmowers should run only during the day, because hedgehogs are out at night.

begriffe.erklaerung: Hard, pointed hairs that protect the hedgehog.
A long, deep sleep in winter in which the body cools down sharply.
Sleeping during the day and being active at night.
A small shelter in the garden in which hedgehogs can sleep.

gewusst: A hedgehog can walk several kilometres in one night.
Hedgehogs are astonishingly resistant to some poisons, for example bee and wasp stings.
Hedgehogs have existed for millions of years and have hardly changed since.

teile.einleitung: Tree kangaroos are kangaroos that live in trees. They are much smaller than the red kangaroo and climb skilfully through the treetops in the rainforest. Most species live on the island of New Guinea.
wichtigste: Tree kangaroos live mainly in trees in the rainforest.
There are over a dozen species.
They occur in New Guinea and in the north-east of Australia.
They are much smaller than the red kangaroo.
Their long tail helps them to balance.
Many species are endangered by hunting and deforestation.

abschnitte.text: Tree kangaroos belong to the **marsupials**. Depending on the species they weigh about 5 to 15 kilograms. Their forelegs are stronger and their hind legs shorter than in kangaroos on the ground. The paws have curved claws and rough soles that give a grip when climbing. The long, bushy **tail** serves as a counterweight, but it cannot grasp.

Most species of tree kangaroo live in the **rainforest** of New Guinea, often in the mountain forests. Two species occur in the north-east of Australia in the state of Queensland. They spend most of their time high up in the trees. They come down to the ground to move to another tree. There they hop, but are rather clumsy.

Tree kangaroos eat mainly leaves, fruit, buds and bark. They are mostly **loners** and are active mainly at dusk and at night. During the day they sleep curled up on a branch. They can jump to the ground from a great height without hurting themselves. Between branches they make long leaps.

Like all kangaroos, tree kangaroos give birth to a tiny, unfinished young. The young crawls into the mother's **pouch** and drinks milk there. It stays in the pouch for many months and grows up there. Usually a female has only one young per year. That is why the populations grow only slowly.

Many species of tree kangaroo are **endangered** or even threatened with extinction. They are hunted in New Guinea, and their forest is cleared for timber, fields and mining. Matschie's tree kangaroo, for example, is highly endangered. In protected areas and with the help of the local people, attempts are made to save them. Some zoos in Europe take part in breeding programmes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mammal whose young grows up in a pouch of skin on the mother's belly.
A dense forest in warm regions where it rains a great deal.
An animal that usually lives alone.
A large island north of Australia.

gewusst: The ancestors of the tree kangaroos lived on the ground and only later returned to the trees.
Tree kangaroos can move their hind legs one at a time when climbing, but on the ground they hop with both legs at once.
The dingiso, a tree kangaroo species from New Guinea, was only scientifically described in 1995.

teile.einleitung: The rut, in German called Brunft, is the mating season of deer, reindeer, bison, chamois and other even-toed ungulates. In this time the males fight over the females, call loudly and show their strength. In autumn you can hear the impressive roaring of the red deer in Swiss forests.
wichtigste: The rut is the name for the mating season in deer and other even-toed ungulates.
In bison and reindeer too people speak of the rut.
Males fight or show off to be allowed to mate with females.
Red deer roar loudly during the rut.
In many species the rut takes place in autumn.
The young are then born in spring or early summer, when there is enough food.

abschnitte.text: The **rut** is the period in the year in which certain mammals mate. The German word Brunft comes from hunters' language and is used above all for deer, roe deer, chamois, ibex, reindeer and bison. For other animals there are other words, for wild boar for example people say **Rauschzeit**. In the rut the behaviour and bodies of the animals change greatly.

In the red deer the rut lasts roughly from mid-September to mid-October. The males, called stags, give out deep sounds, the **roaring**, which can be heard for kilometres. A strong stag gathers a group of hinds around him, the harem. When two equally strong stags meet, they fight with their antlers, and usually the weaker gives up before anyone is badly injured.

In bison the rut takes place in summer, when the bulls bellow and fight with their heads. In reindeer the rut is in autumn, and the males then carry their largest antlers. The chamois has its rut in November and December, the Alpine ibex in December and January, in the middle of winter. In the roe deer the mating season in summer is also called the **Blattzeit**.

abschnitte.titel: A strenuous time for the males
abschnitte.text: During the rut the males often hardly eat anything, because they constantly guard their females and chase off rivals. A red deer can lose many kilograms of weight in this time. Some stags roll in mud wallows and mark their territory with scent substances. After the rut they are exhausted and have to recover quickly before winter.

In Switzerland you can experience the red deer rut, for example, in the **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine or in other mountain regions. There are guided excursions on which you listen and watch from a safe distance. It is important to be quiet, to stay on the paths and not to disturb the animals. Dogs belong on the lead so that the game is not chased.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mammals that walk on two toes per foot, for example deer, cattle and chamois.
The loud, deep calling of the stags in the rut.
A competitor with the same aim, here another male.
Special words that hunters use for animals and their behaviour.

gewusst: The Alpine ibex has its rut in the middle of winter, often in snow and cold.
The roaring of a red deer can be so loud that it is heard several kilometres away.
In the roe deer the fertilised egg at first hardly grows for months, so that the fawn is only born in spring.

teile.einleitung: The axolotl is a Mexican salamander that looks like a larva all its life. With its feathery gills and its smiling face it is known around the world. It can also regrow lost body parts completely.
wichtigste: The axolotl is called Ambystoma mexicanum scientifically and belongs to the salamanders and newts.
It belongs to the family of mole salamanders and is closely related to the tiger salamander.
It becomes sexually mature as a larva, which is called neoteny.
It breathes with three pairs of external gills, through the skin and with simple lungs.
When grown it is usually about 20 to 30 centimetres long.
It is endemic to Mexico and naturally lived only in Lake Xochimilco and Lake Chalco.
In the wild it is critically endangered today.

abschnitte.text: The axolotl belongs to the **salamanders and newts**, that is, to the same group of amphibians as newts and salamanders. Its family is the mole salamanders, and it is closely related to the North American **tiger salamander**. Other salamanders change from water larva to land animal, but the axolotl does not. It becomes an adult as a larva and has young, a phenomenon called **neoteny**.

A full-grown axolotl is usually about 20 to 30 centimetres long. On its head it has three pairs of external, feather-like **gill branches** with which it takes oxygen from the water. In addition it breathes through the skin and has simple lungs with which it sometimes gulps air at the surface. Its small eyes have no lids. Wild animals are dark grey-brown, but in aquariums there are also pink-white, golden and black forms.

The axolotl is **endemic** to Mexico, that is, it occurs naturally only there in the whole world. It originally lived only in Lake Xochimilco and Lake Chalco near Mexico City. Lake Chalco was almost completely drained, and in the canals of **Xochimilco** the water is often polluted. Added to this are introduced fish such as carp and cichlids that eat young axolotls.

If an axolotl loses a leg, it grows back completely, with bones, muscles and nerves. It can even restore parts of the heart, spinal cord and eye. That is why scientists around the world study how this **regeneration** works. They hope one day to learn something from it for medicine for people.

Normally the axolotl stays in the water all its life. But if it is given the thyroid hormone **thyroxine**, it can change into a land salamander. Then it loses its gills and the fin fringe on its tail. Such transformed animals, however, usually live for a shorter time.

In the old Aztec empire the axolotl was a food and was linked with the god Xolotl, to whom its name is also traced back. Today it is a popular animal in aquariums and laboratories all over the world. While it is very common in captivity, only a few are left in the wild. It is therefore on the Red List as **critically endangered**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sexual maturity in the larval stage, without changing into an adult animal.
Breathing organs with which animals take oxygen from the water.
Occurs naturally only in one particular area of the world.
A hormone of the thyroid gland that controls the transformation of amphibians.
The regrowing of lost body parts.

gewusst: An axolotl is shown on a Mexican 50-peso banknote.
In captivity an axolotl can live to be 10 to 15 years old.
Because it can renew parts of its brain and heart, it is one of the most studied animals in regeneration research.

teile.einleitung: The brown bear is one of the largest predators on land and lives in forests, mountains and the tundra of the Northern Hemisphere. Although it belongs to the carnivores, it eats mainly plants. In Switzerland it was gone for over a hundred years, and since 2005 individual bears have been turning up again.
wichtigste: The brown bear lives in forests, mountains and the tundra.
It is an omnivore, but eats mainly plants such as berries, roots and grasses.
Its fur can be anything from light brown through dark brown to almost black.
Before winter it eats a great deal to build up fat reserves.
In the wild it lives to be about 20 to 30 years old.
Most brown bears today live in Russia.
When it meets a person, it usually retreats shyly.

abschnitte.text: Brown bears have a massive body, a big head and a very short **tail**. On the shoulders they carry a hump of muscle that gives them strength when digging. Their dense, thick fur is light brown, dark brown or almost black. Males in Europe often weigh 150 to 300 kilograms, and the large **Kodiak bears** in Alaska clearly more. Young brown bears often climb better than fully grown ones.

Brown bears live in **forests**, mountains and in the tundra of Europe, Asia and North America. The country with the most brown bears today is Russia. In Europe there are larger populations in Scandinavia, in the Carpathians and in the Balkans. In North America it is also called the grizzly bear.

The brown bear is an **omnivore**. You can see this in its teeth: it has pointed canines and flatter molars for grinding. The largest part of its food is made up of berries, roots, grasses and nuts. In addition there are insects, honey, carrion and sometimes larger animals. In Alaska some bears catch salmon in the river.

In autumn the brown bear eats a great deal in order to build up thick **fat reserves**. It spends the winter in a den in **winter dormancy**, in which its body temperature drops only a little. In January or February the female in the den usually gives birth to two to three tiny young that weigh only about as much as a guinea pig. The young stay with their mother for about two years. A brown bear can live to be about 20 to 30 years old in the wild.

In the past brown bears lived throughout Switzerland. Because they were seen as a danger to livestock, they were hunted, and the last one was shot in 1904 in the Lower Engadine. Since 2005 individual young males have been migrating again from the Italian **Trentino** into the canton of the Grisons. When a bear meets a person, it is usually shy and retreats. It can become dangerous when bears get used to food from rubbish or a mother defends her young.

In many old European legends the bear is regarded as a strong and mighty **forest animal**. The city of Bern carries it in its name and in its coat of arms. For centuries bears have been kept there, today in the **Bear Park** on the Aare. The coat of arms of the canton of Appenzell also shows a bear.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that eats both plants and meat.
A long resting sleep in winter from which the animal can wake easily.
Stores of fat in the body on which the animal lives in times of need.
Cold, treeless landscape in the far north.

gewusst: A brown bear can run short distances faster than a human, up to about 50 kilometres per hour.
Newborn bear cubs weigh only about half a kilogram, although the mother is much heavier than a human.
The grizzly in North America is not a species of its own, but a brown bear.

teile.einleitung: Alpine farming means that farming families bring their animals in summer to high mountain pastures, the Alps. There cows, young cattle, goats, sheep and horses eat fresh mountain grass. In Switzerland, alpine farming has been a tradition for centuries and shapes the mountain landscape to this day.
wichtigste: Alpine farming is the use of mountain pastures in summer.
The grazing of the animals on the Alp is called summering.
An alpine season usually lasts about 100 days, from June to September.
In early summer the animals move to the Alp in the Alpaufzug, in autumn they return in the Alpabfahrt.
On many Alps, alpine cheese is made from fresh milk.
Alpine farming keeps the pastures open and protects against scrub encroachment.
The Confederation supports summering with contributions.

abschnitte.text: In the mountains, a lot of grass grows in summer, which lies under snow in winter. That is why farmers bring their animals up in summer to the **Alp**, a mountain pasture with huts and barns. Down in the valley, hay for the winter can be made during this time. The grazing of animals on the Alp in summer is called **summering**, and this applies to horses too. An Alp often lies at 1,000 to over 2,000 metres above sea level.

On the Alp work **Sennerinnen** and **Senner**, herdswomen and herdsmen. They milk the cows in the morning and evening, herd the animals and look after the fences. Often they make the milk straight into cheese, butter and Ziger (a whey cheese). The work is hard, the days begin early, and there is not electricity or roads everywhere. Many young people from the city today spend a summer as an alpine helper.

From the milk on the Alp comes tangy **alpine cheese**, because the cows eat many mountain herbs. Well known are, for example, Gruyère d’alpage, Bernese alpine cheese or Hobelkäse (a hard cheese that is shaved into curls). The cheese is made in large copper cauldrons over the fire. After that it matures in cool cellars for months. Alpine products are popular and are often sold directly from the Alp.

In June the herds move uphill in the **Alpaufzug**. In September they return to the valley in the **Alpabfahrt**, which in French-speaking Switzerland is called Désalpe. The cows then often wear flower decorations and large bells, the Treicheln. In many villages the Alpabfahrt is a big festival with music and a market. Well known are, for example, the Alpabfahrten in the Appenzellerland and in Charmey in the canton of Fribourg.

The summering areas make up about a third of the agriculturally used area of Switzerland. Without grazing animals, many alpine pastures would slowly be overgrown by bushes and forest. Open pastures offer habitat for many flowers, insects and birds. The Confederation therefore pays **summering contributions** so that the Alps continue to be used. At the same time, care must be taken that not too many animals damage the soils.

Over a thousand years ago, animals were already driven to mountain pastures in summer in the Alps. Many Alps belong to this day to a **cooperative** or a municipality, and the farmers share the grazing rights. Songs, yodels, the alphorn and traditional costumes often have their roots in alpine life. Today alpine farming is an important part of Swiss culture and also attracts many tourists.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mountain pasture with a hut and barn that is used only in summer.
The grazing of animals on the Alp during the summer.
A man who looks after the cows on the Alp and makes cheese, the woman is called a Sennerin.
A large, forged cowbell with a deep sound.

gewusst: On some Alps, the cheese is still made today over an open wood fire.
Many Alps are so remote that material is brought up by cable car or even by helicopter.
Horses, donkeys and llamas can also spend the summer on a Swiss Alp.

teile.einleitung: Cheek pouches are stretchy pouches in the cheeks of some animals in which they keep food for a time. They are best known in hamsters and chipmunks. But baboons and other monkeys also have such handy storage pouches.
wichtigste: Cheek pouches are skin sacs in the cheeks that serve as transport and storage bags.
Hamsters and chipmunks stuff grains and seeds into them to carry to their burrow.
Baboons keep food in them for a time.
In hamsters the full cheek pouches reach as far as the shoulders.
Pocket gophers have cheek pouches that lie on the outside of the head and are lined with fur.
Cheek pouches help animals to collect a lot of food quickly and eat it in a safe place.

abschnitte.text: Cheek pouches are stretchy **skin sacs** on the inside or outside of the cheeks. Animals can collect food in them without swallowing it straight away. They work like a built-in shopping bag. Later the animals take the food out again with their paws or tongue.

The **hamster** is the best-known animal with cheek pouches. When they are completely full, its cheek pouches reach as far as the shoulders and make the head look twice as wide. In autumn the European hamster in this way drags several kilograms of grain into its burrow as a **winter store**. The chipmunk from North America also transports nuts and seeds in this way.
